Published Document: 2026-22525 (91 FR 69535)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily finds that countervailable subsidies were provided to producers and exporters of ripe olives from Spain. The period of review (POR) is January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review, in part, with respect to four companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stefan Smith AD/CVD Operations, Office I, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-4342.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the countervailing duty order on ripe olives from Spain.[1]
On January 21, 2026, Commerce selected Agro Sevilla Aceitunas S.Coop And. (Agro Sevilla) as the mandatory respondent in this administrative review.[2]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[3]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS)
( printed page 69536)
during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[4]
On June 15, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review by 83 days.[5]
Further, on August 27, 2026, we extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review by 30 days.[6]
Accordingly, the deadline for the preliminary results is now November 2, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[7]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included in the Appendix to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
The products covered by the
Order
are ripe olives from Spain. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if the parties that requested the review withdraw their requests within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation. Commerce received a timely filed withdrawal requests for Plasoliva, S.L. (Plasoliva).[8]
Because the withdrawal request was timely filed, and no other parties requested a review of this company, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(1), we are rescinding this review of the
Order
with respect to Plasoliva.
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a countervailing duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[9]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the countervailing duty assessment rate calculated for the POR.[10]
Therefore, for an administrative review of a company to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the countervailing duty assessment rate for the POR.[11]
On August 27, 2026, we issued a memorandum notifying parties of our intent to rescind this administrative review with respect to: (1) Alimentary Group DCoop, S.Coop. And.; (2) Aceitunera del Norte de Caceres, Soc. Coop. LTDA 2° Grado; and (3) Aceitunera del Norte de Cáceres, S.C.L.[12]
We received no comments from interested parties regarding our intention to rescind the review with respect to these companies. Accordingly, in the absence of reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review with respect to these three companies, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each of the subsidy programs found countervailable, Commerce preliminarily determines that there is a subsidy,
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.[13]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions, including our reliance, in part, on facts otherwise available pursuant to sections 776(a) of the Act,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Review-Specific Rate for Non-Selected Companies Under Review
There is one company for which a review was requested and for which Commerce does not intend to rescind review and which was not selected as a mandatory respondent or found to be cross-owned with a mandatory respondent, Angel Camacho Alimentación, S.L. (Camacho). The Act does not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(e)(2) of the Act. However, Commerce's regulation at 19 CFR 351.109(g) states that Commerce will determine the rate for non-selected companies by following the process set forth in 19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)-(2), which generally parallels the process for determining the all-others rate in an investigation under section 705(c)(5) of the Act. Section 705(c)(5)(A) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.109(f) state that for companies not investigated, in general, we will determine an all-others rate by weight averaging the countervailable subsidy rates established for each of the companies individually investigated, excluding zero and
de minimis
rates or any rates based entirely on facts available.
Accordingly, to determine the rate for companies not selected for individual examination, Commerce's practice is to weight average the net subsidy rates for the selected mandatory respondents, excluding rates that are zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available.[14]

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) finds that revocation of the countervailing duty (CVD) order on utility scale wind towers (wind towers) from India would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of countervailable subsidies at the levels indicated in the “Final Results of Sunset Review” section of this notice.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Colton Dulin, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-1222.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On December 6, 2021, Commerce published the CVD order on wind towers from India.[1]
On July 2, 2026, Commerce published the notice of initiation of the first sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and 19 CFR 351.218(c).[2]
On July 17, 2026, Commerce received a notice of intent to participate in this sunset review from the Wind Tower Trade Coalition (the Coalition), within the deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(i).[3]
The Coalition claims that it has interested party status within the meaning of section 771(9)(C) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.102(b)(29)(vii)-(viii) as a group comprised of U.S. producers of the domestic like product.[4]
On August 3, 2026, Commerce received an adequate substantive response from the Coalition, within the 30-day deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3)(i).[5]
Commerce did not receive a substantive response from either the Government of India or a respondent interested party to this proceeding. On August 24, 2026, Commerce notified the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that it did not receive an adequate substantive response from respondent interested parties.[6]
As a result, Commerce conducted an expedited (120-day) sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c)(3)(B) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(e)(1)(ii)(B)(2) and (C)(2).
Scope of the Order
The product covered by this
Order
is wind towers from India. For a full description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Issues and Decisions Memorandum.[7]
Analysis of Comments Received
A complete discussion of all issues raised in this sunset review, including the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of subsidization and the countervailable subsidy rates likely to prevail if the
Order
were to be revoked, is contained in the Issues and Decision Memorandum.[8]
A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is attached as an appendix to this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, complete versions of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.

articles.title: Tesla, Samsung Oppose New US Tariffs on Vietnam as Industry Groups Demand Penalties - Tekedia
articles.summary: Tesla, Samsung Oppose New US Tariffs on Vietnam as Industry Groups Demand Penalties  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
Major US businesses are divided over whether the Trump administration should impose additional tariffs on Vietnamese goods, with Tesla and Samsung warning that higher duties could disrupt supply chains, while American producers and intellectual property groups are urging Washington to take a tougher approach.
The disagreement emerged in submissions to the US government ahead of a November 29 deadline for concluding a trade investigation into Vietnam’s alleged intellectual property violations. The probe, launched in May, follows Washington’s decision to designate Vietnam a “priority foreign country”, placing it in the most serious category of the US intellectual property watchlist for the first time in 13 years.
The United States has accused Vietnam of a “persistent failure to resolve long-standing concerns about IP protection and enforcement”. A separate investigation into alleged excess industrial capacity is also underway, adding another source of trade uncertainty for the Southeast Asian economy.

Vietnam has urged Washington to conduct its investigations objectively. It remains unclear whether any tariffs arising from the intellectual property investigation would apply broadly across Vietnamese imports or target specific industries.
The United States currently imposes a general 12.5% tariff on Vietnamese goods, introduced in July following an investigation into alleged failures to prevent imports of products made with forced labor. Vietnam had previously faced a 20% tariff under President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” trade measures, but the Supreme Court struck down those duties.
Many economists have argued that the administration’s objective is to restore tariffs at least at the level previously imposed before the court ruling. A new trade action linked to intellectual property enforcement could provide another route to higher duties, although the scope and legal basis of any additional measures remain unresolved.
Tesla urged the US Trade Representative to consider the supply chain requirements of American manufacturers before imposing further tariffs. In comments submitted on July 2, the electric vehicle maker said some advanced components and precision manufacturing equipment could not be sourced domestically, even after substantial investment in US production.
The company’s position highlights a constraint facing manufacturers seeking to expand domestic production: US factories remain dependent on international suppliers for certain specialized inputs. Tariffs on Vietnamese goods could therefore raise costs for American companies if affected products or components are difficult to replace with domestic alternatives.
Samsung’s US unit made a similar submission, pointing to Vietnam’s importance in manufacturing smartphones and network equipment supplied to the American market. The South Korean technology group is Vietnam’s largest foreign investor, with approximately $25 billion invested in the country.
Retail organizations and trade associations representing businesses with extensive manufacturing operations in Vietnam also opposed additional tariffs. Their members include footwear and apparel companies, as well as manufacturers of consumer products such as bicycles and video game consoles.
For these businesses, the issue extends beyond the direct cost of imported finished goods. Higher tariffs could affect established production networks, supplier relationships, and the economics of products assembled in Vietnam for US consumers.
Vietnam’s expanding trade position adds to the significance of the investigation. Its exports to the United States increased 42% in the first eight months of this year compared with the corresponding period in 2025, making it the US trading partner with the largest goods surplus, ahead of China and Mexico. At the end of 2025, Vietnam ranked fourth.
The increase has strengthened Vietnam’s importance in US import supply chains, while also bringing greater attention to the trade imbalance and the country’s role in manufacturing goods destined for the American market.
While major manufacturers and retailers have warned against additional tariffs, several US industry groups have called for penalties, arguing that Vietnamese producers benefit from unfair trade practices.
Organizations representing American steel, seafood, plywood, solar panel and wood product manufacturers accused Vietnam of unfair practices and urged the administration to impose new duties.
Intellectual property organizations have also pressed Washington to secure stronger commitments from Hanoi to tackle piracy and improve enforcement. Their submissions point to concerns involving software licensing, online distribution of copyrighted films and television programmes, and access for legitimate content providers.
The Business Software Alliance, whose members include Microsoft, Oracle and IBM, said about three-quarters of software installed on personal computers in Vietnam was unlicensed. It cited a 2017 survey and criticized what it described as inadequate enforcement, arguing that repeated Vietnamese commitments had not sufficiently addressed the problem.
The Motion Picture Association described Vietnam as a major center for online piracy. It said websites hosted in the country that distribute unauthorized films and television programmes attracted more than 12.5 billion visits worldwide last year.
The association called for stronger enforcement against piracy and improved market access for legitimate streaming services.
The competing submissions expose the difficulty facing Washington as it considers how to address intellectual property concerns without imposing costs on American companies that depend on Vietnamese manufacturing. Technology companies and retailers have an interest in maintaining access to production networks, while domestic producers and copyright holders are seeking measures they believe would protect their businesses from unfair competition and unauthorized distribution.
The outcome could also influence the broader US-Vietnam trade relationship. With Vietnam now running a larger goods surplus with the United States than China or Mexico, the administration faces pressure to address trade and intellectual property concerns while managing the potential consequences for American importers and manufacturers.
The November 29 deadline will provide a key point in the investigation, although the submissions do not establish whether Washington will impose additional tariffs, which sectors could be affected, or how any new duties would interact with the existing 12.5% levy.

articles.title: Supply chain diversification & greater regional cooperation are key to stronger maritime inter-dependence amid strained security environment: Raksha Mantri at Indo-Pacific Regional Dialogue 2026 - Technology For You
articles.summary: Supply chain diversification & greater regional cooperation are key to stronger maritime inter-dependence amid strained security environment: Raksha Mantri at Indo-Pacific Regional Dialogue 2026  Technology For You
articles.full_text:
Ministry of Defence
 
“Certain actors & nations seek to exploit the criticality of oceans for narrow unilateral gains; Answer to interconnected world’s vulnerabilities lies in building resilience”
Maritime security must evolve with emerging threats; Leveraging emerging technologies is the need of the hour, says Shri Rajnath Singh
“Technology must not become another source of inequality among nations; Benefits to a few won’t achieve collective resilience”
“Economic development & environmental responsibility must progress together; Oceans cannot be treated as unlimited source of resources”
“Maritime sector to be a key driver of India’s Viksit Bharat journey; Govt striving to develop a comprehensive maritime ecosystem”
प्रविष्टि तिथि: 04 NOV 2026 5:53PM by PIB Delhi
Raksha Mantri Shri Rajnath Singh has called for making inter-dependence among regional partners more secure and resilient through diversification of supply chains, reliable maritime infrastructure, enhanced maritime awareness and greater cooperation, along with the ability to anticipate, withstand and recover from disruptions, amid growing strains in the global maritime security environment. He was delivering the commemorative address at the Indo-Pacific Regional Dialogue (IPRD), the Indian Navy’s annual apex-level international strategic conference, being held in New Delhi on November 4, 2026.
Describing oceans as bridges rather than barriers among nations & civilisations, Raksha Mantri highlighted their role in sustaining livelihoods and facilitating the exchange of goods, knowledge & culture. He stated that despite the international community’s awareness of these universal dependencies, certain actors and nations seek to exploit the criticality of the oceans for narrow unilateral gains. “The global maritime security environment is strained by deliberate trade disruptions. We see blatant challenges to the freedom of navigation and the weaponisation of narrow maritime passages. This growing instability in the maritime domain casts a long shadow over the broader international order,” he added.
Shri Rajnath Singh asserted that the answer to the vulnerabilities of an interconnected world lies in building resilience, emphasising that globalisation cannot be abandoned in response to every disruption, nor should maritime spaces that have enabled human progress be closed. He stressed that the objective must be to make inter-dependence more secure.
Highlighting the evolving nature of maritime security, Raksha Mantri stated that challenges could arise not only from conventional military activities but also from non-traditional threats such as piracy, trafficking, illegal fishing, cyber-attacks and natural disasters. He underscored the need for maritime security to evolve with the changing maritime domain. “Artificial intelligence is changing the way data is processed, while autonomous systems are expanding the possibilities of surveillance & operations. New sensors are improving our ability to observe the oceans. Advances in materials, biotechnology and data analytics are opening new avenues for research and application. These developments have enormous implications for maritime security and economic activity. But technology, by itself, is not the answer. The more important question is how we use technology to address real challenges,” he said.
Shri Rajnath Singh also underlined that technology must not become another source of inequality among nations as the Indo-Pacific includes countries with different levels of technological and economic capability. “Some possess advanced research infrastructure. Others are still developing the institutional and human resources required to participate fully in this transformation. If technological progress benefits only a limited number of countries, we will not achieve the collective resilience that our region requires,” he said.
Raksha Mantri called for promoting cooperation in research, education, innovation and capacity building, stating that a stronger scientific capability in one country can contribute to the security & prosperity of the entire region. Terming it particularly important for smaller maritime nations and developing countries, he said the most useful technology is not necessarily the most expensive or sophisticated; it is the one that solves a real problem.
Shri Rajnath Singh emphasised that as India moves towards Viksit Bharat by 2047, the maritime domain will play a crucial role in the country’s national transformation. He highlighted Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi-led Government’s efforts to develop a comprehensive maritime ecosystem through investments in port infrastructure and connectivity, port-led development under Sagarmala, promotion of coastal economic activities and strengthening of the maritime industrial base. He described the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 as the national blueprint for this transformation, with emphasis on technology, innovation, research, education and skills.
Raksha Mantri underlined the need for economic development and environmental responsibility to progress together, stating that oceans cannot be treated as an unlimited source of resources. He advocated the protection of marine ecosystems, responsible utilisation of ocean resources and placing the interests of coastal communities at the centre of development efforts. “National prosperity and ecological responsibility are not competing objectives. They must reinforce each other,” he said.
Reaffirming India’s commitment to an open, inclusive and rule-based maritime order, Shri Rajnath Singh highlighted the vision of MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions) that recognises the interconnected nature of security and prosperity among nations and underscores that the maritime future of the Indo-Pacific cannot be shaped by any single country acting alone. He also termed the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative, announced by PM Modi in 2019, as a practical framework for advancing maritime cooperation across seven interconnected areas.
Emphasising the need to translate regional cooperation into tangible outcomes, the Raksha Mantri urged the participants of IPRD to move beyond identifying challenges and focus on practical action. He pitched for stronger scientific networks, joint research, exchanges between universities and maritime institutions, and the development of affordable technological solutions to common challenges. Stressing that the deliberations at the IPRD must lead to concrete outcomes, he said ideas emerging from the dialogue must translate into partnerships, projects and measurable outcomes.
“The future of the Indo Pacific will not be shaped by technology alone. It will be shaped by the wisdom with which we use that technology, the partnerships we build and the confidence we create among nations,” Shri Rajnath Singh said, reiterating India’s readiness to contribute to this collective endeavour.
Raksha Mantri expressed hope that the deliberations would lead to meaningful discussions and practical cooperation. He concluded with a call to move “from shared challenges to shared understanding. From shared understanding to shared knowledge. And from shared knowledge to shared resilience and shared prosperity.”
In his address, Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, Chief of the Naval Staff (CNS) highlighted the interconnected nature of the oceans and the uneven distribution of scientific knowledge, research infrastructure and technological capabilities across the Indo-Pacific. He emphasised that maritime cooperation must extend beyond equipment acquisition to building sustainable capabilities, enabling partner nations to operate, maintain, adapt and upgrade technologies.
Underscoring the need for a broader and more integrated approach to maritime challenges, the CNS called for greater collective investment in ocean science and research, enhanced sharing of scientific data and technology, and collaborative research initiatives, including joint scientific expeditions. He also highlighted the importance of strengthening existing regional institutions and mechanisms through trust, transparency and inclusive ocean governance.
The CNS observed that IPRD-2026 provides an important platform for translating shared maritime interests into practical outcomes and generating concrete, forward-looking recommendations to strengthen science, technology and academic cooperation across the Indo-Pacific
Also among the dignitaries present were Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth, Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Ashutosh Dixit, former CNS and Chairman, NMF Admiral Dinesh K Tripathi (Retd).
The three-day IPRD 2026, being conducted by the Indian Navy in association with the National Maritime Foundation (NMF), commenced on November 3, 2026. The second day of the dialogue focused upon two closely connected issues of regional maritime resilience: a better shared understanding of activities at sea and a stronger scientific capacity to anticipate and respond to environmental change.
The day also witnessed a ministerial session featuring a special address by the Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences Dr Jitendra Singh. He also released an NMF publication titled ‘Alternative Hull Forms for the Future Indian Navy’.
Adding a Naval perspective to the overarching theme of IPRD 2026, an interactive session ‘Perspectives from the Flag Bridge’ brought together former Indian Navy chiefs Admiral RK Dhowan, Admiral Sunil Lanba, Admiral Karambir Singh and Admiral Dinesh K Tripathi, and former Commander of the Sri Lanka Navy, Admiral Jayantha Perera, in a conversation hosted by Director General, NMF Vice Admiral Pradeep Chauhan. articles.title: A Democratic Congress could curb the Iran war but not Trump's tariffs, former ambassador says - Fortune
articles.summary: A Democratic Congress could curb the Iran war but not Trump's tariffs, former ambassador says  Fortune
articles.full_text:
As U.S. voters headed to the polls on Tuesday, former U.S. ambassador to Vietnam Ted Osius predicted that a Democratic-controlled Congress could curb President Donald Trump’s ability to wage war in the Middle East, but would likely struggle to unwind his tariffs.
The U.S. midterm elections could have major implications for both the Iran war and the global economy, Osius said at Fortune’s Southeast Asia 500 Summit in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam on Nov. 3.
“The Iran war is extremely unpopular in the United States, and it’s one of the factors that will be decisive in this election,” said Osius, who served as ambassador to Vietnam from 2014 to 2017. “I expect that Congress would use the power of the purse to curb the president’s ability to wage war in the Middle East.”
About 65% of Americans disapprove of how Trump is handling the U.S. military action in Iran, according to a Pew Research Center survey released on Oct. 8. The polling outfit noted that the war has been unpopular since it began; a March survey reported 61% disapproval of his handling of the conflict.
Most polling averages put the Democratic Party ahead of the Republican Party on the generic ballot; several independent forecasts suggest the Democrats will retake control of the House of Representatives, with control of the Senate being more uncertain.
Tariffs—Trump’s other signature foreign policy—would be harder to touch. “I don’t think we’ll suddenly go back to the status quo ante,” Osius said. “Unfortunately, it’s actually harder to unwind tariffs once you put them in place.”
A Democratic House and Senate might pressure the Trump administration into more predictable trade policy, but Osius conceded that tariff power “rests with the executive.”
Trump’s initial tariffs hit Southeast Asia harder than almost any other region in April 2025, with Vietnam in particular hit with a 46% rate, later cut to 20% in a deal, based on its large trade surplus with the U.S. Since then, Southeast Asian governments have launched negotiations with Washington to get tariffs reduced, offering to lower their trade barriers and to buy more U.S. products.
Since the Supreme Court’s Feb. 20 ruling that Trump’s tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, including his“Liberation Day” levies were unlawful, the administration has resorted to other justifications, including widespread duties imposed following allegations of forced labor and overcapacity.
Still, Osius predicted that a Democratic victory would show that Trump’s more coercive foreign policy doesn’t work. “When you sort of run a state like a mobster, it may work in the short term, but in the long term it doesn’t,” he said. “It’s much more effective, especially in this part of the world, to have predictable policies, and to show that rule of law and rules-driven trade works to everyone’s benefit.”
U.S. protectionism hasn’t dented Vietnam’s growth. The Southeast Asian country grew almost 10% in the third quarter of 2026, following growth rates of 8.2% and 8.8% in the first and second quarters of the year, respectively.
More broadly, the Asian Development Bank expects developing Southeast Asia to grow by 4.7% this year and 4.9% in 2027.
Jens Lottner, the CEO of Vietnamese bank Techcombank, explained that exports were up 30% year-on-year despite the 12.5% tariff currently on Vietnamese exports to the U.S. “If you’re a bank, you’re a proxy on the economy,” he said. “We still have a couple of very good years ahead of us.”
Amol Gupte, Asia South head at Citi, argued that global trade isn’t shrinking under Trump’s tariffs, but is instead being rerouted, often to Southeast Asia. “The aggregate amount of trade in the world is not really reducing; it’s just changing flows,” he said. “Exports from China to the U.S. have shrunk quite drastically, but China’s aggregate exports have not reduced—they’ve actually grown substantially.”
The region still sits at the center of several flashpoints. Lynn Kuok, the Lee Kuan Yew Chair in Southeast Asia Studies at the Brookings Institution, highlighted continued tensions over ownership of the South China Sea. “We see off Vietnam’s coast, for instance, a greater Chinese presence. And after a decade’s pause, China is actually starting its rebuilding of islands off the Vietnamese coast,” she said.
Kuok added that the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz has exposed a second vulnerability: the Strait of Malacca, the narrow passage between Malaysia and Indonesia through which much of Asia’s trade travels. Malaysia, Indonesia, and Singapore have all pledged to keep the strait open, but she warned that “a future more nationalist government might actually seek to close off the strait, or come under pressure from various powers to close off the strait.”
Kuok said members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are invoking international law as a way to defend their interests without taking sides in the rivalry between Washington and Beijing. “They’re not choosing U.S. or China; they’re choosing principles of international law,” she said.

articles.title: Textile-garment industry restructures supply chains to meet rules of origin - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Textile-garment industry restructures supply chains to meet rules of origin  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – More than seven years after taking effect, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) has become an important driver of Vietnam’s exports. However, fully capitalising on its tariff preferences requires businesses, particularly those in the textile and garment industry, to address challenges related to rules of origin, supply chain restructuring and value chain reorganisation. 
In response to supply challenges, textile and garment enterprises have proactively adopted more flexible supply chain strategies. 
Tran Minh Hieu, General Director of TNG Investment and Trading JSC, said that before the CPTPP came into force, the company selected material suppliers mainly based on three criteria: cost, quality and delivery time. However, with the agreement’s “yarn-forward” rule, origin compliance has become a key factor in partner selection. 
TNG has reviewed and categorised its entire supplier network, prioritising long-term cooperation with suppliers meeting origin requirements and establishing strategic partnerships with domestic fabric manufacturers. It has additionally developed an in-house software system to manage origin-related data, and use QR codes and ERP codes for each batch of imported materials and accessories, linked to relevant documents, invoices and contracts to ensure transparency and traceability. 
According to Truong Van Cam, Vice Chairman and General Secretary of the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association (VITAS), the CPTPP, which took effect in January 2019, opened access to 12 member markets. Vietnam’s textile and garment exports to these markets rose from 6.27 billion USD in 2018 to 8.3 billion USD in 2025. 
Nevertheless, the yarn-forward rule remains a major obstacle. While domestic yarn production largely meets local demand, fabric weaving, dyeing and finishing remain significant bottlenecks. Sourcing materials from within the CPTPP bloc is also challenging as member economies are not major suppliers. 
Many Vietnamese garment manufacturers still operate under the cut-make-trim (CMT) model, relying on materials supplied or designated by customers. This limits their ability to shift towards more advanced production arrangements such as free on board (FOB) and original equipment manufacturing (OEM). 
Despite expanding market access, Vietnamese goods account for just over 1% of total imports by CPTPP members. The proportion of exports using preferential CPTPP certificates of origin (C/Os) remains below 10%, despite having quadrupled since the agreement took effect. Experts attribute this low utilisation rate mainly to the yarn-forward requirement. 
Under this rule, all production stages, from spinning and weaving to dyeing, cutting and sewing, must take place within the CPTPP bloc. Vietnam’s textile and garment industry currently meets only around 50% of its demand for materials and accessories domestically, with local fabric production covering just 36% of demand. 
In the first nine months of 2026, the industry spent up to 11.6 billion USD importing fabrics, as compared with 15.2 billion USD in 2025. Meanwhile, imports of materials and accessories from CPTPP members remained virtually unchanged at 1.58-1.59 billion USD annually between 2018 and 2025. 
Ngo Chung Khanh, Deputy Director of the Ministry of Industry and Trade’s Department of Foreign Market Development and Multilateral Trade, said Vietnam has implemented 17 free trade agreements (FTAs) with nearly 70 partners worldwide. Businesses should therefore develop supply chain maps, identifying suppliers, alternative sources and potential disruption points to better respond to trade fluctuations. 
He stressed that the CPTPP should be viewed not only as an export market but also as an important source of raw materials. Trade promotion should increasingly focus on supply chain connectivity, with rules of origin serving as a tool for designing supply chains from the input stage. Shifting from “Made in Vietnam” to “Made in CPTPP” will help create shared added value and improve overall efficiency. 
Experts also recommend that businesses assess their entire supply chains and classify materials according to their potential for immediate domestic or intra-bloc substitution, those requiring further technological development, and those needing new investment. For materials that cannot yet be produced domestically, partnerships and joint ventures with manufacturers from China, Taiwan (China) and the Republic of Korea could help establish production facilities in Vietnam, ensuring domestic origin, stable supplies, cost control and timely delivery./.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that certain oil country tubular goods (OCTG) from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) are being, or are likely to be, sold in the United States at less than fair value (LTFV). The period of investigation (POI) is April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2026. Interested parties are invited to comment on this preliminary determination.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Alexander Rodriguez or Dylan Hill, AD/CVD Operations, Office IV, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0190 or (202) 482-1197, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
This preliminary determination is made in accordance with section 733(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Commerce published the notice of initiation of this investigation on April 28, 2026.[1]
On August 28, 2026, Commerce postponed the preliminary determination of this investigation and the revised deadline is now October 29, 2026.[2]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this investigation,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[3]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included as Appendix II to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Investigation
The product covered by this investigation is OCTG from the UAE. For a complete description of the scope of this investigation,
see
Appendix I.
Scope Comments
In accordance with the
Preamble
to Commerce's regulations,[4]
the
Initiation Notice
set aside a period of time for parties to raise issues regarding product coverage (
i.e.,
scope).[5]
Certain interested parties commented on the scope of the investigation as it appeared in the
Initiation Notice,
whereby they requested that Commerce find certain mechanical pipe products to be outside the scope of this investigation. These products include: mechanical pipe for oilfield tools, mechanical pipe for perforating guns, and expandable mechanical pipe.
We note that there is an ongoing scope inquiry related to the antidumping duty orders on OCTG from Argentina and Mexico with respect to these same mechanical pipe products.[6]
In that inquiry, Commerce preliminarily found that the products were outside the scope of the orders,[7]
based on comments identical to the scope comments received in this investigation. Consistent with that finding, Commerce preliminarily finds and clarifies that mechanical pipe for oilfield tools, mechanical pipe for perforating guns, and expandable mechanical pipe are outside the scope of this investigation. Because this is a clarification, Commerce is not preliminarily modifying the scope language as it appeared in the
Initiation Notice. See
the scope in Appendix I to this notice.
The final determination in the above-referenced scope inquiry is currently scheduled to be made no later than December 22, 2026.[8]
We intend to consider that final determination when making a final scope ruling in this investigation. Case briefs or other written comments regarding the scope of this investigation may be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance no later than 30 after the preliminary determination of this investigation. Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in the case briefs regarding the scope of this investigation, may be filed not later than five days after the date for filing of the scope-related case briefs.[9]
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.310(c), interested parties who wish to request a hearing regarding the scope of this investigation, limited to issues raised in the case and rebuttal, may do so in accordance with the instructions detailed below within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this investigation in accordance with section 731 of the Act. Commerce has calculated export prices in accordance with section 772(a) of the Act. Constructed export prices have been calculated in accordance with section 772(b) of the Act. Normal value is calculated in accordance with section 773 of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying the preliminary determination,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
All-Others Rate
Sections 733(d)(1)(ii) and 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act provide that in the preliminary determination Commerce shall determine an estimated all-others rate for all exporters and producers not individually examined. This rate shall be an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted-average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any zero and
de minimis
margins, and any margins determined entirely under section 776 of the Act.
In this investigation, Commerce calculated estimated weighted-average dumping margins for Universal Tube
( printed page 69540)

articles.title: One deal, two national security reviews: Coordinating CFIUS and Investment Canada Act strategy in US-Canada M&A - Dentons
articles.summary: One deal, two national security reviews: Coordinating CFIUS and Investment Canada Act strategy in US-Canada M&A  Dentons
articles.full_text:
Helping our clients everywhere
Dentons news
One deal, two national security reviews: Coordinating CFIUS and Investment Canada Act strategy in US-Canada M&A
This article was originally published in the American Bar Association’s Deal Points newsletter.
National security review has moved from the edge of cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&A) planning to the center of it. In US-Canada transactions, counsel can no longer assume that a deal involving friendly jurisdictions, familiar investors and commercially ordinary assets will avoid national security scrutiny. A single acquisition may implicate both the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS) and the national security review powers under Canada’s Investment Canada Act. The regimes share a common policy concern, but they differ in jurisdictional triggers, timing, process, remedies and political context. For M&A counsel, the challenge is not merely filing in two countries. It is designing one transaction strategy that can survive two reviews.
The first question is not whether the buyer is “foreign”
Deal teams often begin with the buyer’s nationality. That is necessary, but incomplete. CFIUS analysis may turn on control, noncontrolling investments, governance rights, access to material non-public technical information, board or observer rights and sensitive personal data. Canadian analysis may focus not only on who the investor is, but also on the nature of the Canadian business, the investor’s ownership and influence, links to foreign states and whether the investment could be injurious to national security.
In practical terms, a US buyer acquiring a Canadian business with US subsidiaries, US customer data, controlled technology, defense contracts or critical infrastructure touchpoints may need to analyze both regimes. Likewise, a Canadian buyer with significant non-Canadian ownership, sovereign wealth participation, foreign limited partners or sensitive financing sources should not assume that its Canadian identity ends the inquiry. Counsel should diligence the entire investor stack, including upstream owners, side-letter rights, governance arrangements, financing commitments, and any foreign government nexus.
Sensitive sectors are expanding
The national security perimeter is no longer limited to traditional defense. Current areas of sensitivity include: semiconductors, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, biotechnology, critical minerals, battery supply chains, aerospace, telecommunications, energy infrastructure, ports, geolocation data, health data, financial data and cybersecurity services.
These categories matter because many targets do not view themselves as “national security companies.” A software business may hold sensitive data. A mining company may own an early-stage critical minerals asset. A manufacturer may have a small defense customer. A life sciences target may possess genetic or health information. Each fact can change the risk profile.
This is particularly important in US-Canada M&A because many businesses operate seamlessly across the border. A Canadian target may have US facilities, US government customers, US-origin technology or US persons’ data. A US target may have Canadian mineral rights, Canadian research operations or Canadian customers in regulated sectors. The cross-border nature of the business can expand the review map rather than simplify it.
Timing should be built into the deal model
CFIUS and Investment Canada Act timing do not always align with each other or with antitrust, securities, financing or shareholder approval timelines. Some CFIUS filings are mandatory, others are voluntary but prudent, and some parties may choose a declaration or full notice depending on risk tolerance. In Canada, national security review can arise in connection with a reviewable acquisition, a notifiable investment or in some circumstances, even a minority investment or new business establishment. The Canadian process may also include extended review periods if the government identifies concerns.
The purchase agreement should reflect this uncertainty. Outside dates should be long enough to accommodate potential escalation. Regulatory efforts covenants should identify which filings must be made, who controls strategy, what information must be shared, and what mitigation obligations the parties are required to accept. A generic covenant to use “reasonable best efforts” may be inadequate where one review could require divestitures, access restrictions, proxy arrangements, data localization, supply commitments, security protocols or exclusion of certain investors from governance rights.
Mitigation strategy must be coordinated
A commitment that satisfies one government may create problems in the other. For example, a data access restriction accepted in the United States could affect Canadian operations. A governance limitation imposed on a foreign investor could alter economics or control rights relevant to Canadian analysis. A supply assurance or critical minerals undertaking in Canada could have implications for US customers or export control compliance. Counsel should avoid negotiating mitigation in silos.
A coordinated strategy starts with identifying the likely concern of each regulator and the business assets most relevant to that concern. The parties should decide early which mitigation proposals are commercially tolerable, which would defeat the transaction rationale, and which require lender or board approval. They should also anticipate the information-sharing problem: submissions to CFIUS and Canadian authorities should be consistent but not casually copied across regimes without considering differences in legal standards, confidentiality and government expectations.
Purchase agreement drafting is the control room
  National security risk should be allocated in the purchase agreement with more precision than a standard regulatory approvals condition. The agreement should identify required filings and approvals, define the parties’ cooperation obligations, specify who prepares and controls submissions, and address whether the buyer must litigate, accept mitigation, divest assets, restructure ownership or exclude particular financing sources. If the seller is running a competitive process, bidders should be compared not only on price but also on regulatory certainty, ownership transparency and mitigation capacity.
Termination rights also deserve attention. A seller may want a reverse termination fee if the buyer’s ownership profile creates the principal national security risk. A buyer may resist an unconditional hell-or-high-water obligation if mitigation could materially impair the target. Both sides should consider whether national security covenants should be separate from antitrust covenants, given that the remedies and policy concerns differ.
Minority investments are not always low risk
Venture capital, private equity, private investments in public equity (PIPEs), joint ventures and strategic minority investments can trigger national security questions even when the investor does not acquire outright control. Governance rights, access to technical information, board observer seats, veto rights, commercial agreements and data access may matter as much as percentage ownership. This is especially relevant for emerging companies in AI, quantum, cybersecurity, defense-adjacent software, life sciences and critical minerals. Counsel should analyze whether the investment documents create rights that regulators may view as sensitive. A minority investor’s information rights may be narrowed, board rights may be modified or technical data access may be restricted. These adjustments are easier to draft before signing than to retrofit after a regulator asks questions.
Practical takeaways
The best cross-border national security strategy begins before the letter of intent. Counsel should map the target’s sensitive assets, customer base, data, technology, locations and government touchpoints. They should diligence the investor’s ownership, control, financing and foreign government connections. They should prepare an integrated filing and communications plan for CFIUS and Investment Canada Act issues, while preserving flexibility to address each regime’s distinct concerns.
For US and Canadian M&A lawyers, the central lesson is that national security review is no longer a specialist issue to be checked late in the deal. It is a transaction structuring issue, a diligence issue, a covenant issue and a closing certainty issue. The deals that fare best are those in which counsel treat CFIUS and Investment Canada Act analyses as related but not interchangeable. One deal may face two national security reviews. It needs one coordinated strategy.
For more information on this topic, please reach out to the authors, Myron Mallia-Dare and Nick Bushelle.

articles.title: Temu & IACC launch programme to tackle IP disputes - Australia
articles.summary: Temu & IACC launch programme to tackle IP disputes  Australia
articles.full_text:
Temu and the International AntiCounterfeiting Coalition have launched the IACC-Temu Program, giving IACC member brands a new way to raise complex intellectual property disputes on the marketplace.
The programme adds a dedicated process alongside Temu's existing reporting channels for rights holders. IACC members can escalate disputed notices through the IACC Global Portal, submit keywords and images to support detection work, and hold regular check-ins with Temu on enforcement issues.
Under the arrangement, participants get direct one-to-one access to Temu intellectual property specialists for cases that need further review. Temu said each escalation filed through the programme will receive a response within 48 hours.
The move deepens ties between the eCommerce platform and the anti-counterfeiting group after Temu joined the IACC as a General Member earlier this year. The IACC represents brands concerned with trademark counterfeiting and related intellectual property theft.
For brands, the new channel is meant for cases that go beyond routine takedown requests, including pending notices, rejected notices and complaints a rights holder wants reviewed again.
Enforcement data
Temu said the programme forms part of a wider effort to identify suspect listings before rights holders report them. According to its 2026 Intellectual Property Protection Report, proactive removals of potentially infringing listings outnumbered complaint-based takedowns by 331 to one.
The report also said Temu's proactive monitoring database now covers more than 15,000 brands, about three times the level a year earlier. According to the company, that monitoring uses more than 47 million images and 9.5 million keywords, with material submitted through the new programme feeding into the process.
Temu said its intellectual property controls span seller vetting and pre-listing screening to round-the-clock monitoring after products go live. The company operates in more than 90 markets.
The IACC said the joint work had already produced early results for participating brands.
“Temu underscored its commitment to brand protection and collaboration with the IACC when its Co-Founder, Dada Sun, met with me and my team. That discussion marked an important step in strengthening our relationship and ultimately led to the launch of the IACC-Temu Program,” said Bob Barchiesi, President, International AntiCounterfeiting Coalition.
“Early results from our joint program have been positive for our member brands, demonstrating the immense value of collaboration between all stakeholders in addressing IP challenges,” Barchiesi said.
The programme reflects a broader push by large online marketplaces to show brand owners and regulators they can respond more quickly to counterfeit and other allegedly infringing goods. In practice, that often means combining notice-and-takedown systems with automated screening tools and direct communication channels for major rights holders.
For Temu, which has expanded rapidly in international markets, intellectual property enforcement has become a closely watched issue as its merchant network and product listings have grown. The company said the programme is voluntary and is intended to improve the handling of more difficult cases rather than replace standard reporting routes.
The IACC has long worked with marketplaces, payment groups and social media companies through industry agreements and advisory efforts focused on online trade in counterfeit and pirated goods. That gives it a role as an intermediary for brands seeking quicker responses from large platforms.
A Temu spokesperson said the partnership was designed to combine direct enforcement with brand input.
“Effective IP protection requires both strong enforcement measures and close collaboration with rights holders,” the spokesperson said.
“The IACC-Temu Program brings these efforts together to better address complex cases and support proactive enforcement.”
