articles.title: How China turned its own ‘Trade War’ into a ‘Global Franchise’ - The CSR Journal
articles.summary: How China turned its own ‘Trade War’ into a ‘Global Franchise’  The CSR Journal
articles.full_text:
For 6 years we have been fed a comforting bedtime story. Multinationals are packing up. Supply chains are being “de-risked”. India, Vietnam and Mexico are the happy heirs of a great factory migration, and all we need to do is hold the door open and smile.
Then you open the trade data and the story gets awkward.
India’s trade deficit with China touched a record $112.6 billion in 2025-26, with imports rising 16% to $131.63 billion while exports reached $19.47 billion. China also overtook the United States as India’s largest trading partner. The supposed winner of the great escape is buying more from the jailer than at any point in its history. That is not a glitch. I think it is the design.
Rerouting is not leaving
China+1 sounds like arithmetic: one factory in China, plus one somewhere else. In practice it works more like a relay race. Chinese components, machines and increasingly Chinese engineers move to Vietnam, Mexico, Thailand or India. Something gets assembled, a new country of origin is printed on the box, and it ships onward. Procurement people have a dry name for the result, “paper China+1”. Final assembly moves, but the circuit boards, semiconductors and specialty materials still come from China, so the tariff and policy exposure is unchanged.
Look at Mexico and Vietnam. Mexico imposed tariffs of up to 50% on non-FTA countries across 1,463 tariff lines from January 2026, and its imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of the year, exactly the pattern that makes customs officers suspect relabelled Chinese goods. Washington’s answer has been blunt, with a 40% tariff on transshipment and AI-assisted customs mapping of supply chains.
And the escape route is not comfortable for the Chinese firms that took it either. A survey circulated in April found about 40% of Chinese-invested manufacturers in Vietnam were running at a loss. Hardly a triumphant migration.
China did not lose its factories. Its supply chains became longer, more spread out and harder to sanction, while the “plus one” countries absorbed the political risk and the customs scrutiny. Beijing outsourced the exposure and kept the core. If you were designing a hedge, you could do worse.
Wolf Warriors with a plan
The name comes from a 2017 action film in which a Chinese special forces soldier rescues civilians abroad and humiliates foreign villains. Diplomats like Zhao Lijian turned that swagger into a diplomatic style, roughly from 2019 onward: combative tweets, public scoldings, ambassadors summoned and ambassadors lecturing. Western commentators concluded that Beijing had lost its patience and its manners.
I think they read it backwards. The shouting was the visible half. The invisible half was paperwork: export licences, dual-use lists, customs inspections, approval delays that never quite amount to a ban.
Japan is the cleanest example. In January 2026, after Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s remarks about a possible Japanese response in a Taiwan contingency, China announced export controls on dual-use items aimed at Japan and put them into effect immediately. Shipments of controlled rare earth compounds and metals to Japan have stayed near historic lows since, while South Korea has received increasing amounts. Nobody had to shout. A licensing office did the talking. Reward the friendly, starve the unfriendly. That is “wolf warrior diplomacy” with a briefcase instead of a megaphone.
And it is the real lesson for any country dreaming of diversification. Moving away from China is a negotiation in which China holds the pen on your inputs.
The theory, as Beijing would argue it
Fairness matters here, because the Chinese defence of all this is coherent, and treating it as plain aggression misses how Chinese strategists think.
Start with Deng Xiaoping’s old line, tao guang yang hui, usually translated as hide your light and bide your time. For three decades China built capacity quietly while the West called it a “responsible stakeholder”. Wolf warrior looks like a break from that line. A Chinese strategist would say the line was never about silence. It was about sequencing. Stay modest until the dependencies are in place, then you can afford a louder voice.
Qin Yaqing’s relational theory pushes the same way. In his account, world politics is made of relationships, and power flows to whoever sits at the centre of the most ties, not to whoever hoards the most. A Vietnamese plant that needs Chinese inputs and a Mexican factory that needs Chinese machinery are not defeats for Beijing under this logic. They are new ties, and every tie is a form of leverage.
Yan Xuetong’s moral realism argues that rising powers win through credible leadership, what he calls humane authority, and official Chinese messaging does describe integrated supply chains as a public good: cheap solar panels, batteries and phones for the whole planet. Zhao Tingyang’s tianxia, “all under heaven”, imagines a hierarchical harmony instead of a contest of equals, and its modern echo is the belief that a world organised around Chinese industrial capacity is stable rather than coercive. Plenty of neighbours hear that harmony and see a landlord. Fair enough. But that is the argument.
Then there is Sun Tzu, always. The supreme excellence is to win without fighting. Chinese strategists also lean on the idea of shi, the potential energy of a position, like water piling up behind a dam. You do not push the boulder. You arrange the slope. Strategists have long contrasted weiqi (Go) with Western chess, too: chess hunts the king, while Go places stones across the whole board until the opponent has no room to move. China+1, from this angle, is a slope. Every country that “diversifies” rolls downhill towards Chinese inputs anyway.
The proverbs make the defence even sharper.
Jiao tu san ku: the cunning rabbit has three burrows. Chinese firms digging into Vietnam, Mexico, Indonesia and India are the rabbit. China+1 was never a Western invention, they would say. It is what any sensible firm does.
Jie ling hai xu ji ling ren: whoever tied the bell must be the one to untie it. If Washington started the tariff war, Washington must end it, and nobody should blame Chinese firms for routing around the wall.
Fu chao zhi xia wu wan luan: under an overturned nest, no egg stays whole. Break the integrated system and everyone pays, not only China. This is the mutual hostage argument in a single line.
Qian li zhi di hui yu yi xue: a thousand-mile dyke collapses through an ant hole. The tiny dependency, a magnet, a rare earth oxide, a pharmaceutical ingredient, can bring down the big structure. Ask Tokyo.
You can hate every one of these arguments and still admit they hang together. That is exactly why they are dangerous to ignore.
What it does to the dollar?
Does any of this touch the dollar? Yes, but slowly, and not in the way breathless headlines claim. The dollar is not going anywhere next year. It still dominates reserves, invoicing and debt markets, and the yuan’s share of global payments remains in the low single digits.
What changes is the mood. Every tariff, sanctions package and transshipment rule teaches trading nations the same thing: dollar plumbing can be turned into a weapon. The response is not a grand switch to the yuan. It is a thousand small hedges. More bilateral settlement in local currencies, more swap lines, more gold in central bank vaults. India’s own gold import bill rose 24.1% to $71.98 billion in 2025-26, though that was driven by price rather than volume. I would not call that a Delhi policy choice, but it tells you how the world’s savers feel.
Notice the irony as well. China+1 rerouting keeps the final sale to American customers priced in dollars, so Chinese firms keep earning dollars through third countries. The dollar is not defeated. It is being slowly bypassed, at the margins, by people who have stopped assuming it will always be neutral. Erosion, not collapse. But erosion is how most empires of money have ended.
Japan and South Korea: two ways to get squeezed
Japan is the cautionary tale, and it is a painful one because Japan learned this lesson early. After the rare earth scare of 2010, Tokyo built stockpiles and funded alternative sources. Even so, a country that hosts the largest, rare earth magnet industry outside China is still heavily exposed, and one report puts its reliance on Chinese rare earth supply at about 70 percent. Japanese buyers have reportedly paid sharply higher prices for yttrium oxide they could find at all. Fifteen years of preparation, and the ant hole still opened.
South Korea faces a different and more subtle squeeze. Seoul is getting more of the controlled materials Tokyo is not, which sounds like good news until you ask what it is being asked to give in return. Korean analysts openly describe a dilemma between trilateral cooperation with the United States and Japan and cooperation with China. Samsung, Hyundai and the battery makers need both the American market and Chinese inputs, graphite and processing capacity above all. Beijing’s message to Korea is simple: be a friend and the door stays open.
Put the two together and you see the actual method. Split the American alliance system at the seam, reward the one who hedges, punish the one who commits. No tank required.
And now, India
The official story is that China+1 is our moment. Production linked incentives, Make in India, global phone brands opening lines, ministers on stages. The data tells a different story. India’s deficit with China rose from $44 billion in FY2021 to $112.1 billion in FY2026, a rise of 155 percent. In electronics alone, the deficit under HS Chapter 85 reached $43.1 billion in FY26, up from around $20 billion in FY19, which analysts called structural rather than cyclical.
And 2026 is on track to beat even that: imports from China hit a record $79.41 billion in the first half, and the January to September deficit has already reached $105.93 billion.
We are assembling,

articles.title: “Tariff pressure to persist ... Scrutiny of U.S. investment project selection and execution to intensify” [U.S. Midterm Elections] - 파이낸셜뉴스
articles.summary: “Tariff pressure to persist ... Scrutiny of U.S. investment project selection and execution to intensify” [U.S. Midterm Elections]  파이낸셜뉴스
articles.full_text:
Although the Democrats regained majority control of both the House and Senate in the U.S. midterm elections, the Trump administration is expected to maintain its protectionist stance. The administration still holds the authority to impose tariffs, and protecting domestic manufacturing and restructuring supply chains are common policy goals of both parties. However, concerns have been raised that the Democrats’ control of Congress could lead to greater scrutiny of the selection and implementation of projects under South Korea’s pledged $200 billion strategic investment in the United States.
■ Outlook: Tariff pressure to persist
According to foreign media reports and other sources on the 4th, the Democrats regained both the House and Senate majorities previously held by the Republicans in the midterm elections held on the 3rd, local time. As a result, President Trump will have to pursue trade and industrial policies with an opposition-led Congress for the remainder of his term.
The shift in the balance of power in Congress is not expected to lead to an immediate change in tariff policy. The administration can exercise considerable authority over tariffs imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act and Section 301 of the Trade Act, among other provisions. Analysts say it would be difficult to immediately repeal existing tariffs even if the Democrats control Congress.
In a recently published report, the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) forecast that the push to expand production in the United States and bring supply chains for key industries back under domestic control would continue even if the Democrats control Congress. This is because creating manufacturing jobs and reducing reliance on China for supply chains are common policy goals of both parties.
Cho Sung-dae, head of the Trade Research Institute at the Korea International Trade Association, also said at a seminar titled “Outlook and Market Entry Strategies After the U.S. Midterm Elections,” held last month, “Even if the Democrats regain both chambers in the midterm elections, the Trump administration’s America First trade policy, pursued through executive orders, is likely to continue.”
There are also expectations that, separately from the continuation of the protectionist stance, trade pressure specifically targeting South Korea could intensify. An immediate concern for South Korea is the Office of the United States Trade Representative’s (USTR) ongoing Section 301 investigation into structural overcapacity. With 16 economies, including South Korea, among those being investigated, the key question is whether South Korea can maintain the level of burden under the existing U.S.-South Korea tariff agreement if additional tariffs are proposed.
Professor Koo Ki-bo of the Department of Global Commerce at Soongsil University said, “The Democrats have traditionally tended to take a somewhat tougher line on trade pressure than the Republicans, so I think they will become somewhat tougher on the details. In areas such as semiconductors, I think pressure may intensify for South Korea to expand investment in U.S. factories further and reduce its trade surplus.”
■ $20 billion in investment in the U.S.: Congressional scrutiny a wild card
The new balance of power in Congress is also expected to affect the $200 billion strategic investment in the United States pledged by South Korea. Analysts say that as the Democrats step up scrutiny of the Trump administration, political factors could also emerge in the implementation of the existing investment agreement.
Tom Orlik, chief economist at Bloomberg Economics, said at the “2026 U.S. Midterm Elections and Macroeconomic Outlook” webinar hosted that day by the Korea Financial Investment Association that, as the Democrats focus on scrutinizing the Trump administration, the U.S. government’s acquisition of stakes in private companies and investment agreements with foreign companies could face closer examination.
This could also affect the implementation of the U.S.-South Korea investment agreement. Since the U.S. side plays a leading role in selecting projects for South Korea’s strategic investment in the United States, greater congressional scrutiny could affect the process of moving those projects forward.
An official from the Ministry of Trade and Industry said, “We will closely monitor developments in the U.S. Congress and administration and actively pursue outreach to ensure the stable management of U.S.-South Korea trade relations.” The official added, “On the basis of the agreements between the two countries, we will continue to pursue strategic investment in the United States and strengthen economic security cooperation and our strategic partnership.”
aber@fnnews.com Ji-young Park Reporter

articles.title: Section 301 port fees on Chinese vessels - Squire Patton Boggs
articles.summary: Section 301 port fees on Chinese vessels  Squire Patton Boggs
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways
- The suspension of the Section 301 port fees and related measures, due to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on November 9, 2026, is set to be extended by two months to January 9, 2027, following an agreement reached during the September 24 Trump-Xi summit in Washington DC.
- On October 23, 2026, the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) issued a Federal Register notice opening a short public comment period that ran from October 23, 2026, and closed on October 30, 2026. (Docket USTR-2026-0694; 91 Fed. Reg. 67388, published October 26). Comments filed can be found in the USTR Comments Portal under Docket ID: USTR-2026-0694.
- Formal approval of the extension is widely expected. The notice-and-comment process is required under the Administrative Procedures Act (APA) to gather stakeholder input when USTR is considering tariff adjustments or trade actions pursuant to Section 301 and is largely a ministerial act.
- The key question is what happens on or before January 9, 2027. The consensus in Washington DC is that further short extensions of two to three months are likely, with the imposition of port fees kept in reserve (suspended) as negotiating leverage with China.
Background
The Section 301 investigation at issue was initiated in April 2024, and focused on China’s acts, policies and practices targeting the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors for dominance. A notice of proposed action was published in February 2025, and formal notices of proposed action issued in April 2025, with final modifications announced in June 2025, and then in October 2025.1 As noted above, the Section 301 measures took effect on October 14, 2025, but were suspended for one year from November 10, 2025, pursuant to an agreement reached by Presidents Donald J. Trump and Xi at the 2025 Summit in Busan, Korea.
The original one-year suspension, and this most recent two month suspension, cover all of the Section 301 related measures. The most visible and impactful were the broadport fees that target Chinese-owned, Chinese-operated and Chinese-built vessels calling at US ports. The fee structure includes per-call charges of up to US$1 million or more for vessels owned or operated by Chinese entities, and for Chinese-built vessels operated by non-Chinese companies. However, the proposed measures go well beyond Chinese-built vessels. The measures also include up to 100% tariffs on specific Chinese-built ship-to-shore (STS) cranes and tariffs of up to 150% on other cargo handling equipment (including rubber-tired gantry (RTG) cranes, rail-mounted gantry cranes and automatic stacking cranes).
Finally, one of the more controversial measures in the Proposed Section 301 remedies is Annex III, which sets out port fees for car or vehicle carrying vessels (ro-ro vessels). The fees provided for in Annex III apply to all foreign-built vehicle carrier vessels, not just those built in China or those owned or operated by Chinese entities. As a result, Annex III appears to be detached from Section 301’s purpose of securing the removal of China’s actionable acts, policies and practices, and is designed to punish the owners and operators of all vehicle carrying vessels.
The proposed further suspension
At the September 24, 2026 summit, the two governments agreed to extend the moratorium on these Section 301 measures by two months. USTR proposes suspending the measures (port fees, tariffs on cranes and cargo handling equipment, as well as the Annex III fees on all vehicle carrying vessels) from 12 a.m. ET on November 10, 2026, through 11:59 p.m. ET on January 9, 2027. USTR requested comments on a very compressed timetable. The approach mirrors the procedure USTR followed for the original one-year suspension in November 2025.
Summary of public comments
Most submissions support the extension. Many also ask USTR to suspend the fees permanently or indefinitely. Some of the principal submissions are summarized below.
| Commenter(s) | Position | Key arguments | 
| World Shipping Council | Supports; urges permanent suspension | The fees would raise freight costs and act as a regressive tax. Annex III should be revoked in full. Fees on vessels already built or ordered penalize past decisions. | 
| International Chamber of Shipping (ICS); European Shipowners (ECSA) | Supports | Represents about 34.5% of the global fleet. Hopes the suspension evolves into a permanent US-China agreement. Endorses the ICS submission. | 
| Norwegian Shipowners’Association | Supports | The fees and Chinese countermeasures disrupted global trade and harmed US interests. Seeks a long-term agreement that permanently withdraws the fees. | 
| National Grain and Feed Association (NGFA) | Supports; seeks permanent elimination or at least a further one year delay | Bulk grain freight is currently stable because the market expects an extension. Bulk carriers above the exemption thresholds were hit hard by cost increases in 2025. If fees resume, agriculture should be exempted. | 
| Agriculture Transportation Coalition (AgTC) | Supports | The fees would price US farm and forest exports out of markets and reduce calls at smaller ports. Bulk shipping is especially price sensitive. | 
| USA Shipbuilding Coalition | Opposes | The pause allowed Chinese orderbooks to recover. Further delay creates uncertainty for US shipbuilding investment. The measures should apply immediately. | 
Outlook
Even before this latest notice and comment period, Washington DC observers and shipping industry stakeholders consistently indicated that major new trade measures were unlikely before the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. Even after the coming elections, the prevailing view is that the administration will continue to use the port fees as leverage in its negotiations with China. A further short extension of two to three months is therefore likely in January 2027. Unfortunately, successive, short extensions offer little predictability for owners and charterers.
Factors pointing toward potential reinstatement of the port fees and other measures remain. These include bipartisan pressure from Congress to support the US shipbuilding and maritime transportation sector, slowly building momentum behind the SHIPS for America Act and its proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund, and the February 2026 Maritime Action Plan issued by the White House, which relies in part on fee revenue. The plan also proposes a universal cargo-weight-based fee on all foreign-built vessels, not only Chinese vessels.
Practical considerations for vessel owners and operators
- Plan commercially for possible reinstatement after January 9, 2027, and review the allocation of Section 301 fee risk in charter parties and contracts of affreightment that run past that date
- Monitor the Federal Register and USTR announcements from mid-December, since decisions have typically come close to deadlines
- Consider whether to make submissions on any future USTR proposals, including on the exemption thresholds for bulk vessels and on relief for agricultural trade, and on the legality of the proposed fees for vehicle carrying vessels regardless of country of origin and on any efforts to impose a universal cargo-weight-based fee on all foreign-built vessels
This alert is based on publicly filed comments and our discussions with Washington DC maritime contacts. It is not legal advice. Developments are fluid.
- Our firm has previously prepared a series of alerts on the Section 301 investigation of Chinese shipbuilding and maritime sectors. See for example: US Trade Representative Announces Section 301 Investigation in Chinese Shipbuilding and Maritime Transportation (March 2024); Rough Seas Ahead – An Overview of the Section 301 Investigation Into China’s Maritime and Shipbuilding Sectors (March 2025).

articles.title: Section 301 Investigations Up as Congress Eyes Trade Authority - Legis1
articles.summary: Section 301 Investigations Up as Congress Eyes Trade Authority  Legis1
articles.full_text:
Why It Matters
The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) may use findings from two Section 301 investigations it opened after the Supreme Court invalidated tariffs based on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) in February. The intent was to impose a country-specific tariff regime similar in scope to the 2025 IEEPA tariffs, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. Four of those six investigations remain ongoing; two concluded in June with tariff actions finalized in July. The question before Congress is whether simultaneously investigating dozens of trading partners fits the authority Congress originally delegated. 
The Big Picture
From the World Trade Organization's establishment in 1995 until the first Trump administration, the United States used Section 301 primarily to build cases and pursue WTO dispute settlement.
On February 20, the Supreme Court issued its opinion in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, which addresses whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) authorizes the President to impose tariffs. Following that ruling, USTR initiated two Section 301 investigations in March on an "accelerated timeframe" into structural excess capacity across 16 economies and forced-labor import-ban enforcement across 60 economies.
The six investigations break down as follows:
- Brazil, various trade practices (July 2025): concluded June; 25% tariff with exemptions imposed July.
- China, Phase One agreement implementation (October 2025): ongoing.
- 16 economies, structural excess capacity (March): ongoing.
- 60 economies, forced-labor import bans (March): concluded June 2026; 10%-12.5% tariffs finalized July.
- Vietnam, intellectual property protection (May): ongoing.
- Germany, pharmaceutical underpayment (June): ongoing.
Section 301 does not specify a tariff exclusion process, and actions terminate after four years unless USTR receives a continuation request and conducts a review. H.R.2665 and S.1272, both titled the Trade Review Act of 2025, would require congressional notification and review of tariffs. Both were referred to committee, with their latest recorded actions in April 2025 and no action since.
The Bottom Line
Four investigations remain ongoing, including the excess-capacity investigation covering 16 economies and the China Phase One investigation, and USTR may use the findings of its March investigations to impose a country-specific tariff regime similar in scope to the global tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act in 2025. USTR's second four-year review of China Section 301 tariff actions, initiated May 6, is also underway with no completion date stated in the CRS report.

articles.title: Vietnam–EFTA FTA: What It Means for Cross-Border Investment - Vietnam Briefing
articles.summary: Vietnam–EFTA FTA: What It Means for Cross-Border Investment  Vietnam Briefing
articles.full_text:
The Vietnam-EFTA investment framework offers national treatment in specified non-services sectors but excludes investment protection. Businesses from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland should assess sector coverage, licensing requirements, and capital transfer rules ahead of the agreement’s targeted entry into force in early 2027.
Vietnam and the four member states of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) – Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, and Switzerland – signed a free trade agreement in Hanoi on 18 October 2026. Most attention has focused on tariffs, but for investors the longer-term change sits in the agreement’s investment and services chapters.
Those chapters set the terms on which EFTA companies can buy, build, or expand operations in Vietnam, and on which Vietnamese companies can do the same in EFTA markets. However, they leave one major question to separate treaties: how an investment is protected once it is made.
This article explains what the investment chapter covers, where its limits lie, and what foreign investors should review before the Vietnam-EFTA trade agreement takes effect. For agreed upon Vietnam-EFTA tariff schedules and rules of origin, see our earlier overview.
Plan Your Investment
Assess how the Vietnam–EFTA FTA applies to your planned market entry, acquisition, or expansion.
How significant is EFTA investment in Vietnam?
The Vietnam-EFTA FTA’s investment chapter builds on an established base, led by Swiss capital. Registered investment from the EFTA states with reported figures is summarised below.
| EFTA Investment in Vietnam: Registered Projects and Capital |  |  |  | 
| EFTA state | Projects | Registered capital | As of | 
| Switzerland | 244 active projects | About US$2.5 billion | End-September 2026 | 
| Norway | 62 projects | More than US$201 million | End-2025 | 
| Liechtenstein | 1 project | US$4 million | End-July 2026 | 
Around 89 percent of Swiss investment is in manufacturing and processing, the type of activity the investment chapter covers. Switzerland ranks 20th among the countries and territories investing in Vietnam.
What does the investment chapter of the Vietnam–EFTA FTA cover?
Chapter 5 of the Vietnam–EFTA FTA covers investment through commercial presence in specified non-services sectors, including agriculture, fishing, mining and quarrying, and manufacturing. Its main commitment is national treatment: investors from the other parties must receive treatment no less favourable than domestic investors, subject to the sectors and reservations in each party’s schedule. Services are covered separately under Chapter 4.
Does national treatment apply to every investment?
No. According to the EFTA Secretariat’s summary, coverage depends on three conditions:
- A positive list sets the sectors: The listed sectors include agriculture, fishing, mining and quarrying, and manufacturing.
- Reservations narrow it further: Within those sectors, the parties kept exceptions, for example on land acquisition and investment screening.
- Acquisitions and branches are covered: National treatment applies to buying an existing company and setting up a branch, not only to new projects.
An activity that is not listed receives no guarantee under the chapter. Investors should therefore check their specific activity against Vietnam’s schedule, not just its broad sector.
The chapter also contains rules that matter once the business is running:
- Payments and transfers: No party may restrict current payments and capital movements relating to commercial presence. Transfers may be made in any freely convertible currency at the market rate, subject to balance-of-payments and prudential exceptions.
- Key personnel: Subject to its laws, each party grants temporary entry and stay to key personnel employed by the other parties’ investors, and to their spouses and minor children.
- Room to improve: A party may amend its schedule at any time, on its own initiative or at another party’s request, to offer more favourable treatment. The chapter is also reviewed periodically.
Each party keeps its right to regulate for legitimate aims such as public health, safety, the environment, and climate change. A separate exception allows measures to protect critical public infrastructure.
For manufacturers deciding where to place new capacity, the investment rules work alongside the agreement’s origin rules. These allow extended accumulation for non-agricultural inputs from the EU, or from ASEAN members with which a preferential agreement is in force. A Vietnam plant using such inputs may find it easier to qualify for preferential access to EFTA markets.
Structure Capital Flows
Confirm account routes, tax treaty claims, and licensing steps before committing capital in Vietnam.
How does the Vietnam-EFTA FTA treat investment in services?
Service businesses fall under the trade in services chapter, not the investment chapter. The two work as a pair: one covers commercial presence outside services, the other covers commercial presence by service suppliers.
The services chapter builds on World Trade Organisation (WTO) practice, with annexes on financial services, telecommunications, maritime transport, and the movement of natural persons. Its main points for investors are:
- Better than WTO terms in some sectors: Improved market access was agreed for financial, transport and business services, and for supplying services through the presence of natural persons.
- Parity with competitors: The parties will provide market access equivalent to or better than that offered to competitors in their markets.
- Wider eligibility: The benefits extend to permanent residents of the EFTA states.
The detail sits in each party’s schedule of commitments. A service company should confirm the ownership limits and licensing conditions Vietnam has scheduled for its sector before relying on the agreement.
Does the Vietnam–EFTA FTA provide investment protection?
No. The Vietnam–EFTA FTA’s investment chapter expressly excludes investment protection and does not allow investors to bring claims directly against a government. It leaves other investment and taxation agreements between the parties unaffected.
The investment chapter also prevents investors from using dispute mechanisms in existing investment protection agreements to pursue alleged breaches of this chapter.
FTA disputes can be brought only by governments, through consultations and, if unresolved, a three-member arbitration panel. Companies cannot initiate these proceedings themselves.
Investors seeking treaty protection against measures such as expropriation must therefore assess any applicable bilateral investment treaty (BIT). Coverage and access to investor–state arbitration depend on the relevant treaty and its conditions; they should not be assumed to be identical across the four EFTA states.
| Vietnam–EFTA FTA: Treaty Coverage by EFTA State |  |  |  | 
| Investor’s home state | BIT with Vietnam | Double taxation agreement | What the FTA adds | 
| Switzerland | In force since 3 December 1992; replacement under negotiation | In force since 12 October 1997 | Market access on equal terms; BIT protection continues | 
| Iceland | In force since 10 July 2003 | In force since 27 December 2002 | Market access on equal terms; BIT protection continues | 
| Norway | None | In force since 14 April 1996 | Market access on equal terms only | 
| Liechtenstein | None | Signed 18 October 2026; not yet in force | Market access on equal terms only | 
Norwegian and Liechtenstein investors face a clear gap. The FTA gives them a new legal basis for entering Vietnam, but no treaty-based protection once they are established.
For Swiss investors, the picture may change. Vietnam and Switzerland are negotiating a new investment protection agreement to replace the 1992 treaty. The Ministry of Finance reported progress on its scope, protection standards and investor-state dispute settlement, with direct talks scheduled for 30 October 2026.
Investors should not assume that routing an investment through another jurisdiction secures treaty benefits. Under the FTA, a company qualifies as a juridical person of a party only if it has substantive business operations there. Tax treaty rates are likewise tied to beneficial ownership, and each BIT has its own definition of a protected investor.
What still depends on Vietnamese law?
The FTA sets the standard of treatment, but the procedures remain domestic. EFTA investors will follow the same steps as other foreign investors, under rules that changed substantially in 2026.
Investment licensing
The Law on Investment No. 143/2025/QH15 took effect on 1 March 2026. It lets foreign investors set up a company before obtaining or amending the Investment Registration Certificate, provided they meet market access conditions.
Decree No. 96/2026/ND-CP of 31 March 2026 guides the law and lists the sectors with restricted market access for foreign investors. The FTA does not remove the need for either certificate or for sector licences.
Capital contributions and profit remittances
The FTA’s transfer rule works through Vietnam’s foreign exchange framework. Under Circular No. 38/2026/TT-NHNN, in force since 18 August 2026, capital contributions and transfers abroad of capital and profits generally pass through a foreign investment capital account.
The account is required for companies set up by foreign investors, and for those in which foreign investors hold more than 50 percent after a contribution or acquisition. Holdings of 50 percent or less use the indirect investment account route, which matters for minority acquisitions.
Key personnel
The FTA’s commitment on key personnel applies subject to domestic law, so work permit rules still govern. From 5 December 2026, Decree No. 393/2026/ND-CP limits the intra-corporate transferee category to managers, executive directors and experts with at least 12 months’ prior service in the overseas company.
The work permit exemptio

articles.full_text:
The fact that import and export turnover has surpassed the 1 trillion USD mark affirms the scale of Vietnam's integration, while also highlighting the need to enhance the domestic value and competitiveness of goods.
After 10 months of 2026, the total value of goods exports and imports nationwide is estimated to exceed 1 trillion USD, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. This is an important milestone, reflecting the scale of trade and the increasingly deep integration of the economy .
According to Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), the above results are a combination of many factors, most notably the recovery and growth of domestic production, especially the processing and manufacturing industries. As production capacity expands, businesses have more opportunities to take advantage of demand from international markets and maintain export growth.
Foreign-invested enterprises continue to play a crucial role in key sectors such as electronics, machinery, equipment, textiles, and footwear, contributing to maintaining export growth and integrating Vietnam more deeply into global supply chains.
Another driving force is the exploitation of free trade agreements (FTAs) and market expansion. Besides traditional markets, businesses are increasingly interested in regions with significant potential such as the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
"It's impossible not to mention the proactive and flexible approach of the business community in adapting to the fluctuations of global trade, from changing market demands, technical standards requirements, green transitions to adjustments in the trade policies of various countries," Mr. Son emphasized.
The structure of export goods also shows the increasing role of the processing and manufacturing industry group. According to data from the Customs Department ( Ministry of Finance ), as of October 15th, the two groups of computers, electronic products and components; and telephones of all types and components reached a total export value of US$189.65 billion, accounting for approximately 40% of the country's total export value.
In the labor-intensive sector, textiles and garments have maintained their competitiveness. The latest figures from the Vietnam Textile and Garment Association show that in the first nine months of 2026, the industry's export turnover reached approximately US$37.3 billion, an increase of about 3% compared to the same period.
To support import and export activities, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has implemented numerous solutions to develop markets, exploit FTAs, and remove difficulties for businesses. In particular, the Ministry has intensified efforts to disseminate commitments under FTAs, guide businesses in utilizing tariff preferences and rules of origin; promote trade, connect businesses, and respond to trade defense measures…
You may also like
Improving the quality of export growth
Despite achieving a large trade volume, the quality of export growth remains a concern. According to Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, the added value created domestically is not commensurate with the export value, especially in sectors with large export volumes such as electronics, machinery and equipment, textiles, and footwear.
The main reason is that domestic businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), have limited capacity to participate in global supply chains. They have not yet met the requirements in terms of scale, technical standards, quality management, technology, and stable supply sources.
The links between domestic businesses and the FDI sector are not strong; some industries depend on imported raw materials and components, limiting their export potential.
To address this, experts suggest developing supporting industries in sectors with high added value potential, such as electronics, semiconductors, precision mechanics, electrical equipment, and processing industries.
Along with technological innovation, improved governance, and adherence to international standards, it is necessary to promote linkages between FDI enterprises and Vietnamese businesses, creating conditions for domestic suppliers to participate more deeply in global production chains. Attracting foreign investment should also focus on high-tech projects with a commitment to developing the domestic supply chain ecosystem and creating spillover effects.
Regarding priority solutions to further promote import and export in the coming period, economist and Doctor Le Quoc Phuong suggested that the Ministry should exploit FTAs more effectively, clearly identifying industries, markets, and business groups capable of effectively utilizing each agreement to focus resources on support, instead of just generalizing about the commitments.
For green transition, support policies need to be designed according to the specific characteristics of each industry. For example, with coffee and rubber, the focus should be on tracing the origin of the growing region, controlling the risk of deforestation, and building a data system.
In the textile and footwear industries, emphasis should be placed on sustainable materials, water conservation, pollution reduction, chemical control, and the use of clean energy.
Regarding trade promotion, Dr. Le Quoc Phuong also proposed shifting from broad to deep connections, prioritizing connections with businesses that have green products, sustainable processes, and low emissions.
You may also like
This also includes developing infrastructure for laboratories, testing, quality certification, green logistics, and appropriate credit mechanisms to enable businesses to invest in energy-saving technologies and renewable energy.
According to Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, in the context of continued global economic fluctuations, the goal in the coming period is not only to maintain the growth rate of trade turnover but also to improve the quality and efficiency of trade; diversify markets and minimize risks.
In addition, proactively securing raw materials helps businesses adapt to requirements regarding quality, traceability, and sustainable development.
"Following the expansion of the FTA network, the current requirement is to delve deeper, helping businesses not only take advantage of tariff preferences but also gain better access to supply chains, investment flows, and business cooperation opportunities from partner markets," Mr. Son said.
Vietnam's import and export volume has surpassed the $1 trillion mark, but a more important measure is the value Vietnam creates in each product and the increasingly significant role of domestic businesses in the global trade chain.

articles.title: Can a Democratic Congress Roll Back Trump's Tariffs? - Multibagg AI
articles.summary: Can a Democratic Congress Roll Back Trump's Tariffs?  Multibagg AI
articles.full_text:
Key highlights
- A veto override needs 290 of 435 House members and 67 of 100 senators with full attendance.
- The Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 on 20 February 2026 that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs.
- Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% took effect on 24 July 2026 on 60 economies.
- India faces an additional 10% under Section 301, against 12.5% for China, Vietnam and Thailand.
powered by IRIS
A Democratic Congress, projected to take office in January 2027, is unlikely to roll back President Donald Trump's tariffs on its own. Overriding a veto needs 290 of 435 House members and 67 of 100 senators. The 10% to 12.5% Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies also rest on a trade law the administration can apply without a new vote.
Who controls tariff powers, Congress or the president?
The Supreme Court has said the power to tariff is an exercise of Congress's taxing authority, but Congress has written parts of it into laws that the president and trade officials can use. Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 lets a president impose a temporary global tariff for up to 150 days unless Congress votes to extend it. Section 301 lets the US Trade Representative (USTR) act on findings from its own investigations.
Democrats argue that Trump imposed tariffs without following legally required procedures and bypassed Congress, according to a commentary by William Alan Reinsch of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS). It adds that the party is split between trade sceptics and centrists, and that some tariffs are acceptable to Democrats.
What did the Supreme Court rule, and what replaced those tariffs?
On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that IEEPA (the International Emergency Economic Powers Act) does not let the president impose tariffs, according to law firm Hogan Lovells. A temporary 10% global tariff under Section 122 replaced those duties until it expired on 24 July. That day, Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% took effect on 60 economies that USTR said had failed to ban imports made with forced labour, according to EY and USTR. A coalition of 25 US states has challenged them at the Court of International Trade (the US court for trade disputes), calling them a workaround for the Supreme Court ruling, according to Construction Dive.
Refunds of the struck-down tariffs are under way. As of 2 October, US Customs had sent about $126 billion to the Treasury for disbursement, according to Supply Chain Dive. The Justice Department is appealing the trade court's order that refunds go to all importers, not only those who sued.
What can a Democratic Congress do about tariffs in practice?
It can investigate and vote, but it cannot change a tariff without the president's signature or a veto override. According to CSIS, Congress can hold hearings, amend bills in committee, control funding and subpoena documents. The commentary names Canada tariffs as the most obvious target, and says Democrats may seek ways to pass refunds to consumers and examine whether exemptions were tied to campaign contributions.
Votes on trade bills are likely to be symbolic, Reuters reported on 1 November. Senator Chuck Schumer's End Trump's Tariff Tax Act, with 28 co-sponsors, would repeal Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 and Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the law behind the current tariffs on Canada, and refund duties collected under them. CSIS's William Reinsch told Reuters that neither party will have a "veto-proof majority in any scenario". In February the House passed a Democratic resolution rejecting Trump's tariffs on Canada by 219 to 211, with six Republicans joining, according to Rep. Richard Neal's office. That vote came before the Supreme Court ruling. CSIS calls the Democratic measures reactive rather than a trade policy.
Got a follow-up? Ask IRIS
Get more from Multibagg
Create a free account to ask IRIS follow-up questions and get alerts.
Can Congress override a Trump veto on tariffs?
Only if two-thirds of each chamber vote for it, which is 290 of 435 House members and 67 of 100 senators with full attendance. In late October Trump said he would "veto everything" if Democrats won Congress and then make a deal, according to CQ-Roll Call.
Projections point to Democratic control of both chambers, not two-thirds majorities, and counting continues. CSIS wrote on 20 October that nothing that passes is likely to get a presidential signature. The more realistic near-term changes may come from courts, as the February ruling showed, or from the administration itself.
What does this mean for trading partners, including India?
Little changes soon, because trading partners negotiate with the USTR and the White House, not with Congress. India and the US had not signed a trade deal by early October, when Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said both sides had reached "a plateau", according to CNBC. On 1 November Reuters named India among trade deal holdouts, alongside Vietnam and Canada.
Under the Section 301 action, the EU and Taiwan face a 10% rate that includes normal duties, and Japan, South Korea and Switzerland face 12.5%, according to RVIA. An additional 10% applies on top of existing duties for 17 countries including India, and an additional 12.5% for 38 economies including China, Vietnam and Thailand. India's additional rate is therefore below the rate on China, Vietnam and Thailand.
Reuters also reported a forthcoming investigation into excess industrial capacity in 16 major trading partners, so new tariffs remain possible even if Congress objects. For Indian exporters and the stocks tied to them, USTR notices and court rulings are likelier to move tariffs than congressional votes.
Conclusion
Congress holds the formal tariff power, but it has delegated much of it, and a projected Democratic majority does not change the veto arithmetic. The Supreme Court closed the emergency-law route in February, the administration moved to Section 301 within months, and Democrats' tools are hearings, resolutions and bills that a veto can stop. The likelier result is pressure and investigation rather than repeal.
Several dates frame the next steps. Final seat counts are still being confirmed, and the current Republican-led Congress sits in a lame-duck session until the new Congress takes office in January 2027. The stopgap funding law runs to 11 December, and the Federal Reserve meets on 8 and 9 December. Beyond that, watch for court action on the Section 301 tariffs, the government's refund appeal, and any new USTR notices.

articles.title: Democrats Win Congress but Costa Rica’s US Tariff Stays - The Tico Times
articles.summary: Democrats Win Congress but Costa Rica’s US Tariff Stays  The Tico Times
articles.full_text:
Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The result hands President Donald Trump a divided government for his final two years in office. It does not lower the 12.5% duty Washington charges on most Costa Rican goods. The US trade office imposed that duty under a 1974 law that gives the decision to the executive branch.
The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday after the party flipped several Republican seats. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown unseated Sen. Jon Husted, and in North Carolina former Gov. Roy Cooper won the seat Thom Tillis is leaving.
NBC News and CBS News projected that Democrats will also hold a majority in the House. The new Congress is seated in January. Trump told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept” the results and said, “We’ll work with the Democrats.” He also posted an image of his campaign hat bearing the word “VETO.” On Fox News, he said Democrats were “really not in control.”
Exit polls cited by CBS News put his approval among midterm voters at 38%. Costa Rica’s current rate comes from a Section 301 investigation the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) opened on March 12 into 60 economies. On June 2, the agency concluded that Costa Rica had failed to impose and enforce a ban on imports of goods made with forced labor.
The 12.5% rate took effect on July 24. It replaced the 10% surcharge Costa Rica had paid since April 2025. The USTR set two tiers. Economies with no forced-labor import ban pay 12.5%, and those with a ban that is weakly enforced pay 10%. The action has no expiration date and stays in place unless the agency amends it.
Coffee, pineapple, bananas, orange juice, plant cuttings, fruit and vegetable seeds and certain refined sugars are excluded, according to the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex). Textiles and apparel entering duty-free under the CAFTA-DR trade agreement are also exempt. Because Section 301 places the decision with the president and the USTR, a Democratic majority cannot repeal the duty by voting. A bill limiting it would need Trump’s signature, or two-thirds of both chambers to override a veto.
What Democrats gain is oversight: hearings, subpoenas and leverage over spending bills. Those tools can raise the political cost of trade measures without removing them. The same limits apply to the other US decisions that weigh most on Costa Rica. Visa rules, immigration enforcement and deportation flights are all set by the executive branch.
So are entry requirements such as the health declaration for US-bound air travelers, which took effect at 10:59 p.m. Costa Rica time Tuesday. That leaves Costa Rica’s own case before the USTR as the more direct route. On July 6, Comex asked the agency in written comments to drop the 12.5% rate and keep the market access Costa Rica negotiated under CAFTA-DR. The higher rate took effect 18 days later.
The government has since issued Decree 45941-H-MTSS-COMEX, published Sept. 28. It orders Comex and the Ministry of Labor and Social Security to create an official public list of goods at risk of being made with forced labor, and importers must check their purchases against it. The two ministries have 60 calendar days from the decree’s entry into force to set the parameters for the first list. The USTR has not said whether the measure would change Costa Rica’s tier.
That work now falls to new leadership at Comex. Arianna Arce Camacho is serving as interim Foreign Trade Minister after Indiana Trejos was removed on Oct. 28. That was the same day President Laura Fernández announced that Costa Rica would not pursue membership in the CPTPP. First Vice President Francisco Gamboa signed both orders while Fernández was in Europe. They were published in La Gaceta on Tuesday.
For now, the duty remains in place and Congress changes hands in January. Any change to Costa Rica’s rate will depend on how Washington’s trade office judges the measures the country is now building. As the analysts consulted before the vote expected, that decision still sits with the White House rather than Capitol Hill.

articles.title: Deputy PM calls for export-import market diversification, better trade governance - vietnamnews.vn
articles.summary: Deputy PM calls for export-import market diversification, better trade governance  vietnamnews.vn
articles.full_text:
| Standing Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Gia Túc speaks at the meeting on Tuesday. — VNA/VNS Photo | 
HÀ NỘI — Permanent Deputy Prime Minister Phạm Gia Túc has called for the diversification of export-import markets, more effective trade governance and stronger measures to prevent trade fraud and violations in cross-border commerce while drafting a government resolution on balanced trade promotion.
Chairing a meeting with ministries and agencies on Tuesday to discuss the draft resolution, Túc stressed the need for the document to address key and urgent issues, with practical and effective solutions that can be implemented immediately after its issuance.
He said the resolution must closely follow resolutions and conclusions of the Party Central Committee and the Politburo, as well as directives from competent authorities.
In particular, Conclusion No. 106-KL/TW dated October 15, 2026, issued by the 14th Party Central Committee on socio-economic development and State budget performance in 2026 and plans for 2027, calls for diversifying export and import markets while increasing added value, engaging more deeply in regional and global supply chains, and reducing dependence on a small number of markets.
The Deputy PM called for timely handling of trade and tariff issues and effective solutions to address trade deficit. He also asked the drafting agency to continue reviewing the scope, title and content of the draft to ensure a balanced approach to trade governance that takes into account both trade surplus and deficit.
Tasks and solutions must be feasible, effective and substantive, contributing to market diversification, improved trade governance, proactive risk prevention and the prevention of fraud and legal violations in import-export activities, he said.
According to Deputy Minister of Industry and Trade Lương Hoàng Thái, the ministry has worked with relevant agencies to prepare a draft government resolution on a master plan to promote balanced trade, prevent risks of excess capacity, combat trade circumvention and illegal transshipment, and control goods produced using forced labour. The plan aims to improve the management of import-export activities, proactively prevent trade risks and diversify markets.
The draft sets targets for export growth management, a reasonable trade balance, market diversification, stronger control over goods origin and the prevention of trade fraud. It outlines seven groups of key tasks and solutions, including tighter review and management of foreign investment projects that may pose risks of trade fraud, more effective inspection and verification of goods origin, and promotion of sustainable trade. It also proposes facilitating imports of goods, machinery, equipment and technology in line with the plan's objectives and the economy's development needs.
Other measures include expanding export markets, making better use of signed free trade agreements and exploring new markets; strengthening information provision and early warnings; and helping businesses comply with international trade regulations and respond proactively to trade defence measures.
The draft also emphasises improving State management capacity, strengthening coordination and data sharing among relevant agencies, and reviewing and refining legal regulations on investment, trade and related fields.
At the meeting, representatives of ministries and agencies broadly agreed on the need for the resolution, while recommending further review of its targets and task assignments to ensure they match the functions and authority of each agency and are practical to implement. They stressed that stronger controls should go hand in hand with facilitating legitimate production and business activities.
Participants also called for better inter-agency coordination in handling trade defence issues, closer alignment of labour policies with international standards, improved international cooperation and data sharing on imports and exports, and more effective monitoring of cross-border supply chains and goods traceability.
They stressed the need to clarify definitions of trade defence circumvention and illegal transshipment to distinguish such violations from legitimate transport and transit activities. — VNA/VNS

articles.title: Vietnam eyes opportunities amid supply chain shifts in Southeast Asia - Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.summary: Vietnam eyes opportunities amid supply chain shifts in Southeast Asia  Vietnam+ (VietnamPlus)
articles.full_text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) – Vietnam has a prime opportunity to attract investment in high-tech industries, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, data centres, and logistics, while enhancing its role in global value chains as Southeast Asia becomes an increasingly significant destination for international investment.
The issue was discussed by business leaders, experts, and international corporate representatives at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit, organised by Fortune magazine in Ho Chi Minh City on November 3.
Supply chains shift towards Southeast Asia 
Geopolitical tensions, trade protectionism, tariff changes and technological competition are prompting global businesses to adjust production, sourcing and investment strategies, diversify manufacturing locations and strengthen supply chain resilience. 
Thomas Knudsen, Executive Chairman of Toll Group, noted that supply chains are gradually shifting from traditional manufacturing hubs to Southeast Asia. He expects the trend of moving production from China to ASEAN to continue, supported by stronger regional connectivity and infrastructure development, as well as rising investment demands.
Building resilient supply chains requires flexible transport options, transit warehousing and better cross-border connectivity, he said, noting that the region's dynamism, expanding real-time payment systems and free trade agreements offer significant advantages.
However, to fully capitalise on its advantages, the region needs to strengthen its connectivity with global markets and establish effective links between the public and private sectors.
James Nesbitt, Managing Director and Head of Global Subsidiaries for Singapore and ASEAN at Standard Chartered, said businesses are diversifying suppliers and customer markets, increasing inventories and adjusting production methods to minimise supply chain disruptions, while security and political factors are increasingly influencing investment decisions and production organisation.
According to Thammasak Sethaudom, President and CEO of SCG, competition from excess manufacturing capacity in China is spreading across the region. Businesses need to expand production, leverage free trade agreements, cut costs and increase added value. He said automation could improve precision, product quality and resource efficiency, allowing companies to focus more on design, research and development.
Vietnam ready to welcome new waves of investment
Deputy Minister of Finance Le Tan Can said Vietnam aims to become a regional hub for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, as well as a destination for multinational corporations, international investment funds and financial institutions. 
To realise this goal, the country is focusing on building a new-generation investment ecosystem that connects foreign-invested enterprises with domestic businesses, while developing logistics, data and clean energy infrastructure and a high-quality workforce.
It aims to attract foreign investors as partners in technology research, innovation and product development, rather than merely producers for the domestic market. Priority areas include semiconductors, electronics, sustainable value chains and high-quality workforce training.
Nguyen Loc Ha, Standing Vice Chairman of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee, highlighted the city's strengths in finance, trade, services, industry, high-tech industrial parks and the Cai Mep – Thi Vai deep-water port, saying that these create favourable conditions for connecting production chains and development of logistics, trade and financial services.
In the first nine months of 2026, the city's GRDP grew 9.06%, while registered foreign investment exceeded 19 billion USD, four times the figure recorded in the same period last year and accounting for over 30% of the national total.
Ha said the southern metropolis seeks stronger links between investors and local businesses, suppliers, and partners in automation, AI, energy management and workforce training. It is also developing an international financial centre, free trade zones and logistics infrastructure.
Businesses stressed that opportunities from global supply chain shifts lie not only in attracting investment but also in converting it into technology, knowledge, production capacity and domestic added value, helping Vietnam boost competitiveness and strengthen its role in regional and global production and trade networks./.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that Shanghai Yueda Nails Co., Ltd., (Shanghai Yueda) and Shanghai Yueda Nails (Chuzhou) Ltd. (Chuzhou Yueda) (collectively, Yueda Nails), an exporter of certain steel nails (nails) from the People's Republic of China (China), made sales of subject merchandise at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR), August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025. In addition, we are rescinding the review with respect to nine companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results of review.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Joshua Nixon, AD/CVD Operations, Office VIII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-8361.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2026, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty order on nails from China.[1]
On January 28, 2026, Commerce selected Yueda Nails as the mandatory respondent in this review.
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days,[2]
and, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and
( printed page 69542)
Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[3]
On June 4, 2026, Commerce extended the preliminary results deadline by 90 days.[4]
On September 4, 2026, Commerce extended the preliminary results deadline an additional 22 days.[5]
Accordingly, the deadline for these preliminary results is now October 30, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[6]
A list of the topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Order
7
The products covered by the scope of this
Order
are nails from China. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of an antidumping duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[8]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.[9]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the calculated antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.[10]
Commerce notified all interested parties of its intent to rescind the instant review regarding the companies listed in Appendix II because there were no reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, and invited interested parties to comment.[11]
No party commented on this memorandum. In the absence of any suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review for the companies listed in Appendix II, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) of the Act. We calculated export prices in accordance with section 772 of the Act. Because China is a non-market economy (NME) country within the meaning of section 771(18) of the Act, we calculated normal value in accordance with section 773(c) of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Separate Rates
In the
Initiation Notice,
we informed parties that firms for which the review was initiated that wished to qualify for separate rate status must complete, as appropriate, either a separate rate application or a separate rate certification.[12]
We preliminarily determine that Yueda Nails is eligible for a separate rate in this review. For further discussion,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
The China-Wide Entity
Commerce's policy regarding conditional review of the China-wide entity applies to this administrative review.[13]
Under this policy, the China-wide entity will not be under review unless a party specifically requests, or Commerce self-initiates, a review of the entity. Because no party requested a review of the China-wide entity, the entity is not under review, and the entity's rate (
i.e.,
118.04 percent) [14]
is not subject to change.

Published Document: 2026-22523 (91 FR 69531)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) finds that revocation of the antidumping duty (AD) orders on magnesia carbon bricks (bricks) from Mexico and the People's Republic of China (China) would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, at the levels indicated in the “Final Results of Sunset Reviews” section of this notice.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Samuel Evans, AD/CVD Operations, Office IX, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-2420.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 20, 2010, Commerce published the
Orders
in the
Federal Register
.[1]
On July 2, 2026, Commerce published the notice of initiation of this third sunset reviews of the
Orders,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).[2]
On July 14, 2026, Commerce received timely and complete notices of intent to participate in the sunset review from domestic interested parties within the deadline specified in the 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(i).[3]
The domestic interested party claimed the interested party status within the meaning of sections 771(9)(E) and 771(9)(C) of the Act as an
ad hoc
association comprised of U.S. producers of bricks.[4]
On July 30, 2026, Commerce notified the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that it had received notices of intent to participate from the domestic interested party.[5]
On July 31, 2026, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3)(i), the domestic interested party filed timely and adequate substantive responses.[6]
Commerce did not receive a substantive response from any respondent interested party. On August 24, 2026, Commerce notified the ITC that it did not receive a substantive response from any respondent interested parties.[7]
As a result, pursuant to section 751(c)(3)(B) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(e)(1)(ii)(C)(2), Commerce is conducting an expedited (120-day) sunset review of the
Orders.
Scope of the Orders
The product covered by these
Orders
is bricks from Mexico and China. For the full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the Issues and Decisions Memorandum.[8]
Analysis of Comments Received
A complete discussion of all issues raised in these sunset reviews, including the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping in the event of revocation of the
Orders
and the magnitude of the margins likely to prevail if the
Orders
were to be revoked, is provided in the accompanying Issues and Decision Memorandum.[9]
A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is attached in the Appendix to this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be directly accessed at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Final Results of Sunset Reviews
Pursuant to sections 751(c)(1), 752(c)(1) and (3) of the Act, Commerce determines that revocation of the
Orders
would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, and that the magnitude of the dumping margins likely to prevail would be weighted-average dumping margins up to 57.90 percent for Mexico and 236.00 percent for China.
This notice also serves as the only reminder to parties subject to administrative protective order (APO) of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305. Timely notification of the return or destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective orders, is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation which is subject to sanction.
( printed page 69532)
Notification to Interested Parties
We are issuing and publishing these final results in accordance with sections 751(c), 752(c), and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.218 and 19 CFR 351.221(c)(5)(ii).
Dated: October 30, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.

Orders

Published Document: 2026-22512 (91 FR 69636)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of application for exemption; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
FMCSA requests public comment on an application from Metronet for an exemption from the requirement that all exterior lighting devices be steady burning. The exemption would allow Metronet to use Grote Industries LLC's (Grote) amber brake-activated pulsating lamp on its commercial motor vehicles (CMVs), including pickup truck service vehicles not covered by the exemption FMCSA previously granted to Grote, in addition to the steady-burning brake lamps required by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs).
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before December 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by Docket Number FMCSA-2026-2707 by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal: www.regulations.gov. See the Public Participation and Request for Comments section below for further information.
Mail:
Dockets Operations, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, West Building, Washington, DC 20590-0001.
Hand Delivery or Courier:
1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, West Building, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
Each submission must include the Agency name and the docket number (FMCSA-2026-2707) for this notice. Note that DOT posts all comments received without change towww.regulations.gov, including any personal information included in a comment. Please see the Privacy Act heading below.
Privacy Act: In accordance with 49 U.S.C. 31315(b), DOT solicits comments from the public to better inform its exemption process. DOT posts these comments, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov, as described in the system of records notice DOT/ALL-14 FDMS (Federal Docket Management System (FDMS)), which can be reviewed at
https://www.transportation.gov/individuals/privacy/privacy-act-system-records-notices. The comments are posted without edit and are searchable by the name of the submitter.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mr. David Sutula, Chief, Vehicle and Roadside Operations Division, Office of Carrier, Driver, and Vehicle Safety, FMCSA;
MCPSV@dot.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation and Request for Comments
FMCSA encourages you to participate by submitting comments and related materials.
A. Submitting Comments
If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this notice (FMCSA-2026-2707), indicate the specific section of this document to which the comment applies, and provide a reason for your suggestions or recommendations. You may submit your comments and material online or by fax, mail, or hand delivery, but please use only one of these means. FMCSA recommends that you include your name and a mailing address, an email address, or a phone number in the body of your document so the Agency can contact you if it has questions regarding your submission.
If you submit your comments by mail or hand delivery, submit them in an unbound format, no larger than 8
1/2
by 11 inches, suitable for copying and electronic filing.
( printed page 69637)
FMCSA will consider all comments and material received during the comment period. Comments received after the comment closing date will be filed in the public docket and will be considered to the extent practicable.
B. Confidential Business Information (CBI)
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. 552), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to the notice contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to the notice, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission that constitutes CBI as “PROPIN” to indicate it contains proprietary information. FMCSA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the Freedom of Information Act, and they will not be placed in the public docket of the notice. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Sarah Stella, Chief, Regulatory Development Division, Office of Policy, FMCSA, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001 or via email at
sarah.stella@dot.gov. At this time, you need not send a duplicate hardcopy of your electronic CBI submissions to FMCSA headquarters. Any comments FMCSA receives not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this notice.
C. Viewing Comments and Documents
To view comments, as well as any documents mentioned in this preamble as being available in the docket, go to
https://www.regulations.gov, insert FMCSA-2026-2707 in the keyword box, select the document tab and choose the document to review. To view comments, click this notice, then click “Browse Comments.” If you do not have access to the internet, you may view the docket by visiting Dockets Operations in the DOT West Building, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.

Federal Register
(49 CFR 381.315(a)). The Agency must provide the public an opportunity to inspect the information relevant to the application, including the applicant's safety analysis. The Agency must provide an opportunity for public comment on the request.
