AGENCY:
Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, we, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), are proposing to revise an existing information collection.
DATES:
Interested persons are invited to submit comments on or before December 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function. Please provide a copy of your comments to the Service Information Collection Clearance Officer, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, MS: PRB (JAO/3W), 5275 Leesburg Pike, Falls Church, VA 22041-3803 (mail); or by email to
Info_Coll@fws.gov.
Please reference “1018-0186” in the subject line of your comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Madonna L. Baucum, Service Information Collection Clearance Officer, by email at
Info_Coll@fws.gov,
or by telephone at (703) 358-2503. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States. You may also view the information collection request (ICR) at
https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA; 44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.) and its implementing regulations in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at 5 CFR part 1320, all information collections require approval under the PRA. We may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
On June 8, 2026, we published in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 34639) a notice of our intent to request that OMB approve this information collection. In that notice, we solicited comments for 60 days, ending on August 7, 2026. We also published the
Federal Register
notice on
Regulations.gov
(Docket No. FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948). We received the following six comments in response to that notice:
Comment 1:
Electronic comment received from Victoria Lopez submitted via
Regulations.gov
(FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0003) on August 3, 2026. The commenter requests that the Service stop allowing the import of African elephants into the United States and stop authorizing the killing of elephants for trophies. The commenter expresses broader opposition to elephant hunting and trophy imports and raises concerns about threats to African elephant populations. The commenter also cites information regarding elephant populations and trophy hunting in Botswana and other African countries and urges the Service to provide greater protection for elephants and deny permits for the import of elephant trophies.
Agency Response to Comment 1:
The Service appreciates the commenter's concern for the conservation of African elephants. However, the comments regarding whether African elephants should be hunted, whether elephant hunting should be permitted in range countries, and whether the Service should issue permits for the import of elephant specimens are outside the scope of this information collection renewal. The commenter did not address the information collection requirements; therefore, no response is required.
Comment 2:
Anonymous electronic comment submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0004] on August 5, 2026. The commenter states that they are unclear about the changes regarding elephant trophies and generally support sport hunting when conducted within biological limits established by range countries. The commenter opposes unnecessary burdens on hunting and indicates they take no position otherwise. The commenter also states that the action appears to primarily concern live elephants and expresses support for the Service's judgment.
Agency Response to Comment 2:
We appreciate the commenters support regarding the import of African elephant specimens and feel there are no unnecessary burdens on hunting. Therefore, the Service is taking no action in response to the comment.
Comment 3:
Anonymous electronic comment submitted via
Regulations.gov
[FWS-HQ-IA-2026-1948-0005] on August 7, 2026. The commenter recommends prohibiting the import and export of wildlife for hunting purposes and expresses concerns about climate change and the impacts of hunting on threatened species, including elephants.
Agency Response to Comment 3:
This renewal does not propose changes to the African elephant 4(d) rule, the conservation status of African elephants, or the Service's substantive

SUMMARY:
Tenaska Power Services Co. (the Applicant or TPS) has applied for renewed authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada pursuant to the Federal Power Act.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 4, 2026.
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) regulates electricity exports from the United States to foreign countries in accordance with section 202(e) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)) and regulations thereunder (10 CFR 205.300). Sections 301(b) and 402(f) of the DOE Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7151(b) and 7172(f)) transferred this regulatory authority, previously exercised by the now-defunct Federal Power Commission, to DOE.
Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On July 7, 2026, TPS filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for renewal of export authority to transmit electric energy from the United States to Canada for an additional five-year term. App. at 2. TPS was granted export authorization under Order No. EA-243-D on January 7, 2022, which expires on January 11, 2027. According to the Application, TPS is a Nebraska corporation that is authorized to do business in the States of Nebraska, Alabama, Illinois, Texas, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, California, Delaware, Nevada, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Washington. TPS is an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of Tenaska Energy Inc. (Tenaska), which is “an independent developer and owner of power production facilities located throughout the United States.”
Id.
at 3. TPS is a “power marketer authorized by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to make sales of electric power at wholesale in interstate commerce at market-based rates.”
Id.
at 2. In addition, TPS states that it “does not currently own or control electric generation or transmission facilities, and it does not have a power supply of its own in the United States that would cause its electricity exports to have a reliability, fuel use, or system stability impact.” Furthermore, TPS states that it will “purchase the electricity that it may export, on either a firm or an interruptible basis, from wholesale generators, electric utilities, federal power marketing agencies and affiliates through negotiated agreements that have been voluntarily executed by the selling parties after considering their own need for any such electricity.”
Id.
at 5. Thus, “TPS's proposed electricity exports will not impair or tend to impede the sufficiency of electric power supplies in the United States or the regional coordination of electric utility planning or operations.”
Id.
The Applicant also states that it will “make all necessary commercial arrangements and will obtain any and all other regulatory approvals required in order to carry out any electricity exports” and that it “agrees to abide by the export limits contained in the relevant export authorization of any transmission facilities over which TPS exports electricity to Canada.”
Id.
at 6.

articles.title: TAKEAWAYS: Shaping the Future of the Global Supply Chain - Inbound Logistics

articles.full_text:
The Math Behind Holiday Inventory
By Shana Wray
Principal Solutions Architect & Supply Chain Analyst, FourKites
Consumers won’t think about the holidays for months, but by July, retailers had already made the decisions that determine what’s on shelves this winter, and what it costs to get there. Shipping costs from China climbed 61% year-over-year this summer, driven by continued Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz disruption, giving many shippers reason to pull holiday inventory forward.
Earlier isn’t automatically safer. Every extra week in a distribution center adds to carrying costs that commonly run 15% to 25% of inventory value annually once capital, insurance, labor, and space are factored in. For seasonal goods with a hard sell-by window, a few additional weeks of dwell time can erase the savings an early booking was meant to protect.
That’s why freight rate alone is the wrong lens for this decision. Paying a premium to move a shipment now can be justified if a delay threatens a product’s entire selling season. Pulling every SKU forward regardless of risk just trades one cost for another, tying up working capital and warehouse space months before that inventory generates a dollar of revenue.
What matters is whether the team can tell, shipment by shipment, which shipments warrant the early move and which can safely wait. That requires visibility into where inventory sits today, how much buffer remains before it’s needed, and which exceptions actually justify intervention.
By the end of summer, most holiday inventory is already in motion. Retailers now have to make sure they aren’t paying to avoid one risk only to create a costlier one elsewhere in the network.
How Manufacturers Can Close the AI Readiness Gap
By Michael Hart
Head of Product, Industry Strategy & Growth
Rockwell Automation
For years, manufacturing investments focused on isolated automation and task-level execution. Now, as factory floors become more intelligent, digital maturity—the ability to seamlessly connect systems, contextualize data, and act in real time—has emerged as the single biggest differentiator for manufacturers.
According to Rockwell Automation’s latest report*, nearly half of manufacturers rank AI and machine learning as their top outcome drivers over the next five years. Yet, only 43% of collected data is used effectively. Many manufacturers remain trapped in the “connected plant” stage. They have digitized workflows and moved off paper, but decision-making remains reactive and data remains siloed.
While 93% of manufacturers have a manufacturing execution system (MES) in place, only 28% have deployed it enterprise-wide, with just 23% reporting full integration. This suggests that there’s still heavy reliance on manual decision-making, disconnected data, and reactive processes. These organizations typically see little operational improvements as any new AI initiative will face resistance and be difficult to scale.
The difference between the “connected plant” stage and the next stage of digital maturity that enables predictive analytics is huge—systems can proactively guide decisions, enable supply chain visibility in real-time, and model outcomes before they happen. Manufacturers become closer to enabling true autonomous operations, where systems are modular, closed-loop, and capable of self-optimizing with minimal intervention.
Intelligent industrial environments require contextualized data from connected shop floors to learn, adapt, self-optimize, and have visibility of operations anywhere and anytime as well as a high degree of predictability. Digital maturity enables faster response times, resilience, better quality, and less downtime.
*This report gathered input from 1,560 hardware, software, and services decision-makers across manufacturing and industrial operations globally. Respondents represent 17 leading manufacturing countries, spanning discrete, process, and hybrid industries; 54% are primary decision-makers.
Diversification Tops Domestication
Despite years of pressure to bring production closer to home, reshoring remains near the bottom of the priority list for supply chain leaders, according to Accenture’s latest Pulse of Change survey.
Surveying 3,000 C-suite leaders across 20 countries and 19 industries, including 322 supply chain and operations executives, the report finds that fewer than one in three leaders plan to reshore or nearshore operations. Investing in domestic production ranks last among strategic priorities, even as 78% of supply chain leaders say operations have become materially harder over the past six months.
Instead, leaders are building resilience within the networks they already have. Two-thirds have already renegotiated or restructured partnerships based on a supplier’s country of origin, and nearly half are diversifying their supplier networks. Forecasting, scenario planning, and risk management are top priorities for the majority of supply chain executives.
There is a notable split between supply chain leaders and the broader C-suite. Operations executives are most focused on supply chain continuity and rising costs, while the broader C-suite is prioritizing AI and digital tech investments. While both groups are increasing AI spending, supply chain leaders are approaching it through a more workforce-focused lens.
Regional pressures differ, too. In the Americas, 56% of supply chain executives name labor and talent shortages as the disruption most likely to force a strategy change in 2026. This number is well above what is reported in Asia-Pacific (45%) and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (32%).
Reshoring makes for good headlines, but it isn’t a practical solution for the majority of companies, the report stresses. Instead, leaders are leaning into stronger forecasting, diversified suppliers, and resilient partnerships.
Robots Are Coming for Warehousing’s Hardest Jobs
Warehousing jobs are getting harder to fill. According to the 2026 MHI Annual Industry Report, 90% of supply chain organizations cite talent acquisition and workforce issues as a top challenge. Companies are responding by automating the jobs that are the most physically demanding and the hardest to staff.
FedEx and Amazon made major robotics announcements within days of each other this summer. FedEx and physical AI company Dexterity (bottom) are expanding their partnership beyond the pilot phase, moving Dexterity’s trailer-loading robot, Mech, into full production at the FedEx Hagerstown Hub in Maryland. Trailer loading has historically been one of the hardest tasks to automate because no two loads are alike. Mech uses a spatial reasoning system called Foresight to decide how to place packages for space, stability, and speed.
Amazon (top), meanwhile, is more than doubling its fleet of Cardinal and Sparrow robotic arms in 2026. Cardinal loads packages into carts, while Sparrow picks individual items from containers into totes. The company also introduced Vulcan, its first robot with a sense of touch, capable of stowing and retrieving items at the highest and lowest levels of inventory pods. Amazon says more than 40% of its items were delivered same-day or overnight in the first half of 2026, and credits robotics as a driver behind that metric.
FedEx and Amazon aren’t alone. The Association for Advancing Automation reports that collaborative robot orders jumped 55.6% in Q1 2026, even as automotive orders fell. This is a sign that demand is spreading well beyond the industries that have dominated the robotics market in the past.
The global warehouse automation market is currently projected to double by 2030. The companies moving now are building an advantage that will be difficult to close later.
Industrial Real Estate Stages a Comeback
The U.S. industrial real estate market is on the path to recovery, according to Savills Research’s Q2 2026 State of the U.S. Industrial Market report. Leasing activity in the first half of 2026 reached 490.6 million square feet, up 27.1% from the same period last year. It’s the strongest first half since the 2021-2022 boom.
The report highlights the following trends:
The supply-demand gap that defined the past two years is closing. New space coming online outpaced demand by just 2.6% in the first half of 2026, the closest those two lines have been in four years. Vacancy held at 8.2% and asking rents nudged up to $9.74 per square foot.
3PLs and manufacturers account for 65% of leasing over the past four quarters. The tightest segment of the market is large-format space of 750,000 square feet and above, where vacancy has dropped 160 basis points YoY.
Regionally, the Sun Belt still leads on absorption, but the Heartland is closing the gap. Chicago, Columbus, Denver, Detroit, and Salt Lake City are attracting a broadening tenant base as companies look for alternatives to coastal and Sun Belt markets.
The data center boom is an emerging driver to watch. Companies that build, cool, power, and equip data centers have become major industrial tenants in markets such as Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, and Atlanta, leasing large blocks of space for manufacturing and logistics operations tied to AI infrastructure.
Construction starts are creeping back up, led by speculative development. The pipeline is rising, but it remains 61.2% below its 2022 peak, so any supply response will be gradual.
Freight Fraud Takes a New Form
For years, the fight against freight fraud focused largely on catching fabricated carrier identities. Today, the approach is changing. As it becomes harder to fabricate a fake carrier from scratch, criminals increasingly hijack the trust already built into legitimate operations, according to the Q2 2026 Freight Fraud Index Report from Highway.
The new focus is on communication-based attacks, including compromised inboxes, spoofed emails, account takeovers, and impersonation calls, which now make up half of all classified fraud vectors, according to the report.

articles.title: Securing The Supply Chain: A Survey Of Contrasting Global Approaches To Critical Minerals Strategic Reserves - JD Supra
articles.summary: Securing The Supply Chain: A Survey Of Contrasting Global Approaches To Critical Minerals Strategic Reserves  JD Supra
articles.full_text:
[co-author: Natalie Doray]
What you need to know
- The US's US$12 billion Project Vault is now operating. On 23 September 2026, two commodity traders each committed US$500 million to the reserve for the supply of critical minerals.
- Project Vault is a physical stockpile financed by industry and backed by US-EXIM. Manufacturers pay for access to stock, and traders source and hold it.
- Australia's A$1.2 billion Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve is scheduled to be operational by the end of 2026. It is primarily a price-support model, using offtakes, forward contracts and price floors, with antimony, gallium and rare earths first.
- The EU, Japan, South Korea and Canada each use different models, ranging from joint purchasing and long-running stockpiles to equity-backed offtake rights.
What you need to do
- Prepare to deal with governments as commercial counterparties, as they increasingly act as buyers, financiers and offtakers.
- Review your offtake strategy so that reserve arrangements fit with your existing contracts and financing terms.
- Know where the risk sits: look closely at pricing, specifications, take-or-pay terms and termination rights.
- Explore funding options in Australia, the US, the EU and Canada.
The United States has moved its US$12 billion strategic critical minerals reserve, known as Project Vault, into its operational and procurement phase, with two global commodity traders committing US$1 billion of critical minerals to VaultCo. Australia's A$1.2 billion reserve is promised for the second half of 2026. As governments move from policy to implementation, we compare how six jurisdictions are building their critical minerals reserves, and what that means for producers, traders and offtakers.
Why now
Critical minerals underpin defense materiel, high-tech manufacturing and the energy transition. China's 2025 export controls on gallium, germanium, antimony and rare earth processing technology have turned long-discussed supply chain risks into real commercial disruption. Governments are no longer just promoting these markets. They are now buying, financing and holding stock themselves.
On 23 September 2026, two major global commodity traders each committed US$500 million to VaultCo, the operating entity of Project Vault. Project Vault is a US$12 billion public-private partnership backed by the Export-Import Bank of the United States (US-EXIM). Other countries have announced or already run their own reserves, but the models differ widely. The US is building a physical stockpile financed by industry. Australia's reserve is primarily a market-making and price-support mechanism. Other countries and regions – such as the EU, Japan, South Korea and Canada – have each taken a different approach again. The structure of each model will decide where the commercial risk falls, and which contracts market participants will be asked to sign.
Australia
Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve
The A$1.2 billion Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve (CMSR) is primarily a market-making and price-support mechanism, not a physical stockpile. It will secure rights to critical minerals produced in Australia and on-sell those rights to meet demand for Australia and its key international partners.1 Its toolkit includes fixed or floating price offtake agreements, trading in forward offtake contracts, demand and supply aggregation, physical stockpiling and contracts for difference (CfD) with price floors and ceilings. The 10% Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive, which starts in July 2027, provides further support.2 The US-Australia Critical Minerals Framework gives a further platform for cooperation.3
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the CMSR on 24 April 2025 to strengthen the security and resilience of critical minerals supply chains.4 The government allocated A$1.2 billion to the reserve in the 2025-26 federal budget, and said it would be operational from the second half of 2026. Responsibility for the taskforce has moved from the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources, and Export Finance Australia now has an expanded range of financial tools to support implementation.
The reserve will first focus on antimony, gallium and rare earth elements. These are critical to clean energy, high-technology manufacturing and advanced military equipment. Rather than holding stock, the reserve will mainly secure rights to minerals produced in Australia and sell those rights on to buyers.5 A$1 billion for these transactions comes from the A$5 billion Critical Minerals Facility, which provides government-backed loans and equity. A$185 million is set aside for selective stockpiling and implementation.6 Australia's plan has been described as a "market stabilising" model, in which the government acts as a guaranteed buyer to reduce investor risk.7
Key insights
Australian producers of antimony, gallium and rare earths are the first likely counterparties, and the CMSR can act as a guaranteed buyer to help projects reach financial close. Producers should expect offtake, forward and CfD terms, and should consider how price floors and ceilings interact with existing offtakes and finance covenants. Because the CMSR will on-sell rights to Australia’s international partners, overseas offtakers and traders will find themselves buying from the Commonwealth rather than the mine.
- Department of Industry, Science and Resources, “Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve”, Department of Industry, Science and Resources website.
- Australian Taxation Office, “Critical Minerals Production Tax Incentive”, last updated March 3, 2026, Australian Taxation Office website.
- Department of Industry, Science and Resources, “United States–Australia Framework for Securing of Supply in the Mining and Processing of Critical Minerals and Rare Earths”, October 21, 2025, Department of Industry, Science and Resources website.
- Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, “Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve”, Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet website.
- Export Finance Australia, “Delivering Australia’s critical minerals supply”, January 12, 2026, Export Finance Australia website.
- Department of Industry, Science and Resources, “Strategic reserve to secure Australia’s critical mineral supply”, January 12, 2026, Department of Industry, Science and Resources website.
- Saloni Sachdeva Michael and Akanksha Golchha, “Building critical mineral stockpiles: A key priority for India”, June 28, 2025, Institute of Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) website.
Canada
Critical Minerals Accelerator
Rather than establishing a dedicated reserve agency, Canada is building its critical minerals stockpile through investment, domestic powers and international partnerships. Natural Resources Canada launched the Canada Critical Minerals Accelerator (CCMA), introduced in Budget 2025, on 7 July 2026.1 Delivered by Export Development Canada, the CCMA invests in projects across the value chain, from extraction to processing. One of its stated purposes is to help advance a national stockpile of critical minerals that will contribute to the supply needs of both Canada and its allies.2
The first agreement under the CCMA is between a Canadian resource company, the Canada Growth Fund and the CCMA. The Canada Growth Fund will establish the commercial framework for an equity-like investment of up to US$400 million into the resource company's smelting operations to support expanding production capacity for germanium, gallium and antimony. The operation is a fully integrated polymetallic smelting and refining complex, with a long history of critical minerals production. The agreement also enables the Government of Canada to negotiate an offtake structure that could include rights to a portion of future germanium, antimony and gallium production.
At the Canada Investment Summit in September 2026, Prime Minister Carney said Canada had signed more than 50 critical minerals agreements with over 15 countries in the past year, unlocking C$20 billion of investment.3 In October 2025, the then Energy and Natural Resources Minister, Tim Hodgson, announced Canada would launch its own stockpiling effort and support those of trusted partners.4 Minister Hodgson announced 26 new investments, partnerships and measures to accelerate and unlock C$6.4 billion of critical minerals projects. Natural Resources Canada is exploring stockpiling options and negotiating offtake agreements with producers. The first two are with a global mining company for scandium and a Canadian graphite developer for graphite.
Key insights
Direct government investment can help fill gaps and crowd in other investment. It should lead to additional critical minerals stock on the market.
- Natural Resources Canada, "Canada announces first agreement under new Canada Critical Minerals Accelerator", July 7, 2026, Government of Canada website.
- Government of Canada, “Government Response to the Third Report of the Standing Committee on Natural Resources titled: 'An Extraordinary Opportunity for Canada': The Development of Critical Minerals”, House of Commons of Canada report, 5.
- Jackson Chen, “Canada’s critical minerals push opens new frontiers in the North”, September 28, 2026, Mining.com.au website.
- Natural Resources Canada, “Canada unlocks 26 new investments and partnerships with 9 allied countries to secure critical minerals supply chains”, October 31, 2025, Government of Canada website.
European Union
RESourceEU
The EU relies on coordination under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) and RESourceEU.1 A new European Critical Raw Materials Centre will act as a coordination hub, supporting strategic stockpiling and joint purchasing alongside work with Member States on a coordinated EU stockpiling approach.
The EU's approach is set out in the RESourceEU Action Plan, adopted on 3 December 2025, which builds on the CRMA.2 The Plan aims to accelerate implementation

- Non-Dilutive Deal: An option agreement on the Monument Peak project in Idaho brings cash, shares, exploration spending and a retained royalty.
- Balanced Backdrop: Funding needs, early-stage project status and low trading Liquidity remain the main considerations.
Global Energy Metals Corp. (TSXV:GEMC) is a Canadian critical minerals explorer with projects in Canada, Australia, Norway and the United States. Its shares advanced 33.33% to CAD 0.02 on 3 November 2026, a large percentage move for a stock at that price.
The company concentrates on battery metals including copper, nickel, cobalt, lithium and uranium, and has recently used partnerships and option deals to advance Assets with limited spending of its own.
Why Did Global Energy Metals Corp. (TSXV:GEMC) Rise by 33.33% on 3 November, 2026?
Global Energy Metals Corp. (TSXV:GEMC) advanced by 33.33% to CAD 0.02 on 3 November 2026. At such a low price, the smallest price increment produces a large percentage change.
The company's recent disclosures reviewed do not identify a new announcement for that session.
Earlier 2026 news may keep the stock on watchlists, including graphite results at Millennium and the Monument Peak option agreement that brings non-dilutive consideration.
Interest in critical minerals and battery Supply chains can lift small explorers together.
A sustained advance would need new project news or funding clarity.
The Business model of Global Energy Metals
Global Energy Metals is an exploration company with no operating revenue. It builds a portfolio of critical mineral properties, then advances them through partners, option agreements or sales.
Its Millennium copper-cobalt-gold project near Cloncurry in northwest Queensland is operated by joint venture partner Metal Bank Ltd. Global Energy Metals holds 49% and is fully carried on exploration spending under Metal Bank's earn-in.
The Monument Peak silver-copper-gold project in Lemhi County, Idaho, is 50% owned by the company and has been optioned to Grounded People Apparel Inc. on a staged four-year basis, with the company retaining a 1.0% net smelter returns royalty.
The company has also held interests in uranium and lithium related assets and a portfolio holding with Athabasca Basin uranium exposure, reflecting its multi-commodity approach.
Major Reasons Behind Upside
Millennium Graphite: Four drill holes completed in December 2025 returned near-surface graphite, including intercepts of 13.1 metres at 12.23% total graphitic carbon and 30.85 metres at 14.11% total graphitic carbon. The company describes the graphite as potentially a by-product of the existing resource.
Graphite Zone Extent: The graphitic zone extends over about two kilometres of strike, running parallel to the copper-cobalt-gold resource.
Government Funding: A Queensland Collaborative Exploration Initiative grant of up to AUD 275,000 majority-funded the drilling and assaying.
Fully Carried Interest: Global Energy Metals does not need to fund its share of Millennium exploration during Metal Bank's earn-in period.
Monument Peak Option: The April 2026 agreement offers CAD 650,000 in cash, CAD 750,000 in shares and at least CAD 250,000 in first-year exploration spending, which the company says preserves its balance sheet.
Retained Royalty: The 1.0% net smelter returns Royalty provides lasting exposure to any discovery, with a buy-back right for the optionee.
Board Nominee Right: After closing, the company will have a right to nominate a director to the optionee's board.
Latest official announcements: In February 2026 the company reported the Millennium graphite results, and in March 2026 it announced an exploration permit application at Millennium and a portfolio company's exercise of an option on an Athabasca Basin uranium portfolio.
In April 2026 it announced the Monument Peak option agreement. No Sept-Oct 2026 announcements were identified.
What Are the Major Risks Investors Should Consider?
Exploration Risk: Graphite intercepts and mineral resources do not guarantee economic extraction.
Funding Risk: The company needs Capital for general costs and any non-carried programmes.
Partner Risk: Progress depends on partners, including Metal Bank at Millennium and the optionee at Monument Peak.
Execution Risk: Option payments and exploration spending might not be completed.
Commodity Risk: Graphite, copper and battery metal prices can change sharply.
Liquidity Risk: The very low price and thin trading can magnify losses as well as gains.
What Is the Dividend Outlook?
Global Energy Metals does not pay a dividend and has no stated policy for one. Its priorities are portfolio management, project partnerships and keeping costs low.
Income distributions would depend on future royalties or asset sales generating sustained cash flow.
How Does Global Energy Metals Compare With Other Industry Peers?
Global Energy Metals shares themes with other battery metals explorers. Electra Battery Materials is building cobalt refining capacity in Ontario, and Canada Nickel Company is advancing the Crawford nickel project.
In graphite, Graphite One is developing an Alaska project, offering a comparison for the Millennium by-product story.
Global Energy Metals is far smaller and works mainly through partnerships rather than advancing a single project itself.
Its competitive standing will rest on the carried Millennium interest, royalty exposure and deal execution.
What Are the Bull and Bear Cases for TSXV:GEMC?
Bull Case:
- Near-surface graphite adds a second Commodity angle to Millennium.
- The Monument Peak option adds cash and shares without dilution.
- A Carried Interest limits spending at Millennium.
- A retained royalty offers exposure to Monument Peak discoveries.
Bear Case:
- Graphite Economics are unproven and metallurgical testing is early.
- Optionee payments may be delayed or fail.
- The company still needs funding for its own costs.
- Low trading liquidity may deepen any decline.
Technical Levels to Watch
- Support Zone: The range where the stock traded before the jump is the first area watchers look for stability.
- Resistance Levels: Earlier trading highs may attract sellers.
- Volume Trends: Higher turnover over several sessions would show wider interest.
- Momentum Indicators: Moving averages and relative strength gauges help show whether the move is extending, though less reliable for low-priced shares.
Outlook
Global Energy Metals Corp. (TSXV:GEMC) maintains a cautiously constructive tone after its latest rise, with graphite findings and a structured option deal supporting its profile.
Items to watch include metallurgical results on the graphite, progress on Monument Peak payments and spending, and permit decisions at Millennium.
Funding needs and early-stage risk remain.
Company announcements will be the clearest guide.

articles.full_text:
Japan’s industry minister, Ryosei Akazawa, criticised China’s controls on rare earth exports during Tuesday’s online Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) ministerial meeting.
He argued against arbitrary restrictions on critical mineral shipments that could interrupt supply chains.
China will host APEC leaders in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, on November 18–19.
Cooperation on artificial intelligence and the digital economy will be central to the summit’s agenda, according to the APEC Secretariat.
China’s commerce minister, Wang Wentao, called for a commitment to free trade.
His fellow co-chair, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, emphasised the importance of maintaining the multilateral trading system.
Wang Yi also pointed to difficulties facing economic globalisation, apparently referring to a US trade policy that prioritises the country’s own interests.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi’s appeal appeared to reflect concerns about protectionism and economic coercion.
Japan’s Foreign Ministry quoted him on Wednesday as linking growing global economic uncertainty to the need for a stronger international economic order.
“In today's world, where uncertainty in the global economy is ever-increasing, it is crucial to strengthen a free, fair and rules-based international economic order,” Motegi told the meeting.

articles.title: Japan Envoy Urges Thailand to Protect its Car Export Hub as Cheap EV Imports Surge - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Japan Envoy Urges Thailand to Protect its Car Export Hub as Cheap EV Imports Surge  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Ambassador Otaka Masato tells The Standard forum that two Japanese carmakers have quit Thailand and calls for joint work on green, space and health industries.
Japan’s ambassador to Thailand has urged the government to protect the country’s automotive export hub, warning that a rising tide of cheap imported cars, particularly electric vehicles (EVs), threatens the industry that anchors Japan–Thailand economic ties.
Otaka Masato delivered a keynote titled “Japan–Thailand: Co-Creating the Next Economy” at the opening of “Economic Forum 2026: Reinvent Thailand”, hosted by The Standard.
“Once you open the gate to the domestic market for cheap cars, it will have some adverse impact on the existing automotive sector, and this will impact the capability of the Thai industry to export,” he said.
A healthy home market, he argued, is needed to sustain overseas sales.
Otaka said the industry remains vital. His slides put its contribution at about 9% of GDP and its workforce, including parts makers, at about 800,000 people. Local content reaches as high as 94–95% for some pickups and eco cars, he noted, so most of the value stays in Thailand.
Exporting cars and trucks has also earned the country valuable foreign currency. But his presentation showed domestic sales trending down while imported fully built units gained share.
The slides said weaker demand and rising imports have left the manufacturing supply chain in a “very difficult situation”. Last year, two of the eight major Japanese carmakers, Suzuki and Subaru, stopped producing cars in Thailand.
“That’s a significant impact,” he said.
The sector has also been hit by the Middle East conflict, which has curbed exports, and by flooding in late September that forced Japanese makers to halt assembly lines for two weeks because parts from affected areas were unavailable.
A little over 150 Japanese companies were affected, mostly around Chon Buri, compared with more than 500 in the 2011 floods.
Otaka acknowledged that EVs benefit the environment. But he said Thailand does not yet have the cheap green electricity that has driven EV adoption in countries such as Norway.
He urged officials to examine the sector carefully and decide how it should be sustained. His first takeaway was to value Thailand’s role as an export hub.
Thailand Japanese investment overseas remains strong, Otaka said, but Thailand has slipped to fifth place among foreign investors since 2022–2023.
That is not because Japanese capital has fallen, he said, but because other countries are investing more. Japanese investment in China has dropped sharply, while investment in the rest of Asia is stable.
Vietnam is Thailand’s most direct rival for investment, and India is rising quickly. Investment in Singapore is growing on the back of social media, AI and data centres.
He said Thailand has been affected by the Middle East situation less than some, though it relies heavily on the region for energy and some products, including naphtha and urea fertiliser, are in short supply.
Thailand’s terms of trade are weakening as import costs outpace export values. In Japan, with the 2% inflation target roughly met, he expected further interest rate rises, which will weigh on growth.
Conditions in Thailand, he said, are “not so bad”. He pointed to success outside the cars. A pet food producer in Thailand employs about 5,000 people, may reach 10,000, and exports 96% of its output, over half of it to the United States.
“Keeping this kind of export hub industry is a great benefit for Thailand,” he said.
His second takeaway was that global and social challenges are business opportunities.
According to his presentation, it showed Thailand's bioethanol output of about 1 billion litres a year and biodiesel of about 2 billion, far behind the United States and Brazil in ethanol and Indonesia in biodiesel. But the country has abundant sugar cane, cassava and palm, and has long blended ethanol into fuel, joining a small group including Brazil, India and Japan.
A biofuel public-private roundtable was agreed at the ASEAN Economic Ministers–METI consultation in September, and Japan is supporting biofuel and bio-industry development. Bio-based alternatives might eventually replace naphtha, he said.
Waste and recycling are another opening. Japan has eight recycling laws and the lowest per-capita municipal waste in the OECD, he said. It recycles 85% of PET bottles, against 19.6% in the United States and 42.7% in Europe, and 97% of construction waste.
Japan taxes older cars more heavily to encourage replacement. It is already supporting, through a JICA project, a system under an end-of-life vehicles act being considered in Thailand.
Otaka said the space industry has become a real business, with launches heading from several a year to several a day. His slides projected the global space economy growing from about US$550 billion today to US$1.8 trillion by 2035.
Thailand, he argued, should focus not just on buying rockets or satellites but on data. More than 40 Japanese companies attended Thailand’s recent space week seeking partners, and data sharing and processing could generate business before Thailand has its own satellite.
Japan is ready to help with capacity building. He also urged Thailand to join early work on optical semiconductors, which use less electricity and could improve satellites and quantum computing, as well as 6G and solid-state batteries.
“You need to join the camp; you need to find your partners,” he said, naming Japan as a good candidate.
Thailand’s fertility rate of 0.86 is “staggering”, he said, against 1.2 to 1.3 in Japan. His slides showed Thailand’s ageing rate rising about threefold in 25 years and noncommunicable diseases accounting for over two-thirds of its disease burden.
Japan is working to narrow the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy so that people can keep working and place less strain on social security.
Life expectancy is 84.3 years in Japan and 77.4 in Thailand, he said, while healthy life expectancy is 72.6 and 67.4, respectively. In health terms, a 67-year-old Thai is equivalent to a 72-year-old Japanese.
Japan is also labelling companies that invest in employee health, and their share prices tend to outperform, he said.
Because the two countries share the same demographic challenge, Otaka said Japan looks forward to working with Thailand on health screening and related industries, an area where Thai conglomerate CP is already active.
It is a new field, he said, that will “benefit the Thai economy for sure”.
Otaka closed on an optimistic note, summing up his three takeaways: keep Thailand’s strength as an export hub, treat global and social challenges as chances to create new business, and stay close to the groundbreaking technologies of the future.
With Japan’s experience and Thailand’s strengths, he suggested, the two countries are well placed to build the next economy together.

articles.title: Dak Lak province is implementing various investment and trade promotion activities in Thailand. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Dak Lak province is implementing various investment and trade promotion activities in Thailand.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
From vast coffee plantations and fruit-laden durian orchards to macadamia and pepper growing regions, Dak Lak possesses a wealth of agricultural products with great potential. However, for these products to reach a wider market, in addition to quality and quantity, finding partners, expanding markets, and building a supply chain from production to processing and distribution are crucial.
 With that orientation, on November 2nd and 3rd, the Dak Lak provincial delegation, led by Mr. Y Giang Gry Niê Knơng, Deputy Secretary of the Provincial Party Committee and Chairman of the Vietnam Fatherland Front Committee of Dak Lak province, held numerous working meetings in Thailand . The activities focused on introducing the potential and advantages of the locality, and seeking opportunities for cooperation in the fields of agriculture, processing industry, trade, services, logistics, and tourism.
 During the working session with the Vietnamese Embassy in Thailand, the delegation provided information on the socio -economic development, outstanding advantages, and investment attraction orientation of the province in the new period.
 According to the information presented, in the first nine months of 2026, Dak Lak 's export turnover to Thailand reached US$27.98 million. By September 2026, Thai investors had nine projects in the province, with a total registered capital of approximately US$76.79 million.
 This serves as a foundation for the locality to continue promoting economic and trade cooperation with Thailand. Dak Lak requested the Embassy's support in promoting the image, potential, strengths, and key products of the province; and connecting Thai businesses and investors to explore cooperation and investment opportunities in the locality.
 Vietnamese Ambassador to Thailand Pham Viet Hung highly appreciated the coordination and thorough preparation of Dak Lak province for the working trip; and expressed his hope that in the future, the province would continue to maintain close ties with the Embassy, regularly providing information on socio-economic development, trade and tourism potential so that the Embassy could support the promotion of the locality, connect with partners and create conditions for Dak Lak businesses to access and expand the market in Thailand. 
 One of the highlights of the business trip was the meeting with BJC Group of Thailand. This is a diversified business group operating in the fields of consumer goods manufacturing, food, trade, distribution, and retail.
 During the meeting, Dak Lak introduced its potential and advantages in agricultural production, raw materials, and the possibility of developing the processing industry. According to data provided by the province, the locality has 217,654 hectares of coffee, producing 580,830 tons; 41,821 hectares of durian, producing 446,214 tons; and 28,804 hectares of pepper, producing 78,745 tons.
 By October 21, 2026, the entire province will have 469 registered growing areas and 84 registered packaging facilities. These are important conditions for developing commodity production, improving traceability, and meeting the requirements of the export market.
 Taking advantage of this, the province proposed that BJC study the opportunity to invest in building a hypermarket in Dak Lak; and at the same time consider introducing key local products into the group's distribution system. The products introduced by the province include coffee, durian, pepper, green vegetables, and processed products.
 The local authorities also hope that BJC will consider investing in agricultural production and processing facilities right in the province. Following this direction, connecting raw materials with processing and distribution systems will not only help expand markets but also create conditions to enhance the value of agricultural products and better exploit the local production potential. 
 BJC highly appreciated Dak Lak's economic potential, agricultural advantages, and regional connectivity; and acknowledged the proposals and expressed a desire to continue discussions to explore suitable areas of cooperation.
 In addition to seeking partners in the distribution sector, the province is also proactively introducing specific projects to attract Thai businesses to invest.
 During the trip, the Dak Lak delegation also worked with the Board of Investment of Thailand (BOI). At this meeting, the delegation presented a list of 257 investment projects for the period 2026–2030. Among these, the province selected key projects with a total estimated investment of approximately VND 6,572 billion to connect with Thai businesses.
 The projects focus on agriculture and raw material development, industrial and logistics infrastructure, agricultural processing, trade, and services. The province also hopes to expand cooperation in the fields of energy, tourism, and resorts.
 Dak Lak's orientation is to attract investors with the appropriate capabilities, experience, and technology, especially in the field of deep processing of agricultural products and the development of infrastructure serving production and logistics. Through this, the province aims to gradually exploit raw materials effectively and increase the linkages between production, processing, and consumption.
 Representatives from BOI highly appreciated the province's potential and development orientation, and expressed their desire to continue exchanging information and connecting Thai businesses to explore the investment environment and research suitable projects in Dak Lak. 
 Alongside efforts to attract investment, the delegation also focused on finding markets for local agricultural products.
 During a meeting with the Thai Chamber of Commerce and the Thai-Vietnam Business Council (TVBC), the delegation requested support in connecting Thai importers, buyers, processors, and distributors with businesses in Dak Lak.
 The products that the province is interested in promoting include coffee, durian, fruits, pepper, macadamia nuts, OCOP products, and processed foods. The locality hopes to find partners who not only consume the products but also participate in processing and developing high value-added products.
 Notably, Ms. Jariya Chirathivat, a member of the Executive Board of the Thai Chamber of Commerce, Vice Chairperson of the Border Trade Committee (Vietnam), and Chairperson of TVBC, stated that processed coffee and macadamia products are popular among Thai consumers; several Thai businesses currently have factories processing these products.
 Initially, the Thai side wishes to connect with businesses in Dak Lak to explore and import coffee and macadamia nuts for production and processing in Thailand. The TVBC representative also requested that the province provide a list of exporting businesses to facilitate contact and discussion of specific cooperation opportunities. 
 In response, Dak Lak hopes that the Thai Chamber of Commerce and TVBC will support it in connecting with industry associations, importers, distributors, and processing businesses; sharing information on market demand, consumer trends, quality standards, and import requirements in Thailand. This will give local businesses more opportunities to access partners, understand the market, and introduce their products.
 From working sessions with the Vietnamese Embassy in Thailand, BJC Group, BOI, the Thai Chamber of Commerce, and TVBC, it is evident that Dak Lak's promotional activities are being implemented in multiple directions: promoting the local image, introducing investment projects, connecting distribution systems, and seeking partners to import agricultural products.
 The meeting was the first step for both sides to strengthen direct connections and gradually realize cooperation opportunities in the field of raw material supply and agricultural product processing.

articles.title: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion: Impressive growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion: Impressive growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Exports continue to grow.
 According to estimates from the Ministry of Industry and Trade , Vietnam's total import and export turnover in the first 10 months of 2026 reached US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. Notably, in October alone, the economy's exports reached approximately US$499 billion, an increase of 27.4% compared to the same period. This growth rate creates a favorable basis for Vietnam to strive to achieve, or even surpass, its export growth target of 15-16% in 2026.
 This import-export achievement is remarkable considering the volatile global economic and trade environment. Geopolitical conflicts, instability on international shipping routes, energy prices, inflation, and interest rates continue to put pressure on production costs, logistics, and purchasing power in many markets. Furthermore, increasingly stringent environmental standards, traceability requirements, and trade protection measures present export businesses with numerous new challenges.
 Under these circumstances, maintaining a high export growth rate demonstrates the adaptability of the economy , from production activities to market organization and the utilization of free trade agreements (FTAs).
 Export growth was recorded in both the domestic and foreign direct investment (FDI) sectors. Many major markets such as China, the United States , the EU, South Korea, and ASEAN continued to record positive growth.
 Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), noted that in recent years, Vietnam's export structure has shifted positively towards increasing the proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods, gradually reducing dependence on exports heavily reliant on resources and unskilled labor. This is the result of attracting investment, developing production, and participating more deeply in the global supply chain.
 However, despite the achievements, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed. One of the important issues is that the added value created domestically is not commensurate with the scale of export turnover, especially in some high-value sectors such as electronics, machinery and equipment, textiles, and footwear.
 In reality, surpassing the $1 trillion mark is not simply an increase in trade volume. Behind this figure lies the effort of millions of businesses, production facilities, and workers in maintaining orders, ensuring supply, seeking markets, and meeting the increasingly high standards of international partners.
 Take advantage of FTAs.
 Increasingly deep participation in the network of FTAs helps Vietnamese goods expand their market space, gain more competitive advantages in terms of tariffs, and have opportunities to participate in global supply chains.
 However, the benefits of integration lie not only in expanding markets or taking advantage of tariff preferences, but more importantly in the ability to improve production capacity, increase domestic value, and participate more deeply in the supply chain.
 Mr. Truong Van Cam, Vice President and General Secretary of the Vietnam Textile and Garment Association, believes that FTAs are creating a change in how businesses approach integration. The benefits of these agreements are not only export opportunities but also encourage businesses to invest, reorganize production, and be more proactive in securing raw materials.
 For example, the rules of origin from yarn onward in the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) create incentives for businesses to invest in yarn and fabric production, gradually developing domestic supply sources. Meanwhile, the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), with its requirement of origin from fabric onward, necessitates investment in fabric production, which remains one of the weaknesses of the textile and garment industry. The cumulation of origin mechanism for Korean fabrics also opens up opportunities for businesses to utilize raw materials that meet the conditions for preferential treatment.
 However, alongside the positive results, the fact that trade volume has exceeded $1 trillion also poses new demands for sustainable development. This requires not only growth in scale but also a continued improvement in the quality of growth, increasing the value created domestically, reducing dependence on external supply sources, and enhancing the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
 In the fourth quarter of 2026, the Ministry of Industry and Trade identified key priorities to further boost exports, diversify markets, and enhance the compliance capacity of businesses. The focus will be on effectively utilizing signed FTAs, expanding into new markets, strengthening early warning systems for trade defense cases, tariff barriers, green standards, traceability, and rules of origin. Simultaneously, support will be provided to businesses to improve product quality, build brands, and ensure transparency in the supply chain.

articles.title: Gulf Economic Resilience: How GCC Weathered US-Iran Conflict - World Economic Forum
articles.summary: Gulf Economic Resilience: How GCC Weathered US-Iran Conflict  World Economic Forum
articles.full_text:
- Efforts in the Gulf to bolster trade, digital and economic infrastructure have paid dividends while the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupted the global economic landscape
The US-Iran conflict has sent shockwaves throughout the world, adding to an already uncertain global landscape marked by shifting trade dynamics, technological disruption and economic fragmentation. Much of the coverage has centred on the vulnerability of global trade and energy networks, rising inflationary pressures and slower economic growth.
One piece of good news is the resilience demonstrated by the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) in the face of the crisis, both within their own economies and through regional cooperation.
When the conflict first began, the immediate priority in Bahrain was the safety and well-being of citizens and residents. First up was implementing precautionary measures, such as maintaining public services and ensuring access to essential healthcare, food supplies and critical infrastructure. We ensured government services stayed accessible, the private sector continued to operate, and alternative trade routes were activated – helping maintain economic activity and daily life.
This is the result of resilience-building policies and contingency plans that have been constructed over decades and have weathered their greatest stress test to date. Bahrain and its GCC neighbours have invested not only in diversifying their economies, but also in building trusted international partnerships, expanding global trade relationships and creating the institutional agility to adapt to changing conditions. Economic diversification has therefore been as much a resilience strategy as a growth strategy. Non-oil activities now make up around 55% of Saudi Arabia’s GDP and more than 75% of the UAE’s. In Bahrain, where this approach has shaped economic policy since the 1960s, the figure is 85.8%, with no single sector contributing more than 20%.
The rerouting of regional trade
Logistics is crucial to the GCC’s economy. It is also one of the sectors perhaps most affected by the conflict. Through regional coordination and contingency planning, both public infrastructure and private operators adapted rapidly, keeping vital industries running.
The King Fahd Causeway connecting Bahrain to Saudi Arabia remained open, while in parallel the GCC launched a temporary logistics fast-track scheme linking major ports and airports – using sealed trucks and exchanging documentation online – to streamline the flow of goods between member states.
This was further strengthened by the rapid launch of the Gulf Shuttle service by Mawani, the Saudi ports authority. With a capacity of up to 3,000 standard containers, the maritime route connects King Abdulaziz Port in Dammam to Khalifa Bin Salman Port in Bahrain, as well as key ports in the UAE and other neighbouring countries. This helped strengthen regional supply chains and maintain the flow of vital consumer and industrial goods across the GCC.
The private sector also stepped in to help maintain essential supplies. LuLu retail, for example, airlifted over 100 tonnes of fresh produce from international suppliers to Bahrain. This multimodal strategy made regional supply chains more resilient, maintaining the flow of vital consumer and industrial goods across the GCC.
In terms of exports, Saudi Arabia was also able to restore around 70% of oil shipments by utilizing its existing pipeline to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. By helping stabilize regional energy markets, this reduced economic pressure on the GCC as a whole. Meanwhile, state-owned Bapco Energies maintained domestic energy supply through contingency planning developed specifically for scenarios of regional disruption – an approach mirrored throughout the GCC.
The resilience of these systems was forged by cooperation at every level, from the rapid coordination between governments and infrastructure operators to deeper financial and economic integration. This included initiatives such as the $5.4 billion currency swap between the central banks of Bahrain and the UAE, designed to facilitate cross-border transactions and strengthen monetary cooperation during periods of uncertainty.
Despite the undeniable economic impact of the conflict, the bloc’s shared logistics infrastructure, joint initiatives and trade integration enabled it to adapt rapidly and mitigate some of the disruption.
Digital infrastructure for resilience
Digital infrastructure provided another layer of resilience. Across the Gulf, resilience and continuity have remained defining strengths. In Bahrain, financial services and the wider investor ecosystem continued to function without interruption, civil courts maintained proceedings remotely, and government services remained digitally accessible. Education moved online, too: Within days of the conflict starting, every school and university across the UAE switched to online, aided by routines carried over from the pandemic.
None of this was improvised. In Bahrain, the Cloud-First Policy, introduced in 2017, had already migrated approximately 85% of government operations to the cloud; coupled with nationwide 5G coverage, it kept courts sitting, classes running and payments flowing. These outcomes were made possible by years of planning, investment in infrastructure and a regulatory framework that enabled swift action when crisis struck.
Economic cushioning across the region
Alongside infrastructure resilience and regional coordination, targeted support measures played a critical role in maintaining business continuity across the GCC economy.
Dubai announced a $272 million stimulus package to support its tourism sector, while Qatar introduced a package of financial, regulatory and operational relief measures for businesses, alongside working-capital support and guarantee programmes for Qatari and Qatar-based companies. Meanwhile, Bahrain’s Labour Fund, Tamkeen, introduced a targeted finance and liquidity support package designed to assist more than 7,000 Bahraini small, medium and micro enterprises affected by the conflict.
At the same time, the Central Bank of Bahrain announced a $19 billion liquidity support package, alongside temporary loan deferrals, to reinforce financial stability and ease pressure on businesses and individuals. Central banks in the UAE and Qatar reacted in a similar fashion, easing liquidity rules and allowing loan deferrals. By the end of July, UAE banks had deferred repayments on $3.67 billion of loans for more than 135,000 customers.
These measures helped cushion the immediate economic impact of the crisis, while reinforcing confidence across the private sector. More broadly, they reflected the region’s increasingly proactive approach to economic resilience.
Signs of confidence
We are also seeing encouraging signs of continued investment across the region. Aluminium Bahrain, a Mumtalakat (Bahrain’s sovereign wealth fund) portfolio company, announced a deal worth $2.2 billion to acquire Aluminium Dunkerque – the largest aluminum smelter in the European Union. In financial services, over 60 memorandums of understanding, strategic agreements and key announcements were signed in Bahrain in October. Across the wider GCC, Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company is set to expand into global logistics, with a $300 million co-investment alongside Stonepeak to support the acquisition of Seaco, forming one of the world's largest container leasing platforms. In Saudi Arabia, Indonesia’s sovereign fund Danantara completed a $533 million deal to purchase a hotel and development plots in Mecca.
While uncertainty and disruption remain, attention is also turning to the longer term. The resilience demonstrated is now being translated into continued investment in economic diversification, stronger international partnerships and the sectors that will drive long-term growth.
In a global economy that continues to be shaped by geopolitical tension, the economies best positioned for long-term success will be those that can turn resilience and preparedness into sustained economic momentum. As we’ve seen, deals continue to be executed, partnerships are being strengthened, and investments are moving forward, reflecting long-term investor confidence in the GCC market.

articles.title: ADIPEC 2026 Day Two: Energy Infrastructure Investment and Supply Chain Resilience - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: ADIPEC 2026 Day Two: Energy Infrastructure Investment and Supply Chain Resilience - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
ADIPEC 2026 Day Two: Leaders Call for Investment in Grids, Storage and Supply Chains
Day two of ADIPEC 2026 concentrated on strengthening global energy infrastructure, with ministers, chief executives and industry leaders urging more investment in grids, transmission networks, storage and supply chains to meet rising demand and improve energy security, according to TradeArabia News Service.
Discussions at the event centred on modernising energy systems as industrial electrification, expanding economies and artificial intelligence push electricity consumption higher. Speakers stressed international collaboration, diversified supply chains and resilient infrastructure as means of ensuring reliable energy delivery amid geopolitical and logistical uncertainty.
Ministers weigh connected systems
In a ministerial panel on whether national energy strategies can deliver a connected global system, ministers examined how national priorities could be aligned to support a more connected and secure global energy system. Karim Badawi, Egypt's Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, said the world needs more energy and that unlocking and delivering it requires collaboration and partnership, adding that no single country or company can manage this alone.
Supply chain resilience in focus
Dr Christian Bruch, President and CEO of Siemens Energy, highlighted the need to strengthen local capabilities and global supply chains during his session on energy for a changing world. He indicated that new criteria are emerging in the design of energy systems and that the region would lead in building resilient systems. He also said the key question is how to ensure more resilient supply chains during global logistics disruptions, which requires understanding local capability needs, which global supply chains can be leveraged and what storage is required.
Efficiency and digitalisation
Digitalisation and energy efficiency featured prominently in discussions on meeting growing electricity demand. In a panel on energy productivity, Olivier Blum, CEO of Schneider Electric, pointed to the role of digital technologies and AI in improving consumption and system performance. He said electricity generation must increase because demand keeps rising, with industries electrifying, cities expanding and electric cars becoming more common, and that more energy must be produced while consuming it more efficiently.
The relationship between AI and energy infrastructure was explored further in a session on planning infrastructure for an accelerating growth curve. Caspar Herzberg, CEO of AVEVA, said AI requires significant power and its infrastructure is being deployed quickly while other resources and infrastructure develop more slowly, describing the challenge as one of coordination rather than simply speed.
Diversifying supply sources
Energy security and supply chain resilience were central to a CEO panel on turning disruption into advantage. Lorenzo Simonelli, Chairman and CEO of Baker Hughes, stressed the importance of diversifying supply sources and identifying vulnerabilities. He said vulnerabilities and alternatives should be examined continuously across the supply chain and logistics, with secondary, tertiary and even fourth sources of supply, and that dependence on single choke points should be avoided so that different circumstances can be navigated and addressed.
Across the exhibition halls, companies showcased technologies and capabilities spanning critical infrastructure, digitalisation, lower-carbon solutions, maritime and logistics. The event also featured 30 country pavilions highlighting national investment opportunities and industrial capabilities, alongside four specialised zones showcasing solutions across the energy value chain. Strategic Leadership Roundtables continued at the Global Energy Club, bringing together ministers, CEOs and senior industry representatives to discuss infrastructure development, investment and supply continuity.
Day three will focus on technologies transforming the energy sector, with discussions on how AI, automation and advanced analytics can improve infrastructure efficiency, intelligence and resilience.

articles.title: With imports and exports exceeding $1 trillion, how can we increase the value added to Vietnamese exports? - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: With imports and exports exceeding $1 trillion, how can we increase the value added to Vietnamese exports?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
According to Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Vietnam's total import and export turnover is estimated to exceed 1,000 billion USD after 10 months of 2026, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. This is an important milestone, reflecting the scale of trade and the increasingly deep integration of the Vietnamese economy .
 According to Mr. Son, this result stems from the recovery and sustained growth of domestic production, especially the processing and manufacturing industries – a key sector in exports.
 Along with expanding production capacity, businesses have taken advantage of opportunities from international market demand, contributing to maintaining export growth momentum.
 The foreign direct investment (FDI) sector continues to play a crucial role in key export industries such as electronics, machinery and equipment, textiles and footwear, thereby promoting Vietnam's deeper participation in global supply chains. 
 Another driving force is the exploitation of free trade agreements (FTAs), combined with the expansion and diversification of export markets.
 Besides traditional markets, Vietnamese businesses are increasingly interested in regions with significant potential such as the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
 Mr. Son assessed that the business community has demonstrated proactiveness and flexibility in the face of fluctuations in global trade, from changes in market demand and technical standards to requirements for green transitions and adjustments in trade policies of various countries.
 However, according to the Director of the Import-Export Department, a trade volume exceeding $1 trillion also places new demands on the quality of growth.
 The key is not only to continue increasing export turnover but also to enhance the value created domestically, reduce dependence on external supply sources, and improve the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
 Regarding the role of managing and supporting businesses, Mr. Nguyen Anh Son said that the Ministry of Industry and Trade has implemented many solutions to develop the market, enhance competitiveness, and remove difficulties in import and export activities.
 In this context, the Ministry of Industry and Trade focuses on supporting businesses to effectively utilize the signed FTAs, through disseminating commitments, guiding them to take advantage of tariff preferences, rules of origin, and market access opportunities.
 Trade promotion activities, business networking, and support for businesses to participate in international distribution systems continue to be implemented according to each product category and market.
 Along with maintaining traditional export markets, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is focusing on expanding into areas with significant growth potential.
 According to Mr. Son, diversifying markets not only creates more growth opportunities but also helps businesses minimize risks from fluctuations in international trade.
 The Ministry of Industry and Trade also regularly monitors production and import-export activities, identifies difficulties faced by businesses, and coordinates the handling of issues related to technical standards, trade defense, and new requirements from importing markets.
 In the coming period, one of the key tasks is to shift from simply exploiting tariff preferences to more comprehensively leveraging the opportunities that FTAs offer, especially in investment, economic cooperation, and participation in supply chains.
 Mr. Son believes that Vietnamese businesses need to continue improving their competitiveness, meeting international standards on quality, sustainable development, green transformation, and traceability.
 These are increasingly important factors for Vietnamese goods to maintain and expand their market share in the international market.
 Although the export structure has shifted positively towards increasing the proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods, Mr. Nguyen Anh Son believes that the added value created domestically is still not commensurate with the scale of export turnover.
 This is clearly evident in several high-value export sectors such as electronics, machinery, equipment, textiles, and footwear.
 According to Mr. Son, one of the bottlenecks is the limited capacity of domestic businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, to participate in global supply chains.
 Many businesses have not fully met the requirements regarding production scale, technical standards, quality management, technological innovation, and the ability to maintain a stable supply.
 Furthermore, the linkages between domestic and FDI enterprises have not met expectations. Some export sectors still depend significantly on imported raw materials and components, limiting the potential for the spillover effects of exports to the domestic business sector.
 To address these bottlenecks, the Director of the Import-Export Department emphasized the need to develop supporting industries, especially those with the potential to create high added value such as electronics, semiconductors, precision mechanics, electrical equipment, and processing industries.
 At the same time, it is necessary to support Vietnamese businesses in technological innovation, improving management capacity, meeting international standards, and gradually participating more deeply in global production chains.
 Another important solution is to promote linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises, creating conditions for Vietnamese enterprises to become suppliers in production chains, instead of mainly participating in low value-added stages.
 Regarding attracting foreign investment, Mr. Son suggested prioritizing projects with high technological content, a commitment to developing the domestic supply chain ecosystem, and creating a spillover effect on the economy.
 In the context of Vietnam's goal of double-digit economic growth, import and export continue to be identified as important drivers. However, trade growth needs to go hand in hand with improving domestic production capacity and the ability to adapt to external fluctuations.
 The Ministry of Industry and Trade will continue to coordinate with ministries, sectors, localities, and the business community to develop export markets, exploit integration opportunities, enhance competitiveness, and promote the sustainable shift in the structure of import and export.
 According to Mr. Son, the long-term goal is not only to maintain the growth rate of export turnover but also to increase the Vietnamese value content in each exported product, thereby strengthening the position of Vietnamese businesses in the international market. 
 With exports and imports exceeding 1 trillion USD, Vietnamese goods have reached more than 200 countries and territories.
 According to estimates by the Import-Export Department (Ministry of Industry and Trade), Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods in the first 10 months of 2026 will reach US$1,010.6 billion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period in 2025, surpassing the US$1,000 billion mark.
 This result marks a new stage of development in trade scale, reflecting Vietnam's production capacity, market connectivity, and increasingly deep integration into the global economy.
 Vietnam currently has trade relations with over 200 countries and territories, with goods present in many major markets in Asia, Europe, North America, Latin America, and the Middle East.
 Along with maintaining traditional markets, Vietnamese businesses are expanding exports to markets with significant potential. In this context, free trade agreements (FTAs) continue to play a crucial role, helping businesses take advantage of tariff preferences, rules of origin, and market access opportunities.
 Diversifying markets and effectively utilizing FTAs contributes to maintaining export growth momentum, reducing dependence on a few markets, and opening up more room for Vietnam's trade development after reaching the $1 trillion mark.
