articles.title: IEA: India Can Help Diversify Global Solar PV Supply Chains - TaiyangNews
articles.summary: IEA: India Can Help Diversify Global Solar PV Supply Chains  TaiyangNews
articles.full_text:
India could account for half of global module manufacturing capacity outside China by 2030, according to a new IEA report
The country could have around 135 GW of surplus module manufacturing capacity available for exports by 2030, but China will continue to dominate
Battery storage pipeline continues to expand, but financing, technology access, and project execution remain key challenges
India’s expanding solar PV manufacturing industry could play a growing role in diversifying global supply chains, as the country strengthens its position as a major manufacturing hub, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
In its India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026, the IEA identifies India as the world’s second-largest manufacturer of solar PV modules after China, with annual module manufacturing capacity reaching around 225 GW in September 2026, up from around 22 GW in 2022. It expects the country to maintain this position through 2030 as manufacturing capacity continues to expand, reaching around 250 GW by the end of this decade.
The report notes that India’s growing clean energy manufacturing base is helping diversify international supply chains. This comes as global solar manufacturing remains concentrated in China, particularly in upstream segments of the PV value chain.
The IEA credits India’s industrial policies, including the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and domestic sourcing requirements, with helping mobilize investment in solar PV manufacturing. New policy measures are also targeting strategic upstream segments, where global dependence on imports from China exceeds 95%, the IEA said.
The report focuses on India’s growing importance in the global renewable energy markets, which reduces its reliance on imported fuels. According to the report’s estimates, India’s coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million tons higher without the solar PV, wind, and bioenergy capacity added since 2010. Import dependence for electricity generation would also have exceeded 30%, approximately twice the actual level.
By 2030, the country is forecast to reach around 530 GW of renewable power capacity, with solar PV accounting for more than 80% of new additions. This also opens up new opportunities in the manufacturing space.
The IEA estimates that the country accounted for 40% of global solar module manufacturing capacity outside China and 20% of non-China cell manufacturing capacity in 2025. By 2030, these shares are expected to increase to around 50% and 30%, respectively.
The country’s installed solar PV capacity is likely to exceed 450 GW DC/350 GW AC. Analysts project that by 2030, India could have about 135 GW of surplus solar module manufacturing capacity available for export, making it the world’s second-largest potential exporter after China.
This expansion could create opportunities to serve markets seeking alternatives to Chinese solar PV products, particularly as the European Union and other regions pursue supply chain diversification policies.
China will nevertheless continue to dominate the market with almost 600 GW of spare capacity by the IEA’s estimates. Indian manufacturers will face intense competition in international markets as the report estimates about 780 GW of global module manufacturing capacity will be available for export, against an estimated global import demand of around 130 GW to 160 GW.
Globally, solar PV manufacturing capacity across the supply chain exceeded 1,200 GW in 2025, compared with approximately 630 GW DC of annual installations. China accounted for around 75% of global module manufacturing capacity, 90% of cell capacity, and 95% of wafer and polysilicon capacity.
The IEA expects intense competition in international markets to continue, with Chinese manufacturers retaining a cost advantage. Access to export markets will increasingly depend on cost competitiveness, trade policies, local-content requirements, and supply chain security regulations.
Even as China accounts for the lion’s share of global solar PV manufacturing at lower costs, the IEA estimates India’s integrated solar PV manufacturing costs to reach around $0.15/W, supported by lower labor and energy costs and economies of scale. This would be approximately 10% higher than production costs in China but lower than those in the EU and US without subsidies. However, costs remain around 70% above current global spot market prices, posing a challenge for Indian manufacturers amid global oversupply and intense price competition.
However, the IEA cautions that India’s manufacturing expansion has not been uniform across the PV value chain. While module production capacity has increased rapidly, upstream manufacturing remains underdeveloped.
India’s solar cell imports reached around $2.5 billion in 2025, with approximately 70% sourced from China. Wafer manufacturing was also in its early stages, with the country commissioning its first facility, with around 2 GW of annual capacity, in 2025. India had no operational polysilicon production facility as of 2025.
The IEA expects India’s cell manufacturing capacity to exceed 60 GW by 2030, while wafer capacity could reach around 50 GW based on announced projects. Polysilicon production could also develop sufficiently to support approximately 20 GW of integrated module production annually by the end of the decade.
It identifies technology access, financing requirements, process know-how, scale-up risks and competition from lower-cost imports as challenges to expanding upstream manufacturing. India also remains dependent on imported manufacturing equipment, process technologies and technical expertise, particularly from China.
The IEA also highlights the growing importance of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in supporting India’s renewable energy expansion. As solar and wind capacity increases, storage will be increasingly important for managing variable generation, improving grid flexibility and ensuring a reliable electricity supply.
Battery energy storage deployment in the country is also expected to accelerate, especially during the second half of this decade. According to the IEA, at the beginning of 2026, India’s installed utility-scale battery storage capacity stood at just 350 MW, of which 280 MW was commissioned in 2025.
In 2026, more than 1 GW of additional capacity is expected to come online, with annual installations projected to reach 6 GW to 8 GW by 2030 in line with the growing share of renewable energy. India’s National Electricity Plan sees battery storage capacity rising to nearly 9 GW by 2026-27, and almost 50 GW by 2031-32.
By January 2026, India’s battery storage project pipeline reached around 111 GWh, equivalent to approximately 35 GW of capacity. However, converting announced and tendered projects into operational capacity remains a challenge, the analysts caution, citing financing, grid connectivity, equipment procurement, and project execution as key bottlenecks.
“Improved auction and contract design, accelerated permitting and faster grid connection are critical to converting India’s battery storage pipeline into operating capacity,” recommend the analysts.
The complete IEA report is available on its website for free download.
To discuss India’s upstream solar PV manufacturing challenges and opportunities, TaiyangNews will host the third edition of its Solar Technology Conference.India 2027 on January 20-21 in New Delhi. Registrations will open soon.

articles.title: FTI Backs Government’s 35% EV Import Tax Hike to Support Domestic Manufacturing - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: FTI Backs Government’s 35% EV Import Tax Hike to Support Domestic Manufacturing  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
The Federation of Thai Industries backs a 35% excise tax on imported CBU EVs to ensure market fairness and drive domestic manufacturing from 2027.
The Federation of Thai Industries (FTI) has voiced strong support for the government’s policy direction to safeguard Thailand's automotive sector, endorsing the Cabinet’s decision to increase the excise tax rate on completely built-up (CBU) imported electric vehicles to 35%.
The revised tax structure—approved during an official mobile Cabinet meeting in Udon Thani on 3 November 2026—covers imported Battery Electric Vehicles (BEVs), currently taxed at 10%, and Range Extended Electric Vehicles (REEVs), currently taxed at 15%.
The measure targets imported vehicles produced abroad without domestic manufacturing presence or local content and will take effect on 1 January 2027.
Pimjai Leeissarasakul, chairwoman of the FTI, stated that the 35% excise rate is vital to ensuring trade fairness for vehicle manufacturers that have committed substantial capital to setting up physical production bases in Thailand.
She noted that the policy sends a clear message that Thailand prioritises local industrialisation, advanced technology transfer, and job creation across domestic supply chains.
Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas emphasised that the policy rewards companies that employ local workers and nurture the domestic supply network.
According to Excise Department Director-General Pornchai Thiraveja, the restructuring aligns with earlier resolutions passed by the National Electric Vehicle Policy Committee on 25 November 2025 and 10 September 2026.
"Thailand’s automotive industry accounts for 10% of GDP and supports over 800,000 jobs across the supply chain, including more than 3,000 SMEs," said Pimjai. "Once the new tax structure takes effect in 2027, automotive sector growth is projected at no less than 7%, with annual production reaching at least 1.55 million units, subject to remaining inventory imported prior to the deadline."
The tax adjustment directly supports the FTI’s "Reinvent Thailand" strategy, driven under the Joint Public and Private Sector Consultative Committee (JPPCC).
The strategy aims to transition Thailand’s automotive manufacturing from volume-driven output to high-value creation.
This framework focuses on upgrading multi-powertrain technologies—encompassing commercial pickups alongside xEV variants (BEV, HEV, PHEV, and REEV)—while fostering the production of next-generation electronic components (E-Parts) and Connected and Automated Vehicle (CAV) systems.
Looking ahead, the FTI plans to build upon the government's regulatory framework by actively expanding Thailand’s automotive ecosystem.
The federation will lead proactive investment roadshows and business-matching initiatives, inviting traditional partners from Japan, Europe, and the United States, as well as leading global technology firms, to expand local manufacturing plants and research and development (R&D) centres.
By integrating local component suppliers and SMEs into global supply chains, the FTI aims to sustainably reinforce Thailand's position as a premier global hub for automotive manufacturing and export.

articles.title: Imports and exports exceed $1 trillion: Enhancing the quality of growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports exceed $1 trillion: Enhancing the quality of growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
After 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods is estimated to exceed 1 trillion USD, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year.
This is a significant milestone, affirming the scale and increasingly deep integration of the economy. However, along with the growth in trade turnover, the need to increase added value, develop supporting industries, and strengthen the role of domestic enterprises in the global supply chain is becoming increasingly urgent. Regarding this issue, Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), shared with the press the drivers of growth, solutions for market development, and directions for improving the quality of import-export activities in the coming period.
Sir, according to estimates, after 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods exceeded US$1 trillion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. This is a particularly significant milestone for the economy . In your opinion, what are the driving forces behind this strong growth in import and export activities amidst the volatile global trade environment?
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
It can be affirmed that the fact that the total value of goods exports and imports has surpassed the 1,000 billion USD mark is an important milestone, demonstrating the scale and increasingly deep integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade.
This result is a combination of many factors. One of the key drivers is the recovery and sustained growth of domestic production, especially in the processing and manufacturing industries – the leading sectors in Vietnam's export activities. As production capacity expanded, coupled with businesses effectively capitalizing on opportunities from international market demand, export turnover continued to maintain positive growth.
At the same time, the foreign-invested enterprise sector continues to play a crucial role in key export industries such as electronics, machinery, equipment, textiles, and footwear, contributing to maintaining export growth and enabling Vietnam to participate more deeply in global supply chains.
Notably, the effective utilization of free trade agreements (FTAs), along with efforts to expand and diversify export markets, has created more opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to access larger markets. Besides traditional markets, businesses are increasingly interested in new, potentially lucrative markets in the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
Furthermore, it is impossible to overlook the proactive and flexible approach of the business community in adapting to the fluctuations of global trade, from changing market demands and technical standards requirements to green transitions and adjustments in the trade policies of various countries.
However, alongside the positive results, the fact that trade volume has exceeded $1 trillion also poses new demands for sustainable development. This requires not only growth in scale but also a continued improvement in the quality of growth, increasing the value created domestically, reducing dependence on external supply sources, and enhancing the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
To achieve import and export figures exceeding US$1 trillion, besides the efforts of the business community, the government , ministries, and agencies, especially the Ministry of Industry and Trade, have played a crucial role in managing, supporting, and creating markets. Could you share the key solutions and activities that the Ministry of Industry and Trade has implemented to promote exports, develop markets, leverage FTAs, address business difficulties, and support import and export activities in the past? What priorities will continue to be emphasized in the future?
To achieve the current import and export results, in addition to the efforts of the business community, there has been the coordinated implementation of many solutions by the Government and various ministries and agencies, with the Ministry of Industry and Trade playing a crucial role in developing markets, supporting businesses, and enhancing the competitiveness of Vietnamese goods.
Over the past period, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has focused on implementing many key solutions. One of the key areas of focus is supporting businesses in effectively utilizing the free trade agreements that Vietnam has signed. With an increasingly wide network of FTAs, the Ministry of Industry and Trade has intensified its efforts to disseminate information about commitments and guide businesses in taking advantage of tariff preferences, rules of origin, and market access opportunities.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Simultaneously, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is stepping up efforts to develop export markets, maintaining traditional markets while expanding into areas with significant potential. Trade promotion activities, business networking, and support for businesses participating in international distribution systems continue to be implemented in a focused manner, tailored to each product sector and market.

Monitoring of production and import/export activities has also been strengthened to promptly identify difficulties and obstacles faced by businesses, in order to coordinate with relevant agencies to address them, especially issues related to markets, technical standards, trade defense, and new requirements of import markets.
In the coming period, the Ministry of Industry and Trade will continue to promote the diversification of export markets and product lines, reduce dependence on a few traditional markets, and better exploit new markets.
This also involves further enhancing the effectiveness of FTAs, shifting from simply exploiting tariff preferences to comprehensively leveraging opportunities in investment, supply chains, and economic cooperation.
Another crucial requirement is to support businesses in enhancing their competitiveness, meeting the increasingly stringent demands of international markets regarding quality, technical standards, sustainable development, and green transformation. Furthermore, it is necessary to promote the development of domestic production and supporting industries, and increase the localization rate to enhance Vietnam's value in import and export activities.
Despite impressive growth rates, the current export structure still shows the dominant role of processed and manufactured industrial goods, while domestic enterprises still face numerous challenges in production capacity and participation in supply chains. According to you, what are the biggest bottlenecks that need to be addressed to increase added value, localization rates, and the actual contribution of Vietnamese enterprises to export turnover?
It can be seen that, over the years, Vietnam's export structure has shifted positively towards increasing the proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods, gradually reducing dependence on exports heavily reliant on resources and simple labor. This is the result of attracting investment, developing production, and participating more deeply in global supply chains. However, alongside the achievements, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed. articles.title: Vietnam in the wave of supply chain relocation in Southeast Asia. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Vietnam in the wave of supply chain relocation in Southeast Asia.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Amid geopolitical shifts, trade tensions, and global trends toward supply chain diversification, Southeast Asia is becoming an increasingly important destination for international investment.
Against this backdrop, Vietnam has the opportunity to attract high-tech projects, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, data centers, and logistics, while enhancing its position in the global value chain. These were the issues discussed by international leaders, experts, and business representatives at the Fortune Southeast Asia 500 Summit, organized by Fortune magazine in Ho Chi Minh City on November 3rd.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Supply chains are shifting significantly towards Southeast Asia.
Geopolitical tensions, protectionist trade policies, tariff changes, and technological competition are driving global businesses to adjust their production, sourcing, and investment strategies. The trend toward diversifying production locations, expanding supplier networks, and increasing resilience to external shocks is becoming increasingly evident.
Thomas Knudsen, Executive Chairman of Toll Group, believes that supply chains are gradually shifting from traditional manufacturing hubs to Southeast Asia. This shift from China to ASEAN will continue, while intra-regional connectivity, infrastructure development, and investment demand in the region are increasing.
According to Thomas Knudsen, building a resilient supply chain requires businesses to be flexible in choosing and combining multiple transportation methods, developing transit warehouse systems, and strengthening connectivity between countries. Southeast Asia has many advantages due to its dynamism, rapidly developing real-time payment systems, and network of free trade agreements. However, to capitalize on these advantages, the region needs to improve its connectivity with global markets and build effective bridges between the public and private sectors.
Sharing the same view on the long-term nature of the shift, James Nesbitt, Managing Director and Head of Global Corporate Clients for ASEAN at Standard Chartered Bank, noted that businesses are proactively increasing the number of suppliers, raising inventory levels, adjusting production methods, and diversifying customer markets to reduce the risk of supply chain disruptions. Security and political factors are also increasingly impacting investment decisions and production organization.
You may also like
Meanwhile, Thammasak Sethaudom, Chairman and CEO of SCG Group, believes that competitive pressure from overcapacity in China is spreading throughout the region. To adapt, businesses need to expand production scale, leverage free trade agreements, reduce costs, and increase added value. In particular, automation not only saves labor costs but also improves accuracy, product quality, energy, and raw materials. This allows businesses to focus resources on product design, research, and development, gradually moving up to higher value-added stages in the production chain.
Vietnam is ready to welcome the wave of investment.
Amidst Southeast Asia's growing role in global production and trade networks, Vietnam is considered to have favorable conditions to attract a new wave of investment, especially in high-tech, semiconductor, electronics, AI , data center, clean energy, and logistics sectors.
According to Mr. Le Tan Can, Deputy Minister of Finance, Vietnam aims to become a regional hub for artificial intelligence and data centers, and a destination for multinational corporations, investment funds, and international financial institutions. To realize this goal, Vietnam is focusing on building a new generation investment ecosystem, connecting foreign-invested enterprises with domestic businesses; while also developing logistics infrastructure, data, clean energy, and high-quality human resources.
Vietnam hopes that foreign investors will not only invest, produce, and exploit the domestic market, but also become partners in research, technological innovation, product development, and market expansion at the regional and global levels. Priority areas of cooperation include research, development, and mastery of technology; investment in high technology, semiconductors, and electronics; development of self-reliant and sustainable value chains; training of high-quality human resources; and participation in the development of international financial centers.
From a local perspective, Mr. Nguyen Loc Ha, Permanent Vice Chairman of the People's Committee of Ho Chi Minh City, emphasized that Ho Chi Minh City currently possesses many advantages in finance, trade, services, industry, high-tech industrial parks, and the Cai Mep - Thi Vai deep-water port, creating conditions for connecting production, logistics, trade, and financial service chains.
You may also like
In the first nine months of 2026, the city's GRDP increased by 9.06%; registered foreign investment reached over US$19 billion, four times higher than the same period and accounting for more than 30% of the total registered foreign investment nationwide. These are positive signs, demonstrating the interest and confidence of investors in the business environment in Ho Chi Minh City.
"Besides its advantages in market and production systems, Ho Chi Minh City aims to strengthen connections between new investors and local businesses, suppliers, and partners; promote cooperation in the fields of automation, AI, energy management, and human resource training. The city also aims to develop an international financial center, a free trade zone, logistics, and a transportation-integrated urban area. However, to effectively capitalize on the investment relocation wave, Vietnam needs not only to attract more factories but also to enhance the capacity of domestic businesses, develop supporting industries, strengthen linkages with multinational corporations, and participate more deeply in high value-added stages," Mr. Nguyen Loc Ha further informed.
According to businesses, the opportunities arising from the reshaping of global supply chains lie not only in the ability to attract investment capital but also in the capacity to transform that capital into technology, knowledge, production capacity, and added value domestically. This will be a crucial factor for Vietnam to enhance its competitiveness and strengthen its position in regional and global production and trade networks.

articles.title: Getting US trade deals to spur economic security co-operation - fDi Intelligence
articles.summary: Getting US trade deals to spur economic security co-operation  fDi Intelligence
articles.full_text:
Of the many changes the Donald Trump administration has brought to US trade policy, the one that might ultimately have the most staying power is the integration of economic security commitments into trade deals.
Washington claims to have struck around 20 tariff deals since last year. However, only 10 of these have the more formal status of Agreements on Reciprocal Trade, all of which include a dedicated section on economic security.
These commit the foreign governments to co-operating with the US on the likes of export controls, investment security and sanctions. Although not stated explicitly, such commitments are primarily aimed at countering economic and security threats from China.
But will these novel inclusions in US trade agreements actually shift governments’ behaviour? The results so far are mixed, and provide valuable lessons on how US trade leverage might best be used to advance economic security objectives.
Patchy record
Malaysia was the first country to sign a trade agreement that included binding economic security commitments with the Trump administration. These included a commitment to align with US export controls and help enforce US sanctions. Yet reports recently surfaced that Malaysia was planning a major purchase of chips produced by Huawei, the Chinese tech behemoth sanctioned by the US, to build out its RM2bn ($494mn) sovereign AI plan.
In Taiwan, however, the story is different. In its trade agreement with the Trump administration, the government committed to step up efforts to prevent the smuggling of advanced semiconductors to China and strengthen its export control regulations. Since that deal was signed in February, Taiwan has launched several new investigations into chip smuggling and in October announced plans to expand its chip export controls. Minister of economic affairs Kung Ming-hsin explained the move by telling Bloomberg that “going forward, some of our measures on controlled items will correspond to American ones because we have made quite some commitments in the Agreement on Reciprocal Trade”.
These are both developing stories. Malaysia might still reverse course and drop Huawei, while Taiwan’s newfound focus on export control enforcement could fizzle. But the divergence in these two cases helps reveal broader takeaways on when new economic security commitments in trade agreements will, or will not, deliver results.
Shared threats
One lesson is that simply writing a binding promise to align with US economic security measures into a trade deal provides no guarantee of on-the-ground policy alignment. These commitments touch on sensitive policymaking issues, and governments rightfully guard their sovereignty on matters of national security. A vague commitment in a trade pact will not trump a government’s own analyses of its national interests or convince it to fully delegate economic security decision-making to the US.
Writing a sweeping promise to align with US economic security measures into a trade deal provides no guarantee of on-the-ground policy alignment
These trade agreement commitments will be most valuable when they create frameworks and incentives for ongoing diplomatic engagement to spur co-ordinated action on shared threats. US officials were already working with their Taiwanese counterparts on chip smuggling and export control evasion when they inked their trade agreement earlier this year. The formalised commitment creates a diplomatic hook for US officials to push to strengthen this co-operation, and an impetus for Taiwan to devote more resources and political will to this policy than it otherwise would.
Trade agreements are most likely to induce economic security co-operation when governments are broadly aligned geopolitically but need a nudge to overcome policymaking inertia.
Similarly, alignment is more likely to be durable if both sides see real benefits to ongoing co-operation, rather than it being imposed on a reluctant trading partner as a one-way concession. The Malaysia trade agreement was immediately controversial because Malaysians criticised the deal for sacrificing the country’s sovereignty while producing few tangible benefits in return. Foreign governments will align with US economic security measures if they perceive these deals as facilitating trade and investment flows among trusted partners, not as imperial demands.
The coming months will provide more evidence of how well this new experiment in trade policymaking is working. The ongoing USMCA negotiations will be a key test, because US requests that Canada and Mexico align with US economic security positions are running up against those countries’ demands to maintain more sovereign, autonomous policymaking.
The trade wars of the second Trump administration have demonstrated that the appeal of the US market gives Washington significant geopolitical leverage. But translating this leverage into meaningful economic security alignment remains a work in progress.

articles.title: Thailand Hikes Excise Tax Rates for Overseas EVs to Safeguard Domestic Supply Chain - kaohoon international
articles.summary: Thailand Hikes Excise Tax Rates for Overseas EVs to Safeguard Domestic Supply Chain  kaohoon international
articles.full_text:
Mr. Ekniti Nitithanprapas, Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, disclosed that the Cabinet, during its off-site meeting in Udon Thani, had approved an increase in excise tax rates for imported electric vehicles that do not use domestically manufactured components.
The tax rate for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) manufactured overseas and imported into Thailand will rise from 10% to 35%. Meanwhile, the rate for range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs), which combine fuel and electric power but are driven exclusively by electric motors, will increase from 15% to 35%. Both changes will take effect on January 1, 2027.
Mr. Ekniti said the measure aims to strengthen Thailand’s position as a manufacturing and export hub while protecting the domestic automotive supply chain, which supports substantial employment among both Thai workers and foreign investors operating in the country.
He noted that rapid developments in the global automotive industry and the growing influx of imported vehicles had created an uneven competitive environment for manufacturers with production bases in Thailand. The government therefore intends to safeguard existing manufacturing operations while encouraging additional investment.
The Cabinet has also instructed the Excise Department to negotiate a separate tax structure offering preferential rates to companies undertaking new investments in Thailand. According to Mr. Ekniti, several prospective investors have already approached the government to discuss establishing or expanding production facilities in the country to benefit from available investment incentives.

articles.title: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion, opening up new room for growth. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Imports and exports surpass $1 trillion, opening up new room for growth.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods after 10 months of 2026 is estimated to exceed 1,000 billion USD, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year.
Speaking to the press on November 3rd, Mr. Nguyen Anh Son, Director of the Import-Export Department ( Ministry of Industry and Trade ), said that this milestone marks the need to shift from focusing on scale growth to improving the quality of trade, increasing the localization rate, and enabling Vietnamese businesses to participate more deeply in the global value chain.
Sir, according to estimates, after 10 months of 2026, Vietnam's total import and export turnover of goods exceeded US$1 trillion, an increase of 32.3% compared to the same period last year. This is a particularly significant milestone for the economy . In your opinion, what are the driving forces behind this strong growth in import and export activities amidst the volatile global trade environment?
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
It can be affirmed that the fact that the total value of goods exports and imports has surpassed the 1,000 billion USD mark is an important milestone, demonstrating the scale and increasingly deep integration of the Vietnamese economy into international trade.
This result is a combination of many factors. First and foremost is the recovery and sustained growth of domestic production, especially in the processing and manufacturing industries – the key sectors in Vietnam's export activities. As production capacity expanded, coupled with businesses effectively capitalizing on opportunities from international market demand, export turnover continued to maintain positive growth.
Secondly, the foreign-invested enterprise sector continues to play a crucial role in key export industries such as electronics, machinery, equipment, textiles, and footwear, contributing to maintaining export growth and enabling Vietnam to participate more deeply in global supply chains.
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
Thirdly, the effective utilization of free trade agreements (FTAs), along with efforts to expand and diversify export markets, has created more opportunities for Vietnamese businesses to access larger markets. Besides traditional markets, businesses are increasingly interested in new, potentially lucrative markets in the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America.
Furthermore, it is impossible to overlook the proactive and flexible approach of the business community in adapting to the fluctuations of global trade, from changing market demands and technical standards requirements to green transitions and adjustments in the trade policies of various countries.
However, alongside the positive results, the fact that trade volume has exceeded $1 trillion also poses new demands for sustainable development. This requires not only growth in scale but also a continued improvement in the quality of growth, increasing the value created domestically, reducing dependence on external supply sources, and enhancing the position of Vietnamese businesses in the global value chain.
Despite the impressive growth rate, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed, sir?
Tìm hiểu lịch sử
It can be seen that, over the years, Vietnam's export structure has shifted positively towards increasing the proportion of processed and manufactured industrial goods, gradually reducing dependence on exports that rely heavily on resources and simple labor. This is the result of attracting investment, developing production, and participating more deeply in global supply chains.
However, despite the achievements, Vietnam's export activities still have some limitations that need to be addressed. One of the important issues is that the added value created domestically is not commensurate with the scale of export turnover, especially in some high-value sectors such as electronics, machinery and equipment, textiles, and footwear.
The main reason is the limited capacity of domestic enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, to participate in global supply chains. Many businesses have not fully met the requirements regarding production scale, technical standards, quality management, technological innovation capabilities, and supply stability.
You may also like
Furthermore, the linkages between domestic and foreign-invested enterprises have not yet met expectations. Some export-oriented manufacturing sectors still rely significantly on imported raw materials and components, limiting the potential for spillover effects from export activities to the domestic business sector.
To address these issues, I believe we need to focus on several groups of solutions. First, we must continue to strongly develop supporting industries, especially in sectors with high potential for value-added creation such as electronics, semiconductors, precision mechanics, electrical equipment, and processing industries.
In addition, it is necessary to enhance the capacity of Vietnamese businesses through support for technological innovation, improved management capabilities, meeting international standards, and deeper participation in supply chains.
Promoting linkages between FDI enterprises and domestic enterprises will create conditions for Vietnamese enterprises to gradually become suppliers in global production chains, instead of only participating in low value-added stages.
In attracting foreign investment, it is necessary to continue orienting towards projects with high technological content, a commitment to developing the domestic supply chain ecosystem, and the potential to create spillover effects on the economy.
In the long term, the goal is not only to maintain the growth rate of export turnover, but more importantly to increase the Vietnamese value content in each exported product, thereby enhancing the competitiveness and position of Vietnamese businesses in international trade.
In the context of Vietnam's goal of double-digit economic growth, import and export are identified as crucial drivers. According to you, what breakthrough solutions should be focused on in the coming period to maintain the growth momentum of import and export, diversify markets, proactively secure raw material supplies, and enhance the competitiveness of Vietnamese goods?
In the context of a continuously volatile global economy, the target for import and export growth in the coming period needs to be set with higher requirements: rapid but sustainable development, growth in scale while simultaneously improving the quality and efficiency of trade activities.
In my opinion, we need to focus on several key solutions. Accordingly, we need to continue promoting the diversification of export markets. Vietnam needs to better exploit traditional markets while expanding into regions with significant potential such as the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Diversifying markets will help businesses minimize risks when international markets fluctuate.
Furthermore, it is essential to enhance the effectiveness of utilizing free trade agreements. Following the expansion of the FTA network, the current requirement is to move towards in-depth exploitation, enabling businesses not only to take advantage of tariff preferences but also to better access supply chains, investment capital flows, and business cooperation opportunities from partner markets.
In particular, enhancing domestic production capacity, especially developing supporting industries and proactively securing input material supplies, is crucial for reducing dependence on imports, improving the economy's resilience to external fluctuations, and increasing the domestic value added in exports.
Simultaneously, it is crucial to support businesses in adapting to the new demands of international trade. Markets are increasingly focused on quality standards, sustainable development, green transformation, traceability, and responsibility in the supply chain. Vietnamese businesses need to proactively enhance their capacity to meet these requirements, instead of competing solely on cost.
For the Ministry of Industry and Trade, in the coming period, it will continue to coordinate with other ministries, sectors, localities, and the business community to implement comprehensive solutions to develop export markets, support businesses in taking advantage of opportunities from integration, enhance competitiveness, and promote the sustainable shift in the structure of import and export.
The ultimate goal is not only to continue increasing import and export turnover, but also to build a trade system that is better able to adapt to global fluctuations, in which Vietnamese businesses play an increasingly larger role and create increasingly higher domestic value.

articles.title: RMG industry keeps growing despite challenges, but Bangladesh lags behind on wages - Prothom Alo English
articles.summary: RMG industry keeps growing despite challenges, but Bangladesh lags behind on wages  Prothom Alo English
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh’s garment exports continue to grow despite one crisis after another. The sector is ahead of other industries not only in business growth but also in terms of government support.
However, Bangladesh lags behind competing countries in the minimum wages paid to garment workers. Struggling to meet rising living costs amid persistent high inflation, workers have taken to the streets demanding higher wages.
According to data updated last March by Sweden-based H&M Group, one of Bangladesh’s leading buyers of readymade garments, garment workers in all seven countries—China, Cambodia, Indonesia, Vietnam, Pakistan, India and Turkey—receive higher minimum wages than workers in Bangladesh. The minimum wages in four other sectors in Bangladesh—tanneries, shipbreaking, sawmills and construction—are also higher than those in the garment industry.
In the face of workers’ protests, the Ministry of Labour formed a new wage board last Sunday. Protests have nevertheless continued in various industrial areas. Labour leaders say the unrest could have been avoided if the wage board had been formed earlier and the process of setting new wages had begun in time.
Factory owners, on the other hand, argue that workers’ wages are relatively low because of their lower productivity, the low prices of garments and narrow profit margins in garment manufacturing.
The current minimum wage for garment workers is Tk 12,500. The new wage structure came into effect on 1 December 2023. Previously, wage boards were formed every five years. The current BNP government has amended the labour law, reducing the interval for wage revisions to three years. Accordingly, the new wage structure must come into effect from December this year.
Asked for comment, Taslima Akhter, president of Garment Workers’ Solidarity, told Prothom Alo that rising prices of essential goods had made workers’ lives unbearable. They were being forced to cut food expenses.
Not only that, borrowing to meet household costs has also become more common. Workers had taken to the streets because they had reached the end of their tether, she said.
Garment exports on the rise
Bangladesh’s garment exports have grown despite at least seven major challenges over the past decade and a half. The fire at Tazreen Fashions in 2012 and the Rana Plaza collapse the following year caused a temporary downturn in garment exports. However, buyers’ confidence returned as work was undertaken to improve working conditions in garment factories. Exports also increased.
The garment industry subsequently faced a difficult period during the Covid-19 pandemic, but business recovered again. Over the past five years, the sector has sustained its exports despite the Russia-Ukraine war, political changes in the country, US reciprocal tariffs and the ongoing Middle East crisis.
Garment exports nearly doubled between 2011 and 2025. Last year, Bangladesh exported garments worth USD 38.82 billion, up 0.88 per cent from the previous year.
According to World Trade Organization (WTO) data published last July, China had the largest share of the global garment export market last year, at 27.5 per cent. Bangladesh ranked second, with a 6.76 per cent share. Vietnam accounted for 6.53 per cent, India 3 per cent and Turkey 2.3 per cent.
Tk 60 billion in tax concessions
For more than three decades, entrepreneurs in the garment industry have enjoyed various tax benefits. Citing the need to maintain their competitiveness in the global market, factory owners continue to receive tax concessions worth several billions of taka every year.
According to the latest report of the National Board of Revenue (NBR), the garment and textile sectors received corporate tax concessions worth Tk 58.29 billion in fiscal year 2022–23. This is because the garment sector has the lowest corporate tax rate among businesses, at just 12 per cent.
For environmentally friendly factories, the rate is only 10 per cent. Companies in other sectors, however, have to pay corporate tax ranging from 20 to 45 per cent.
Besides income tax concessions, the garment industry also receives cash incentives for exports to various markets. Factory owners also enjoy bonded warehouse facilities.
Under this arrangement, garment manufacturers do not have to pay customs duties or taxes on raw materials such as yarn, fabric and other goods imported from abroad. Only a handful of other sectors, including the leather industry, enjoy bonded warehouse facilities. Other sectors do not receive these benefits.
Wages lower than in competing countries
When the minimum wage of Tk 12,500 came into effect in the garment industry in December 2023, the exchange rate was Tk 110.50 to the US dollar. At that rate, the minimum wage was equivalent to USD 113. Over the past three years, the price of the dollar has risen to Tk 124. This means the minimum wage is now equivalent to USD 101.
According to H&M Group’s data from last March, however, the minimum wage for garment workers in Bangladesh is USD 102. In neighbouring India, it is USD 124. The figures for other countries are USD 294 in China, USD 208 in Cambodia, USD 172 in Indonesia, USD 163 in Vietnam and USD 135 in Pakistan.
Asked why wages are lower, Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), told Prothom Alo, "Unlike competing countries, Bangladesh has the position of helper in the garment industry. Even people with no work experience can be recruited to this position at Tk 12,500."
"Machine operators earn Tk 18,000 a month without overtime. Experienced workers earn as much as Tk 25,000. Besides, our workers are less productive than those in other countries. The comparatively low wages are also due to the fact that we produce low-priced garments and earn less from cutting and making (CM)," he added.
Cost of living has increased
Although wages in the garment industry were raised three years ago, workers have not benefited because of high inflation. Inflation rose to nearly 9.75 per cent in fiscal year 2023–24. After the government changed in August following the uprising led by students and the public, workers launched a movement demanding higher wages. In response to the movement, workers received a nine per cent annual increment in January last year, instead of five per cent.
Inflation stood at ten per cent in fiscal year 2024–25. It declined somewhat to 8.68 per cent in the outgoing fiscal year. Until last September, wage growth had remained below inflation for 56 consecutive months. After the ongoing Middle East crisis intensified, fuel price increases pushed up the prices of essential goods once again.
A survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), published last month, found that average monthly household expenditure was highest in city corporation areas, at Tk 46,778. The figure was Tk 37,344 for urban households and Tk 32,532 for rural households. At the national level, half of household expenditure goes towards food and the other half towards non-food items.
Asked for comment, Khondaker Golam Moazzem, president of the research organisation Knowledge Hub Institute Trust, told Prothom Alo, "Eleven factors are considered when setting the minimum wage, including the cost of living, inflation, wages in competing countries and productivity."
"Taking these factors into account, we said three years ago that the minimum wage needed to be Tk 17,500 to meet workers’ living costs. Given the high inflation now, there is scope for a substantial increase in wages,” he added.
Khondaker Golam Moazzem also believes that, alongside food and medical allowances, education, transport and recreation allowances should be introduced.

articles.summary: Penang Umno rep urges industrial diversification ahead of possible AI downturn  Free Malaysia Today

Reezal Merican Naina Merican (BN-Bertam) said while the global outlook for semiconductors and AI remained positive, the Penang government must recognise that every industry goes through cycles of growth and decline.
He cited recent market volatility, including a 7.57% drop in South Korea’s Kospi index on Oct 15, when shares of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell by 9.5% and 11.1%, respectively.
Reezal said the Nasdaq Composite fell by 2.6% on Oct 22, while China’s STAR Market lost more than a third of its value compared with its peak in July.
Reezal said these developments did not signal the end of the AI revolution but served as a reminder that market valuations, investor sentiment and demand could change rapidly.
“With more than 80% of Penang’s exports relying on the electrical and electronics (E&E) sector, we need to ask whether the state’s economy is sufficiently prepared for a slowdown in global demand, technological disruptions or shifts in investment priorities.
“We must prepare for the rain while the sun is still shining,” he said when debating the 2027 Penang budget in the state legislative assembly today.
He proposed a comprehensive industrial diversification strategy for the state, saying it was not intended to move Penang away from the E&E sector but to develop complementary, high-value industries based on its existing strengths.
More sectors, more local players
Reezal also proposed increasing local ownership of technology and intellectual property across the semiconductor supply chain.
He said investments in advanced manufacturing and wafer fabrication should go beyond expanding production capacity and creating jobs to include technology transfers, greater participation by local small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and the development of local startups.
Reezal, the Malaysian External Trade Development Corporation chairman, suggested that Penang look into expanding its medical technology and devices industry, which currently has about 40 multinational companies.
He said local talent should be developed in medical electronics, high-precision components, testing, product validation, research and development and specialised manufacturing.
Reezal also called for greater focus on the aerospace and avionics industries, which generated RM25.1 billion in revenue in 2024, up 38.7% from RM18.1 billion in 2023.
“Penang should seize opportunities in high-precision aerospace components, avionics, engineering services, as well as maintenance, repair and overhaul,” he said.
Reezal proposed that the state explore opportunities in green technology, the electric vehicle ecosystem and the halal economy.
He said Penang recorded RM7.68 billion in halal trade last year, placing it third behind Johor (RM34.29 billion) and Selangor (RM30.17 billion).
Penang is heavily reliant on the E&E sector, which accounts for 82.3% of the state’s total merchandise exports. The state also contributes between 56% and 60% of Malaysia’s total E&E exports.

Oil prices fell sharply Wednesday as traders weigh signs — including a widely circulated post by Vice President JD Vance — that the midterm election will add pressure on the White House to find an offramp from the Iran conflict.
Wednesday's price drop — around $8 per barrel — deepened after Vance posted on X that "everyone knows" the war is why Republicans got pummeled and "any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Sen. Chuck Schumer (D), the likely Senate majority leader in the next Congress, vowed that Democrats will push to end the war.
"This crude price drop is entirely about the U.S. election and the belief that Trump will de-escalate rather than escalate on Iran. JD Vance's statement amplified that sentiment," Ben Cahill, a nonresident senior fellow with the Atlantic Council, told Axios via email.
What they're saying: Pavel Molchanov, an analyst with Raymond James, said in remarks circulated to reporters that Vance's post was a "key catalyst" for today's oil price plunge.
"The market is saying that Congress and members of his own administration are likely to start acting as a constraint on President Trump's war in Iran," Seb Barker, a strategist with the hedge fund, Marshall Wace, tells the Financial Times.
Catch up quick: Oil prices were already falling to start the week on signs of new U.S.-Iran diplomacy.
What we're watching: "[I]t remains unclear whether Vance's comments signal a more dovish stance toward Iran," Molchanov said.
"For oil prices to sustainably move lower, a durable off-ramp is needed," he added.

articles.title: Autos hub Thailand approves steep tax hikes on imported EVs - ET Auto
articles.summary: Autos hub Thailand approves steep tax hikes on imported EVs  ET Auto
articles.full_text:
Thailand's cabinet has approved an increase in excise taxes on fully imported electric vehicles to 35 percent. This tax hike will come into effect starting January next year to encourage local production. The government aims to support the auto industry amidst competition from cheaper imports.
                                    
                    
                    
                    
                                        Thailand's cabinet on Tuesday approved an excise tax increase on fully imported battery electric vehicles to 35 per cent from 10 per cent starting January, the finance minister said, a move aimed at encouraging investment and local production.
Excise tax on imported range-extended electric vehicles would also be increased to 35 per cent from 15 per cent, Ekniti Nitithanprapas told a briefing.
In May, Thai auto industry groups warned the industry faced a crisis without changes to EV policy, as local manufacturers struggled to compete with cheaper imports from China.
The government wants to support Thailand as a production and export base, while retaining firms that employ Thai workers, Ekniti said.Thailand is a major regional hub for car manufacturers such as BYD and Toyota Motor.
Thailand's EV policy, which also includes tax breaks and price subsidies, has attracted more than $4 billion in investment, including from Chinese firms BYD and Great Wall Motor.
Cumulative investment approvals in the electric vehicle ecosystem reached $4.59 billion across 189 projects as of August 2026, according to the investment board.
EVs, hybrids and plug-in hybrids accounted for 55 per cent of Thailand's new-car registrations in the first seven months of 2026, surpassing combustion-engine vehicles for the first time, it said.

articles.title: Trump has been humiliated — will he take it out on the world? - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: Trump has been humiliated — will he take it out on the world?  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
"It's a brilliant situation."
That was Donald Trump's bizarrely upbeat summation yesterday of the politically devastating war in Iran, just before the brutal verdict of US midterm voters began rolling in.
"We seem to be getting everything we want," the US president told The Financial Times, talking up the amount of oil now flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.
American voters clearly see things differently. Fed up with what they're paying for that oil, and with another drawn-out foreign entanglement, they've taken their anger out at the ballot box with a stinging rebuke across once reliably Republican states including Texas, Iowa and Kansas.
The question now is what a weakened and famously unpredictable president does next.
Trump's immediate pledge to work with Democrats in Congress was a positive sign. How long that may last is anyone's guess.
If this election was a repudiation of the war, how will Trump respond?
The arguments inside his administration now matter even more. Vice-President JD Vance is seen to be in the de-escalation camp, preferring a negotiated settlement. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is said to favour escalation and a more intense bombing campaign.
Trump's own description of the status quo as "brilliant" suggests there are no easy answers, and he may prefer to muddle along with things as they are.
The voters have just made that considerably harder.
Cost-of-living casualties
What Trump does next won't matter just in Washington.
US allies, including Australia, are becoming increasingly outspoken about this war and its shock wave of inflation.
The Albanese government initially supported the US strikes aimed at denying Iran a nuclear capability. It didn't anticipate the economic damage this would ultimately create. Nor did it expect the conflict to drag on for nine months and counting.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers, with the authorisation of colleagues, has led the escalating rhetorical charge.
"If it was up to me, from an economic point of view, the war in the Middle East would end today," the treasurer told Radio National, "because Australians are the cost-of-living casualties of decisions taken in DC and Tehran."
After this midterm result, expect even bolder calls to end this war.
The risk for the treasurer is the louder he blames the US and Iran, the more he is seen to be passing the buck on his own responsibilities for inflation.
As the Reserve Bank governor made clear, this week's interest rate hike, the fifth this year, was not due to the "direct impact of oil prices on inflation". Michele Bullock said this was about dealing with "domestic capacity pressures".
But the Reserve Bank is hardly pretending global oil price is playing no role here. It clearly is.
Either way, the government knows it must do more to tackle inflation. It's promising spending cuts in what is now looming as a crucial mid-year budget update next month.
If Labor is judged to be unserious about this challenge, when Bullock is warning the next 12 months will "feel like a recession", the government will be in even more political strife.
Analysis from the ABC's experts
The uncertainty of the moment
But this is not as straightforward as it might seem. The economy is at a delicate point, particularly after this latest rate rise. There are real and widespread concerns within the government about cutting too hard.
The downturn in the housing market is proving sharper than was expected when the negative gearing and capital gains tax changes were announced in May. While lower house prices alone aren't seen as a problem, the impact on already soft consumer sentiment and spending is.
There's also a growing concern within the government about the jobs market deteriorating faster than was expected.
This nervousness about tipping an economy that already "feels like a recession" into an actual downturn explains the reluctance to commit to "net savings" in the budget update.
The prime minister remains confident inflation and interest rates will come down in time for the 2028 election. A recession along the way is most definitely not part of his plan.
A mid-year slash and burn to tame the inflation dragon is not on the cards.
The government is left in an awkward situation. Cut too little and look weak on inflation. Cut too hard and risk making a bad economic situation worse.
Even the Reserve Bank governor acknowledges the uncertainty of the moment.
"We do our best with our forecasts," Bullock said after delivering this week's rate hike, "but they're uncertain, and things change, and who knows?"
To all that economic uncertainty, Australia can now add another variable: a wounded Donald Trump.
"Brilliant" is hardly a word the Albanese government would use to describe this outlook.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

articles.title: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine - CNN
articles.summary: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine  CNNWorld leaders who sparred with Trump express relief mixed with caution at Republican election rout  AP NewsDemocrats seize control of Congress: How are the US and the world reacting?  CGTNWhat Trump losing power over Congress means for Iran, Ukraine and foreign policy  CNBCWhat Trump’s Midterm Defeat Means for Iran and Oil Prices  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.
For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.
Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?
Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:
Iran gloats, but gets no guarantee of peace
Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.
Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”
After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.
“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.
Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.
The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.
“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”
Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.
Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.
‘End of an era’ for US-Israel relations
In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.
Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.
“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”
Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.
“We are at the end of an era,” he said.
Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.
The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.
Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.
Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.
Ukraine waits for a post-Trump world
For Kyiv, the reaction came before the election. And on Wednesday there was relative silence.
For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.
And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.
A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.
But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.
There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.
There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. Putin has so far failed to use his apparent great ally, Trump, to secure a battlefield win of note. He may seek to change that while the embers of Trump’s authority burn.

articles.title: CANEX 2026: FG Targets Investment, Jobs, Non-Oil Export Growth Through Creative Economy - TVC News
articles.summary: CANEX 2026: FG Targets Investment, Jobs, Non-Oil Export Growth Through Creative Economy  TVC News
articles.full_text:
The Federal Government is seeking to use Nigeria’s creative industries as a stronger source of foreign exchange, investment, job creation and non-oil export earnings as Lagos prepares to host the 2026 Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) Weekend.
The four-day event, scheduled for November 5 to 8 at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and the Creative Arts, is expected to attract more than 12,000 participants from over 100 countries, providing Nigerian businesses with opportunities to connect with international investors, buyers, distributors and financiers.
Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole, said the government was focused on converting Nigeria’s global cultural influence into commercial opportunities that would generate income, expand businesses and strengthen the country’s economy.
Speaking during a television interview ahead of the event, Oduwole said Nigeria’s music, film, fashion, gastronomy and other creative products had gained international recognition, but the country needed to capture greater economic value from that popularity.
“Now we need the money to come home. We need the prosperity that the creative sector, the talents of Nigerian and African people, can bring home into the pocket,” she said.
ADVERTISEMENT
The minister explained that CANEX was designed to address some of the challenges limiting the growth of creative businesses, particularly inadequate access to finance, international markets, distribution networks and investment.
She said the event would feature deal rooms, a creative value chain and investment hub, commodities buyers’ lounge and exhibitions to connect local entrepreneurs with potential business partners.
According to her, about 20 Nigerian businesses have been selected to showcase their products at the Nigeria pavilion, while agencies including the Nigerian Export Promotion Council, Bank of Industry, Nigerian Export-Import Bank and Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria will participate in supporting businesses.
The commodities buyers’ lounge will also connect local producers with buyers and suppliers of essential inputs such as cotton, polyester and shea, with the aim of strengthening domestic production and keeping more value within the Nigerian economy.
Oduwole said the initiative would create opportunities for Nigerian manufacturers, fashion businesses and beauty-product producers to access raw materials, buyers and wider markets.
ADVERTISEMENT
She cited sportswear manufacturing, textiles, fashion and beauty products as areas where stronger local supply chains could generate employment and reduce dependence on imported finished products.
Boosting non-oil exports
The minister linked the initiative to the Federal Government’s broader economic diversification strategy, saying the creative economy offered opportunities to increase Nigeria’s non-oil exports.
She claimed that the growth rate of non-oil exports had, for the first time in Nigeria’s history, exceeded the growth rate of oil exports, attributing the development to deliberate government policies and efforts to expand access to regional markets.
Oduwole said the ministry had mapped 13 countries in Southern and Eastern Africa to identify products with export potential, including Nigerian snacks, plantain chips, zobo, chin chin, beauty products, shea-based products and fashion items.
ADVERTISEMENT
She added that services such as music, film, hospitality and event planning also offered opportunities for Nigeria to earn foreign exchange.
The minister said the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) agreement remained central to the government’s strategy of expanding market access for Nigerian businesses across the continent.
She also highlighted programmes supporting women-led enterprises, including initiatives on digital trade and export development, as part of efforts to help small businesses participate in international commerce.
Investment and jobs
Beyond exports, the government expects CANEX to attract capital into the creative sector and support businesses to expand their operations.
ADVERTISEMENT
Oduwole disclosed that the investment ambition from the previous edition was about $500 million in announced commercial partnerships and investment transactions.
She said this year’s event would build on that platform through structured engagements between entrepreneurs, investors and financial institutions.
CANEX has previously demonstrated the scale of investment interest in the sector. Its 2024 edition in Algiers, Algeria, brought together nearly 4,000 participants from 81 countries and facilitated deals worth more than $540 million, according to the African Union Commission.
The potential economic benefits extend beyond the creative professionals directly participating in the event. Increased business activity could create opportunities for manufacturers, transport operators, hotels, restaurants, technology providers, event managers and other service businesses.
The expected international attendance could also generate spending within Lagos, while new commercial partnerships could help Nigerian businesses expand production, employ more workers and reach customers outside the country.
ADVERTISEMENT
However, the minister said the ultimate objective was to ensure that businesses left the event with practical outcomes, including investment contacts, signed agreements, distribution arrangements and access to new markets.
Turning creative talent into economic value
Oduwole said the Federal Government was also strengthening intellectual property protection to ensure that creators and businesses could earn from the commercial use of their work.
She noted that the National Intellectual Property Policy, approved by the Federal Executive Council, was being implemented in collaboration with the private sector.
The issue is significant because music, films, designs, fashion and other creative products can generate substantial revenue when their ownership and commercial rights are properly protected.
ADVERTISEMENT
The African Union has also identified limited access to finance, weak intellectual property protection, fragmented markets and infrastructure gaps as major constraints on the continent’s creative industries.
Oduwole said the government hoped CANEX would help Nigerian entrepreneurs improve their competitiveness, attract quality capital and build partnerships that could sustain their businesses beyond the event.
She added that the initiative formed part of the broader ambition to build a $1 trillion Nigerian economy, stressing that economic growth would require deliberate efforts to expand productive sectors, exports and employment.
For Nigeria, the success of CANEX will therefore depend not simply on the number of international delegates attending or the scale of exhibitions, but on how much investment is secured, how many businesses gain access to new markets, and how many jobs and export opportunities emerge from the engagements.
ADVERTISEMENT
The challenge will be to translate the country’s creative popularity into measurable economic gains, with more Nigerian products and services reaching international consumers and a greater share of the resulting value retained within the domestic economy.
