articles.full_text:
News Release
U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, September 2026
The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis announced today that the goods and services deficit was $105.0 billion in September, down $0.7 billion from $105.7 billion in August, revised.
| U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services Deficit |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Deficit: | $105.0 Billion | -0.7%° | 
| Exports: | $321.5 Billion | +1.9%° | 
| Imports: | $426.6 Billion | +1.2%° | 
| Next release: Tuesday, December 8, 2026 (°) Statistical significance is not applicable or not measurable. Data adjusted for seasonality but not price changes Source: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services, November 4, 2026 |  |  | 
Exports, Imports, and Balance (exhibit 1)
September exports were $321.5 billion, $5.8 billion more than August exports. September imports were $426.6 billion, $5.2 billion more than August imports.
The September decrease in the goods and services deficit reflected a decrease in the goods deficit of $0.7 billion to $135.9 billion and a decrease in the services surplus of less than $0.1 billion to $30.9 billion.
Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit decreased $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, from the same period in 2025. Exports increased $297.3 billion or 11.6 percent. Imports increased $204.9 billion or 6.2 percent.
Three-Month Moving Averages (exhibit 2)
The average goods and services deficit increased $11.3 billion to $101.2 billion for the three months ending in September.
- Average exports increased $1.4 billion to $316.0 billion in September.
- Average imports increased $12.7 billion to $417.2 billion in September.
Year-over-year, the average goods and services deficit increased $36.5 billion from the three months ending in September 2025.
- Average exports increased $28.9 billion from September 2025.
- Average imports increased $65.4 billion from September 2025.
Exports (exhibits 3, 6, and 7)
Exports of goods increased $5.1 billion to $211.0 billion in September.
Exports of goods on a Census basis increased $5.0 billion.
- Capital goods increased $3.8 billion.
  - Computers increased $1.3 billion.
  - Computer accessories increased $0.8 billion.
  - Civilian aircraft increased $0.7 billion.
- Foods, feeds, and beverages increased $1.9 billion.
  - Soybeans increased $1.3 billion.
- Consumer goods increased $0.8 billion.
  - Pharmaceutical preparations increased $0.7 billion.
- Industrial supplies and materials decreased $1.0 billion.
  - Nonmonetary gold decreased $3.4 billion.
  - Crude oil increased $1.2 billion.
Net balance of payments adjustments increased $0.1 billion.
When incorporating the statistics in this release into BEA’s National Economic Accounts, including Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, BEA replaces exports and imports of nonmonetary gold with an adjustment calculated as the difference between domestic production and industrial use of gold. For additional information, see “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?” and “How are exports and imports of nonmonetary gold treated in BEA’s National Economic Accounts?”.
Exports of services increased $0.7 billion to $110.5 billion in September.
- Travel increased $0.3 billion.
- Charges for the use of intellectual property increased $0.1 billion.
Imports (exhibits 4, 6, and 8)
Imports of goods increased $4.4 billion to $346.9 billion in September.
Imports of goods on a Census basis increased $8.0 billion.
- Capital goods increased $11.6 billion.
  - Computers increased $7.6 billion.
  - Computer accessories increased $5.7 billion.
  - Semiconductors decreased $1.2 billion.
- Consumer goods increased $2.4 billion.
  - Pharmaceutical preparations increased $2.9 billion.
- Industrial supplies and materials decreased $3.7 billion.
  - Nonmonetary gold decreased $2.7 billion.
  - Crude oil decreased $1.3 billion.
Net balance of payments adjustments decreased $3.6 billion.
Imports of services increased $0.8 billion to $79.7 billion in September.
- Travel increased $0.5 billion.
- Transport increased $0.2 billion.
Real Goods in 2017 Dollars – Census Basis (exhibit 11)
The real goods deficit increased $3.5 billion, or 3.0 percent, to $119.5 billion in September, compared to a 2.2 percent increase in the nominal deficit. (The reason why the Census Basis nominal goods deficit increased, while the BOP nominal goods deficit decreased in September is attributable to a BOP adjustment for nonmonetary gold imports. See “How are exports and imports of gold recorded in BEA’s International Economic Accounts?”.)
- Real exports of goods increased $0.2 billion, or 0.1 percent, to $152.2 billion, compared to a 2.5 percent increase in nominal exports.
- Real imports of goods increased $3.6 billion, or 1.4 percent, to $271.6 billion, compared to a 2.4 percent increase in nominal imports.
Revisions
Revisions to August exports
- Exports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.
- Exports of services were revised up $0.3 billion.
Revisions to August imports
- Imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion.

articles.title: Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Destroyed by Mines Near Strait of Hormuz - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Iran Says Four Oil Tankers Destroyed by Mines Near Strait of Hormuz  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comIran's IRGC says two tankers and tugboat caught fire in Strait of Hormuz  ReutersIRGC: 2 tankers, tugboat attempting to use unauthorized Hormuz routes catch fire  The Times of IsraelIran Turns to Guerrilla Tactics in Bid to Reassert Grip on Strait of Hormuz  WSJFour oil tankers destroyed in Hormuz after hitting mines, Tehran says  France 24
articles.full_text:
Four oil tankers were destroyed after hitting naval mines in an area south of the Strait of Hormuz proscribed by Iran as prohibited for navigation, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, as attacks on vessels in the region intensify while crude oil flows have dipped from recent highs.
The four tankers are still ablaze, while two other vessels have been seized, the Revolutionary Guards said.
While flows have recovered substantially from the lows in the spring, the security situation in and near the Strait of Hormuz has actually deteriorated, with a higher number of attacks on tankers in recent weeks.
Following a post-war peak in September, exports of crude oil, condensate, and fuels from the Middle East slipped to 17.1 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, down from 18.9 million bpd in September, according to data from Vortexa cited by Reuters.
“October data shows Middle East seaborne oil exports have pulled back slightly from recent post-war highs on heightened risks in the Strait of Hormuz,” George Morris, an analyst at Vortexa, said in comments reported by the publication.
Kpler has tracked a 1-million-bpd drop in total crude oil and condensate exports. Crude and condensate flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Oman are estimated, provisionally, to have dropped to 16.1 million bpd in October, from 17.09 million bpd in September.
However, the tanker-tracking services caution that the numbers could be revised up as more details on shipments, especially shuttle shipments, emerge in the coming days.
Oil flows from the Middle East region have materially increased since the lows in April and May, but the heightened security concerns and intensified attacks, mines, and other explosions and incidents are making tracking shipments difficult. Tanker-trackers increasingly rely on satellite imagery to confirm movements because vessels are often switching off transponders to avoid detection when transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

articles.title: Iranian MP tells Euronews Tehran's missiles will strike Europe if US uses its bases there - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Iranian MP tells Euronews Tehran's missiles will strike Europe if US uses its bases there  Euronews.comIran war updates: Tehran warns of ‘crushing response’ if US attacks  Al JazeeraAs Democrats Sweep US Midterms, Iran's Khamenei Issues Warning To Iranians  NDTVIs Europe In Iran's Crosshairs? Tehran Hints At Wider Military Reach  Radio Free Europe/Radio LibertyIran’s war threats now reach Europe, from Cyprus to Britain  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of Iranian parliament’s security committee, said Iran would fire on any European base used against it, including in Italy and Germany. State-run media said any new confrontation could reach “the heart of Europe".
Iranian lawmakers have threatened missile strikes on European countries hosting US military bases, as state-run media warned on Wednesday that any renewed confrontation with the US could reach "the heart of Europe".
"If America uses its bases in Europe, including in Italy and Germany, Iran's missiles will be fired towards Europe," Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of parliament's National Security Committee, told Euronews.
"In the two previous wars we did not do this, but this time we will not let Europe's assistance to America for an attack on Iran go without consequence;" Ardestani added.
Asked whether Europe was entering a new phase of war with Iran, Ardestani said European countries had already been at war with Iran in the previous phase by allowing their bases to be used.
He said Iran would strike any base used against it and would also target "the material and non-material assets of countries that assist America."
A second committee member, Fada Hossein Maleki, said Iran had prepared a new approach and scenario for any renewed conflict that he believed would surprise both the US and European countries.
German embassy message
The IRGC issued a statement on Wednesday — the anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the US embassy in Tehran, marked in Iran as "the day of fighting global arrogance" — pledging "an immediate, effective response without geographical limits to every level and type of threat."
The statement cited orders attributed to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei calling for updating Iran's "target bank" and placing "the enemy's material and non-material assets within range."
Ahead of Wednesday's anniversary marches, government supporters hung a banner outside the German embassy in Tehran carrying a quote from the secretary of Iran's National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, "Europe will pay the price for supporting Israel."
IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency identified those responsible as members of the student Basij at the University of Tehran.
Euronews sought comment from the German embassy in Tehran and Germany's foreign ministry on whether the banner had been placed on the embassy railings. Both were unreachable at the time of publication.
Fars reported separately that Iran had warned Germany its military assets across the region would be treated as "legitimate defensive targets" if Berlin entered open military confrontation with Iran. The claim could not be independently verified.
Tehran has summoned Germany's ambassador in recent weeks over Berlin's support for Israel.
Kayhan newspaper, published under the supervision of a representative of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, wrote that Iran's range of potential targets was no longer confined to US bases in the Middle East and could extend to "the heart of Europe," citing an order attributed to Khamenei for a "military response without geographical limits."
Rezaei wrote on X that the US response to Iran's demands had been "not convincing," saying Washington would need to meet Iran's seven conditions in full before reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf welcomed the Republicans' defeat in Tuesday's congressional elections in a post on X, writing that the American people had "said no to war" and that Iran supported that message.
"If the US government ignores the public will in order to act in favour of managers who pay bribes and engage in international blackmail, it will realise that our 'no' comes with a nightmare," Ghalibaf added.
Asked whether he planned to take a tougher line against Iran, US President Donald Trump gave an ambiguous answer, saying he would examine the matter and act if needed.

articles.title: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes  Al JazeeraIran plays down hope for deal to end war after new U.S. strikes on eve of midterm elections  CBS NewsTehran’s factions weigh Doha talks as hardliners prepare the public for war  Iran InternationalIran Says It Would Reopen Strait of Hormuz in 2 Days as Part of U.S. Deal  The New York TimesIran says contacts over ending war continue after talks finish with no breakthrough&nbs...
articles.full_text:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process“.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
Attack on Qeshm Island
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
Tanker struck in Hormuz
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.title: Chinese fashion brands going global - The Star
articles.summary: Chinese fashion brands going global  The Star
articles.full_text:
For decades, Chinese consumer brands built their success on manufacturing scale, supply-chain efficiency and digital retail. Now, a new generation is building brands that can command attention — and premium prices — overseas.
Icicle, a Shanghai-based fashion label, is among those taking on that challenge. The company is building a globally integrated luxury fashion business — combining Chinese manufacturing capabilities with its design centers in Paris and Shanghai.
"As a global brand, we are only just beginning," said Ye Shouzeng, co-founder and CEO of Icicle. "But we are ready. We are fully prepared for globalization."
Since March 2025, the company has been part of the official presentation calendar of Paris Fashion Week, with plans to join the official show calendar next year, marking a new stage in its push to expand its presence in international markets.
Icicle's ambition reflects a broader shift among Chinese premium brands, which are increasingly seeking to export not only products, but also design, lifestyle concepts and cultural perspectives.
"We're seeing a clear acceleration of Chinese brands going overseas across apparel, leather goods and beauty," said Veronique Yang, managing director and senior partner at Boston Consulting Group Shanghai. "The previous wave was represented by companies such as Shein, which competed through an e-commerce model, or Pop Mart, which built a global following through collectible toys. This time, premium and even luxury brands are leading the way."
She said the shift has been driven by the country's increasingly sophisticated manufacturing capabilities, stronger design talent, rising cultural confidence and digital platforms that allow brands to reach overseas consumers directly.
Brands such as Songmont, which incorporates Chinese architectural and craft traditions into contemporary handbag design, and fragrance brand To Summer, which transforms ingredients such as Longjing tea and osmanthus into modern scents, represent a broader effort to create products with Chinese roots but global appeal.
Beyond exporting products
Many Chinese brands first establish themselves domestically before expanding overseas. Icicle, however, has taken a bolder approach.
Founded in Shanghai in 1997 by Ye and Tao Xiaoma, both graduates of Donghua University, Icicle was built around their belief that clothing should combine quality materials, craftsmanship and comfort.
The company opened its Paris office in 2012 and established a design center there the following year. In 2018, Icicle acquired French fashion house Carven, giving the Chinese company a foothold in the European fashion ecosystem and deeper exposure to international brand management.
Today, its collections are developed through collaboration between teams in Shanghai and Paris.
Ye believes Paris remains a critical testing ground for fashion brands seeking international recognition.
Within a few square kilometers of central Paris, Icicle now operates four boutiques, placing the brand in one of the world's most competitive fashion markets.
"If we tried to internationalize directly from Shanghai, the road would be much longer," Ye said. "France is an important global fashion center. Once we establish ourselves here, entering other markets becomes much easier."
The company's journey in Paris has been a slow climb. Global recognition must ultimately be earned through consumers, said the founder.
"The first thing is whether you can sell," he said. "If consumers don't buy your products, everything else is castles in the air."
The company has been building its presence step by step. At Le Bon Marche, one of the world's most prestigious department stores owned by LVMH, Icicle initially started with only two small display racks. After strong performance, the space expanded to three times its original size.
"The presence in Paris is like we have set up a camp at the foot of Everest," Ye said. "We have not reached the summit yet, but we have built our base here."
The company has also built a substantial domestic foundation. Icicle generates annual sales of more than 300 million euro ($334 million), growing at a double-digit rate annually and operates more than 200 stores across 100 Chinese cities.
"For now, in China, Icicle is influential — it is a relatively successful brand," he said. "Over the past 30 years, consumers in China know our products are not inexpensive, but have kept choosing us because they see the value. We have not let them down."
Yet Ye remains cautious about the company's global position.
The company strengthened its international ambitions earlier this year when Kering became a minority investor.
The partnership provides Icicle access to expertise in leather goods, eyewear, jewelry development and international retail operations as the company expands beyond apparel.
Accessories represent a major opportunity. While accessories can account for a significant share of revenue at many luxury houses, Icicle's business remains heavily concentrated in clothing, with more than 90 percent of sales coming from apparel.
"The growth potential for accessories is enormous," Ye said.
The company plans to build leather goods and accessories factories in Shanghai, extending its vertically integrated model into categories where many luxury brands have traditionally relied on specialized European suppliers.
The company has also strengthened its creative organization, recently appointing former Gucci creative director Sabato De Sarno as creative director. De Sarno will oversee creative direction across womenswear, menswear, accessories and eyewear, with his first collection expected for the autumn/winter 2027-28 season.
"In the past, Chinese companies often exported products," Yang said. "Today they are building global organizations."
Made in Shanghai
One of Icicle's biggest differences from many luxury brands is its control over manufacturing.
While many luxury companies rely heavily on external suppliers, Icicle has invested in a vertically integrated production system covering fabric research and development, material sourcing, manufacturing and retail.
More than 80 percent of its products are manufactured in-house at two production facilities in the Shanghai region.
The company sources premium natural fabrics from Italy, Japan, domestically and other markets before completing manufacturing and finishing processes in Shanghai.
For Icicle, maintaining control over production is not only about efficiency. It is about preserving craftsmanship, shortening product-development cycles and strengthening the credibility of the brand.
This approach comes at a time when luxury consumers are becoming more selective.
After several years of rapid luxury growth, the global sector has entered a more cautious period. Consumers who were previously driven by logos, trends and social visibility are increasingly looking for products with clearer value propositions — including quality materials, durability, design longevity and brand authenticity.
Many international visitors to Icicle's Paris stores are less focused on logos and more interested in fabrics, craftsmanship and comfort, the company said.
Yang of BCG said China's supply chain remains one of the country's strongest advantages.
"The global quality gap has become very small," she said. "The real advantage is flexibility. Chinese companies can respond quickly to market feedback and bring the right products to the right consumers."
Many Chinese fashion brands frequently adjust their positioning in pursuit of short-term sales growth, Yang said. Icicle, by contrast, has maintained a consistent philosophy around natural materials, understated design and comfort for more than two decades.
Icicle's new Five Elements fragrance collection reflects that philosophy.
Inspired by the traditional Chinese concept of metal, wood, water, fire and earth, the collection does not simply translate the concepts into English. Instead, the company uses Chinese pinyin — "jin, mu, shui, huo, tu" — preserving the cultural roots while presenting them through a contemporary format.
The "wood" fragrance captures the freshness and vitality of spring, while "fire" represents energy and intensity.
"Perfume is absolutely the language of French perfumery," Ye said. "A French person can understand it. But what is inside the bottle is Chinese."
A long road ahead
Despite its ambitions, Ye said that becoming a global luxury brand remains a long journey.
Yang of BCG said success cannot be measured only by overseas sales. A global premium brand must also gain recognition from consumers, retailers, fashion media and industry professionals.
A successful global brand, she said, should be able to command premium pricing outside China, enter important retail channels in fashion capitals such as Paris and Milan, and build lasting consumer loyalty.
"Icicle entering mainstream Paris retail isn't simply about selling more products," Yang said. "It shows the local market is beginning to accept the brand."
The company's goal is measured in decades. "We hope that in 10 years we can recreate another Icicle overseas," Ye said. "Only then can Icicle become a truly international brand." - China Daily/ANN

articles.title: RBA hikes interest rates amid clamour from Australian ruling elite for deeper austerity - World Socialist Web Site
articles.summary: RBA hikes interest rates amid clamour from Australian ruling elite for deeper austerity  World Socialist Web Site
articles.full_text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) increased the official interest rate by 25 basis points yesterday, taking it to 4.85 percent, the highest level since 2008.
The rate hike is one component of a multi-pronged offensive against the working class. Workers are already bearing the brunt of persistent inflation through soaring prices, especially for basic necessities. That same inflation is being invoked to justify interest rate increases that drive up mortgage repayments and deliberately suppress economic activity and employment.
At the same time, the corporate and financial elite is seizing on the economic crisis to demand sweeping cuts to social spending by the federal Labor government, which is already imposing major austerity measures.
The most immediate consequence of the rate rise will be to add around $90 a month to repayments on a $600,000 mortgage. That brings the cumulative increase from five rate rises this year to approximately $5,500 annually. Compared with the ultra-low rates prevailing before the tightening of monetary policy began in 2022, annual repayments on such a mortgage are now around $19,000 higher.
According to research firm Roy Morgan, 1.75 million Australian mortgage holders, almost one in three, were at risk of mortgage stress in September, an increase of more than half a million since January. This means their mortgage repayments had reached levels considered financially burdensome relative to household income. Of them, 1.26 million were classified as “extremely at risk.”
RBA governor Michele Bullock made clear that further hardship was in store. “Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track,” she declared in defending the rate rise at the press conference after it was announced.
The RBA sharply revised upwards its inflation forecasts, predicting that headline inflation will reach 4.5 percent by December, compared with its previous forecast of 3.6 percent. Inflation is now expected to remain above the central bank’s 2–3 percent target range until late next year.
For workers, this means further price increases on top of the enormous rises in the cost of living over the past five years. Food, housing, electricity and other necessities already consume a growing proportion of household incomes. Electricity prices alone rose 24.6 percent in the year to August, partly reflecting the withdrawal of government rebates. Even when inflation temporarily subsided, prices did not return to their previous levels.
The RBA itself pointed to the central role of war in the renewed inflationary surge, stating that “materially higher global energy prices as a result of the Middle East conflict have added to inflationary pressures.”
The criminal US-Israeli war against Iran, backed and aided by the Albanese Labor government, has already devastated the country and destabilised the global economy. Washington is now preparing to resume its bombardment, potentially as early as this week, with plans reportedly including attacks on civilian infrastructure that threaten a catastrophic escalation throughout the region.
Higher interest rates cannot reverse these war-driven shocks to the world economy. Instead, the RBA is seeking to suppress domestic economic activity and employment.
The class character of this policy was underscored by Bullock’s response to questions last week about unemployment, which has risen from 4.1 percent at the beginning of the year to 4.7 percent in September.
“We’re not worried about the pace of increase in the unemployment rate at this stage,” she declared.
The RBA now forecasts unemployment reaching 5.1 percent by late 2028, while annual economic growth slows to just 1.3 percent by the end of 2027.
Although the RBA does not forecast a recession, Bullock acknowledged that the conditions confronting millions of people would resemble one.
“Our central forecasts do not see us going into recession, but it does see growth slowing quite markedly,” she said. “It is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer.”
Higher unemployment is not simply an unintended consequence of the RBA’s policies. It is a central mechanism for suppressing wages, by increasing job insecurity and weakening the ability of workers to fight for pay rises. This comes after years of falling real wages. As of June, wages were still 1.4 percent below their level four years earlier, after accounting for inflation.
But the financial and corporate establishment is demanding a far wider offensive. Across the corporate media, business circles and parliamentary opposition, the campaign for sweeping cuts has grown to a fever pitch. Increasingly, Labor’s ability to deliver major austerity measures is being presented as the decisive political test on which its fate hangs.
Yesterday, the Australian Financial Review editorialised: “Chalmers must cut spending to solve inflation problem,” warning that without substantial cuts in December’s mid-year budget update, the RBA could raise rates again. The Australian has issued similar demands, while the Coalition denounces Labor’s supposed “spending addiction.” Economists have floated annual cuts of $7 billion to $10 billion as an alternative to another interest rate rise.
The central claim—that excessive government spending is responsible for the inflationary crisis—is contradicted by the evidence.
As economist Greg Jericho noted in Deepcut News this week, Australia has relatively low levels of taxation and public spending compared with other developed economies, reflecting a tax system that favours big business and the wealthy.
According to Jericho, government revenue would be $100 billion higher annually if Australia collected the OECD average proportion of national income. Yet while the vast profits and accumulated wealth of major corporations and the super-rich, including the gas giants, are protected, the corporate and political establishment insists that essential public services must be slashed.
Moreover, the RBA’s own assessment shows that public demand has weakened while private demand has accelerated. It forecasts business investment growing by 12 percent this year, compared with just 2.1 percent for public demand.
A significant component of this investment is concentrated in the construction of artificial intelligence data centres, which as Jericho also noted, generate relatively few permanent jobs and are bound up with the speculative AI boom fuelling the stock market bubble. The RBA itself has identified this investment as placing pressure on the economy’s productive capacity. Yet the demands for restraint are directed against public spending.
Far from being a technical problem caused by excessive spending on public services, the renewed inflationary surge is bound up with a deepening crisis of the capitalist economy, marked by war-driven price shocks, slowing growth and growing financial instability. The response of the ruling elite is to protect corporate profits and wealth through an intensified assault on workers’ social conditions.
Labor has already made clear its readiness to proceed. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has promised further cuts in December, declaring yesterday that the government would play a “helpful role” in combating inflation. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has warned of “difficult decisions” across government departments.
This follows the government’s announcement in May of approximately $63.8 billion in projected cuts over four years. That includes a $38 billion cut to the National Disability Insurance Scheme; the largest targeting a single government program in Australian history. Hundreds of thousands of vulnerable disabled people are being removed from any support, in a brutal attack that will destroy lives.
Meanwhile, Labor has increased annual military spending to record levels of around $60 billion, with hundreds of billions more earmarked for AUKUS and other measures aimed at completing Australia’s transformation into a launching pad for a US-led war against China.
The same agenda is being advanced in the November 28 Victorian election. Amid a state debt projected to approach $200 billion by 2030, more than 100 business and other prominent figures signed an open letter last week demanding that all parties commit to debt reduction.
The state Labor government has already announced more than $4 billion in cuts and public-sector job losses, while the Liberal-National Coalition proposes a decade-long hiring freeze to slash another $22 billion. One Nation, while seeking to exploit mounting social discontent, likewise advocates swinging cuts to public spending, including through the abolition of major infrastructure projects and reductions in government administration.
The mounting crisis of the political establishment, evident in the Victorian election and federally, is being driven by mass hostility to the relentless assault on workers’ jobs, wages and social conditions. Labor and the other major parties are pursuing the same essential agenda of austerity and militarism being implemented by capitalist governments internationally, amid a deepening global economic crisis.
This hostility will increasingly find expression in major struggles of the working class, as is already emerging in France and across Europe. Such struggles can only be taken forward through an independent socialist perspective directed against the capitalist system itself, the source of the economic crisis, social inequality and war.
Authorised by Cheryl Crisp for the Socialist Equality Party, Level 1/457-459 Elizabeth Street, Surry Hills, NSW, 2010, Australia.

articles.title: Thailand targets Japanese investment in semiconductors and automotive manufacturing - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: Thailand targets Japanese investment in semiconductors and automotive manufacturing  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas will lead a Thai government and business delegation to Japan from November 18–20, 2026, to strengthen investment cooperation in semiconductors, automotive manufacturing and other advanced industries.
Narit Therdsteerasukdi, secretary-general of the Thailand Board of Investment (BOI), announced that the delegation would include the industry minister, the Finance Ministry’s permanent secretary, the Customs Department’s director-general and representatives of the Joint Standing Committee on Commerce, Industry and Banking (JSCCIB).
The heads of the Federation of Thai Industries, the Thai Chamber of Commerce and the Thai Bankers’ Association will join the mission, alongside more than 40 Thai businesspeople.
Narit described Japan as one of Thailand’s most important economic partners, having contributed to the country’s industrial development, technological capabilities and supply chains for more than 50 years.
The visit is intended to reinforce Thailand’s commitment to supporting Japanese investors while encouraging them to expand into higher-technology activities. It will also provide opportunities for Thai companies to develop partnerships with Japanese businesses in priority industries.
The delegation is scheduled to meet six Japanese automotive manufacturers with production operations in Thailand: Toyota, Honda, Isuzu, Mitsubishi, Mazda and Nissan.
Discussions will cover government measures to support the automotive industry, including changes to the vehicle tax structure aimed at ensuring fair competition and encouraging domestic production.
Thai officials will also outline plans to strengthen local automotive parts manufacturers and support the industry's transition towards new vehicle technologies.
The meetings will give Japanese manufacturers an opportunity to discuss their business strategies, future investment plans and recommendations for developing Thailand’s automotive sector.
Narit indicated that the discussions would be important in maintaining confidence in Thailand as a long-term manufacturing and investment base.
The BOI will organise a meeting under the banner of the Thailand–Japan Semiconductor Strategic Partnership, bringing together Thai officials and executives from leading Japanese semiconductor companies.
Thailand will present its recently announced National Semiconductor and Advanced Electronics Strategy, which aims to develop the country's capabilities in higher-technology industries.
The meeting will explore how Japan’s expertise in chip manufacturing can be linked to investment opportunities under Thailand’s industrial strategy.
Discussions will also address technology development, workforce training and cooperation between businesses in the two countries.
The BOI intends to gather recommendations from Japanese industry leaders to help shape future investment and technology partnerships.
The visit will mark the first time the leaders of all three JSCCIB member organisations have joined the same delegation for meetings with Japanese government agencies and businesses.
A central event will be the Thailand–Japan Investment and Business Dialogue 2026, jointly organised by the BOI and Keidanren, also known as the Japan Business Federation.
The forum will allow business leaders and entrepreneurs from both countries to exchange views on trade and investment trends and identify opportunities for cooperation.
Three sectors will receive particular attention: electric and other electrified vehicles (xEVs) and their components; supply chains serving data centres and advanced electronics; and electricity grid modernisation, including equipment used in power transmission and distribution.
The delegation is also scheduled to hold discussions with Japan’s minister of economy, trade and industry and the chairman of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO).
The talks will focus on investment promotion, Thailand’s readiness to accommodate new projects and opportunities to upgrade Japanese companies’ manufacturing operations in Thailand.
A separate meeting with Japan’s finance minister will examine longer-term economic and investment cooperation.
One area for discussion will be Japan’s Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia), an initiative intended to strengthen energy security and supply chain resilience among Asian partners.
Thailand hopes to explore how the framework could support further Japanese investment and the transition towards cleaner energy in the country.
Narit emphasised that bringing together senior government officials and the three major Thai business organisations would demonstrate Thailand’s commitment to its economic relationship with Japan.
“This joint government-private sector roadshow sends a strong signal to Japanese investors, demonstrating the government’s sincerity and determination to strengthen its economic partnership with Japan,” he said.
He added that Thailand was ready to listen to, support and grow alongside Japanese investors.
The JSCCIB would help translate policy-level cooperation into business partnerships, creating opportunities for companies in both countries to collaborate on modern industries, technology development, workforce capabilities and future supply chains.
BOI figures show that Japanese investors submitted applications for investment promotion covering 302 projects worth more than THB113.7 billion in 2025.
The proposed investment value was more than double the previous year’s figure.
During the first nine months of 2026, Japanese companies submitted applications covering another 192 projects, representing more than THB45.4 billion in proposed investment.
Most applications were concentrated in digital industries, agriculture and food, electronics and automotive manufacturing.

articles.title: The market reacts to the RBA's fifth interest rate hike of 2026 - Australian Broker
articles.summary: The market reacts to the RBA's fifth interest rate hike of 2026  Australian Broker
articles.full_text:
The nation's central bank increased the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points on Tuesday, the fifth interest rate hike of the year, bringing rates to 4.85%. That's the highest level in 18 years, equivalent to rates during the Great Financial Crisis (GFC).
And this may not be the end for 2026.
"We don't know yet how this is going to play out," RBA Governor Michele Bullock told reporters Tuesday evening after the decision was revealed. "The underlying assumption is the cash rate part, one more rise. It may work out that that doesn't work out to be enough. It doesn't mean there won't be more interest rate increases.
"I don't know what the next move will be. I don't give forward guidance," she continued. "There's now five interest rate rises in the system. The last three haven't even started to flow through yet. It is probably a good point to take stock for a minute and see what comes in, in terms of the data, see if we're traveling more or less in line with the forecast. What that means for interest rates in the future, I don't know the answer to that. But all I can say is that the board will be watching very closely. Because there is still a bit of a skew on the upside to the inflation risk. And we need to be alert to those materialising.
"Monetary policy will work, but it doesn't work instantaneously," Bullock added. "If we just let inflation run, it will just lead to much worse outcomes: much higher prices, more unemployment and lower growth. We are using the cash rate to stop that from happening. Some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track. Returning inflation to target is our priority and we will do what is necessary to achieve that. It's not a good situation to be in. and we're very uncomfortable with it. It's part of the reason why six members voted for a raise today."
Australian Broker spoke with market participants to get their thoughts on what another interest rate rise means for the nation's loan and housing markets.
Director, mortgage broker and property finance strategist at Sydney-based Strategic Asset and Equipment Finance
"The market is already pretty much close to the bottom in terms of what we're seeing from a consumer action perspective. I just think it's going to be subdued for longer now [with the fifth interest rate hike]. I still think that the market's going to be either soft or softer for the next, probably, six months. But, I mean, it's already soft out there. I have been speaking with a number of different real estate agents, and they say clients are taking a little bit more time to transact. Some people are sitting on the fence. Other people are looking at it going, well, you never know when the bottom is exactly.
The market is just sort of changing [opportunities for brokers]. Brokers are working with refinancers or upgraders. We're staying close with our existing client base and speaking with them, reviewing their loans, seeing what can be done to lower their interest rates, or refinance into another lender that's got potentially a better offer. And then, having discussions with them around what their holistic plans are over the next one, two, three, five years."
"The increase could add approximately $119 a month to repayments on a $731,000 mortgage, equivalent to the national average new owner occupier loan. Every household will experience this decision differently. A positive step borrowers can take today is to understand what it means for their repayments, their budget and their plans. A mortgage broker can review your current loan, compare alternatives and explain the costs, features and lending requirements that matter to your circumstances. You do not have to work through these decisions on your own. A broker is there to help you understand your options and move forward with confidence. For prospective buyers, the conversation starts with what they can comfortably afford, alongside what they may be eligible to borrow. For existing homeowners, a broker can explore a more competitive rate with their current lender or assess whether refinancing makes financial sense. Where refinancing is not suitable or available, that conversation still has value. A broker can help clients understand their position and, where repayment assistance is needed, engage with their lender early."
"I think momentum is going to be pretty soft for the housing market. We downgraded our forecasts for housing prices just last week, actually. We're looking for capital city housing prices to fall 13.5% from their peak in March. We've got Sydney prices falling about 15.5% from their peak. And I think probably the biggest change in our forecast was the fact that we're now more pessimistic on the smaller capitals like Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane, than we were previously. We're seeing that momentum's really come off in those cities. So I think it's going to be a challenging environment over the next half a year or so in particular. If you think about our forecast, we've got housing prices pretty weak over the first half of the year. I think as you move through the second half of the year, you'll start to get a bit of a rebound in Sydney and Melbourne in particular, because they are more rate-sensitive cities. Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide are likely to lag that recovery a little. So I would have those markets, looking soft for most of next year. But we do think that things will start picking up in late 2027 and then into 2028.
We're not forecasting a recession. I think you still have quite a few factors that are contributing to growth. We've got public demand, or government spending. We've also got the AI or data center buildout going on. These things support the economy. I think one of the themes that you're going to really see in the economy is a bifurcation of outcomes across different sectors."
Hobart-based economist
"The rate rise will put further downward pressure on house prices. Whether you think that's a bad or a good thing depends on whether you're an owner or a prospective owner. And it will almost certainly lead to unemployment getting to 5%, maybe a little higher than that, something which Michelle Bullock acknowledged was increasingly likely. And we will almost certainly have more quarters of negative growth in real per capita GDP, that is, after you strip out the impact of population growth. That is consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP. I'm not sure it means a recession. I'm not sure that's inevitable with one more increase in the cash rate, but we will certainly experience slower economic growth, weaker housing prices and higher unemployment."
Senior economist at realestate.com.au
"Higher mortgage costs will continue to weigh on household spending and work to slow economic growth, although a reasonably resilient labour market and growing incomes continue to provide an important buffer. For the housing market, another rate rise will lengthen the downturn already underway. Home prices nationally have declined for seven straight months, and are down 4.3% from peak. Further increases in mortgage rates will reduce borrowing capacities again for prospective buyers, adding to the downward pressure on home prices. However, the downturn, while brisk, remains an orderly adjustment driven by rising rates and affordability pressures, rather than a distressed housing correction. In the near-term, higher mortgage rates and very challenging housing affordability will continue to weigh on home prices; over the longer-term, structural undersupply of housing remains a long-term support for prices.”
"The pressure on household budgets, mortgage holders and consumer confidence continues to grow. For many Australians, a rate rise isn’t simply another adjustment to their repayments. It's another squeeze on already stretched household finances, discretionary spending and their ability to plan for the future. For finance brokers, it reinforces just how important our industry has become. Brokers are often the first point of contact when consumers need guidance, reassurance and options. Whether it's reviewing existing lending arrangements, refinancing, restructuring or simply helping clients understand their position, the value of good advice and genuine relationships has never been greater. But we also need to recognise the pressure this places on brokers and their businesses. Navigating changing lender policies, tighter serviceability requirements, reduced borrowing capacity, and increasingly cautious consumers requires resilience, adaptability and strong business foundations."
"Although disappointing news for mortgage holders, the decision by the RBA to raise the cash rate is unsurprising. This rate hike could add up to nearly $98 a month to repayments on a $600,000 variable-rate mortgage. On top of the September hike, that could be almost $180 per month extra in mortgage repayments. My advice to mortgage holders is that you should speak to your mortgage broker to see if your home loan is still competitive."
Asia head of rates and FX strategy at J.P. Morgan private bank
"The property market downturn and sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment, following both monetary and fiscal tightening earlier this year, constrain the room for further tightening. Against this backdrop, today’s hike is likely to mark the final one of the cycle. If near-term inflation pressures ultimately force the RBA to hike again, we think this would only increase the likelihood of a sharper slowdown and bring forward the case for rate cuts at some point in 2027.
There are several dovish signals beneath the headline hike. The decision was 6-3, with the hold camp pointing to falling house prices and rising unemployment. Governor Bullock also emphasized that the impact of the last couple of hikes 'haven’t even started to flow through yet,' which we think suggests a preference to pause and assess the cumulative impact of tightening."

articles.title: 'No need to sack the governor' and other reasons for the RBA's inflation target - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: 'No need to sack the governor' and other reasons for the RBA's inflation target  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, delivering another blow to indebted households in its efforts to squash inflation.
RBA governor Michele Bullock said inflation was too high and it had to be dragged back down into the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target range.
Headline inflation in Australia is rising at an annual pace of 4.3 per cent.
"We are not looking to tip the economy into recession if we can avoid it, but we do need to get inflation down, and we do have excess demand at the moment, so that is the key," Ms Bullock said yesterday.
But why does the RBA think annual inflation of 2 to 3 per cent is optimal?
Why does it target that particular range for inflation?
Why not inflation of less than 2 per cent? Or slightly higher at 3–4 per cent?
For a number that's so consequential, its origins are surprisingly imprecise.
Copy New Zealand's idea, but with an Australian twist
The RBA adopted its inflation target in the early 1990s.
It copied the idea from New Zealand, which pioneered the concept and became the first country in the world to formally adopt inflation targeting as we know it in 1990.
But the RBA didn't copy New Zealand's model completely.
New Zealand originally picked an inflation target of 0–2 per cent, and senior officials at the RBA thought that was misguided and wanted a different target.
Stephen Grenville, a former RBA deputy governor, recalled the history in 2023 as part of the RBA's oral history collection of interviews.
Dr Grenville worked at the RBA between 1982 and 2001 (his last five years as deputy governor).
"Any inflation target that contemplates getting to zero — or would think that being at, or near, zero is a good thing — just misunderstands the nature of inflation," he said.
"Economies work much better with a little bit of inflation so that relative prices can change, and in any case, quality improvements and a whole lot of those technical issues mean that zero makes no sense.
"So that [lower] end of the New Zealand target was wrong.
"They were also, we thought, 'inflation nutters' in that they thought inflation was the only thing that mattered,"
he said.
Miss the target and the governor gets sacked?
Dr Grenville said there were other reasons why the RBA didn't like New Zealand's 0–2 per cent target.
One reason was that New Zealand's original target was going to have "electric fences" on it — the edges, zero and two, were "very clear penalty areas" — which didn't make sense to RBA officials.
"You could have 1.9 per cent [inflation] and that was OK, but if you slipped over to 2.1 [per cent], various bad things happened, and at least initially there was talk that the governor would be sacked," Dr Grenville recalled.
In the end, New Zealand didn't go ahead with that harsh plan, but they still saw it as a very bad thing if they ever recorded an inflation number bigger than 2 per cent.
"[W]hereas we thought the proper way to think about an inflation target was like an archer's target: that an archer always aims for the centre [and] doesn't expect to hit the centre of the bullseye all the time, but consistently aims for the bullseye," Dr Grenville said.
"[We] thought the right answer was to just mention a single number — which would be the centre of the target — and there wouldn't be any electric fences.
"The presumption, of course, would be the further away you were from the bullseye, the more you needed to do as the more you were off target.
"So it was a much more graduated thing that you could be off the bullseye, and no need to sack the governor," he said.
Inflation under 2pc is too low, above 3pc is too high
That's how the RBA stumbled upon its "2–3 per cent" target.
Dr Grenville said in the early 1990s, after more than a decade of high inflation and economic disruption, RBA officials didn't think they could get Australia's annual inflation down to 2 per cent sustainably, but they still wanted to be ambitious.
"We knew we'd had 'the recession we had to have' and we were going to make a lot of progress on inflation, but we didn't think we'd get much below 3 [per cent]," he said.
"We thought to mention 2 [per cent], which by then some other central bankers were talking about and of course was the top of the New Zealand target.
"[So] 2 [per cent] would be too ambitious, but 3 [per cent] would sound like we weren't trying hard enough, so we suggested 2 to 3 [per cent, but] not as a range, and this was something we had a lot of trouble explaining.
"We didn't think we would stay within 2 to 3 [per cent], because we really thought of it as — I think Glenn [Stevens] invented the term — a 'thick point'.
"We just wanted people to be saying: 'Well, if we had a number starting with 2, most of the time we would regard that as a satisfactory outcome'.
"So that's one advance, as we saw it, over the New Zealand inflation targeting," he said.
Add a time dimension and you're sweet
Dr Grenville said the RBA also included a time dimension in its inflation target to allow for the fact that economies moved in cycles over many years.
"We somehow had to make sense of a single objective, so if people said to us 'don't you care about unemployment?', we would say 'this is where unemployment fits into our single objective,'" he said.
"The critical thing was the time dimension, and I think we were clearly the first to grapple with that idea that you had to get a time dimension into the inflation target.
"The time dimension we introduced was we wanted to get the 2 to 3 [per cent] over the course of the cycle, and that fitted with the idea that, yes, monetary policy does have some influence on the shape of the cycle.
"[And] over time, over the first four or five years of inflation targeting as it spread through more and more countries, everyone adopted our formula of 'over the course of the cycle', or gave themselves some time to get inflation back where it had to be," he said.
An eventual return to lower inflation
So there you have it.
Those are the fascinating origins of Australia's 2–3 per cent inflation target, a concept that is highly consequential in Australia's economy.
Yesterday, after the RBA lifted interest rates for the fifth time in 2026, Ms Bullock acknowledged that home loan borrowers would feel more pain from the higher rates.
But she said if inflation didn't come down, the pain of prolonged high inflation would be worse.
And she said the RBA now expected headline inflation to peak at 4.5 per cent at the end of this year [up from 4.3 per cent currently] and to not return to the RBA's 2–3 per cent inflation target band until late 2027.

articles.title: Shopping on Temu: How to separate good deals from costly mistakes before adding products to your cart - Condia
articles.summary: Shopping on Temu: How to separate good deals from costly mistakes before adding products to your cart  Condia
articles.full_text:
In October 2025, I wanted to venture into content creation, focusing on product reviews, consumer behaviour and product research. I needed a camera but had little money. After earning some money from a small gig, I went on Temu and ordered one for ₦58,000 ($39.71). It took about two weeks to arrive, but when it did, I discovered that it was faulty and performed far below my expectations. The positive customer reviews I had relied on did not reflect the product I received.
I requested a return but was told I had to cover the shipping arrangements and costs. Temu eventually issued me a partial refund of just ₦13,000 ($8.90), leaving me with a loss of ₦45,000 ($30.81) and a camera I never got to use. What looked like a bargain had become an expensive mistake, an experience I have come to call “My Temu Camera Experience.”
That is the risk of Temu online shopping when buying products online without properly checking what is being sold. Temu offers access to thousands of low-priced products, but a low price does not guarantee good quality, and a product photo is not proof of what will arrive at your door.
Read also: Six Nigerian shoppers share their Temu experience
Temu’s growth shows how popular the platform has become. In February 2026, Nigeria’s Data Protection Commission said preliminary findings indicated that Temu processed the personal information of about 12.7 million Nigerians. Sensor Tower also reported strong growth in Temu downloads across Africa in 2025, with Nigeria recording an 84-fold increase. These figures show the platform’s reach, but they do not tell us whether customers are satisfied with what they receive.
So, before adding another product to your cart, here are ten things worth understanding about shopping on Temu.
Understanding how Temu works
Temu is an online marketplace launched in 2022 and owned by PDD Holdings, the parent company of Chinese e-commerce platform Pinduoduo. It connects shoppers with merchants selling products across categories such as electronics, clothing, home appliances, beauty products, toys and accessories.
The company does not manufacture any of the products displayed on its platform. All the listings come from independent sellers and manufacturers, a large number of whom are based in China and other parts of the Asian continent. A product listed under a category on Temu may differ in quality, materials, packaging and performance from another item sold under the same category.
Temu attributes its low prices partly to a business model that connects manufacturers and sellers directly with consumers, reducing some of the costs associated with traditional retail middlemen. But low prices can also reflect cheaper materials like my Temu camera experience.
This is what happens when you shop across a marketplace of different sellers, instead of buying everything from one manufacturer.
Don’t judge a product by its price
A product listed for ₦5,000 ($3.7) may tempt you to think of it as a better deal than the one selling for ₦12,000 ($8.9) elsewhere.
But before buying, you should consider the following:
Is the cheaper product made with the same materials? Does it have the same specifications? Is it the same size? Does the price include delivery and other charges? A cheaper item that breaks after a few uses can cost more in the long run.
How about the amazing discounts you come across with on the app? Temu frequently displays reduced prices, countdowns and limited-time offers to make shoppers feel they need to buy immediately. However, a large percentage discount can be some marketing gimmicks, meaning the original price may not be genuine.
Researchers investigated by comparing the displayed recommended retail prices of 20 Temu products with prices elsewhere. For 15 products, they could not find another retailer selling them at or above the displayed recommended retail price. However, Temu said its reference prices were set by manufacturers and complied with applicable laws.
The lesson is that you should always compare the actual selling price across other stores, rather than allowing a crossed-out price or discount badge to make the decision for you.
Check the product details before buying
Sometimes, a product image can look convincing to the shopper while leaving out the details that determine whether it will work for you.
Ensure to check the dimensions, materials, weight, colour, compatibility and technical specifications. If you are buying a solar power station, for example, look beyond the advertised wattage. Check its battery capacity, output rating, charging options and the appliances it can realistically support.
For clothing, check the measurements rather than relying on labels such as small, medium or large. For phone accessories, confirm that the product supports your particular device. For furniture and storage items, check the actual dimensions before assuming they will fit your space. Buyer photographs are especially useful here.
A few minutes spent reading the listing can prevent the disappointment of receiving something that looks right in a photograph but is unsuitable in practice.
Learn how to read customer reviews
Shoppers always mistake a four- or five-star rating for the whole story. A product may have a high score but still attract complaints about durability, size, missing parts or performance.
Always read the written reviews, particularly those that include photographs or videos from buyers. These can help you compare the actual product with the seller’s promotional images.
Pay attention to recent reviews and repeated complaints. One buyer reporting a damaged item may be an isolated experience. Several buyers describing the same problem suggest a pattern worth taking seriously.
Also check how many people have written reviews about that particular product. A high rating based on very few reviews offers less evidence than a similar rating supported by hundreds of detailed customer experiences.
The aim is not to find a product with perfect reviews. It is to understand what previous buyers received, what worked, what did not and then make a decision.
Know which products to be careful about
It is true not every product carries the same level of risk. But, a decorative item that disappoints is inconvenient; a faulty charger or unsafe children’s toy can create a much bigger problem than you can imagine.
Be very cautious with baby products, children’s toys, cosmetics and skincare. These products can involve choking, chemical, electrical or other safety risks. For items that come into contact with the body or are used by children, an unknown seller and an incomplete product description should be reasons to pause.
In 2025, a European consumer group investigation involving 108 products consisting of USB chargers and baby toys from Temu and Shein found that 96.3% of the tested USB chargers and baby toys failed to meet relevant EU safety requirements. The sample covered products from both platforms, not Temu alone. The findings included concerns about dangerous toy components and chemical substances.
Read also: Shein and Temu face ban campaign in South Africa as unions warn of job losses
Before then, in August 2024, Denmark’s consumer organisation Forbrugerrådet Tænk tested 14 toys and baby products sold on Temu. Twelve failed to meet the relevant safety requirements, with problems including detachable parts that could cause choking, unsafe pacifier chains and baby carriers that could allow babies to fall out.
Also in August 2024, the same Danish consumer organisation tested six electrical products sold on Temu. All six failed compliance checks, with problems including incorrectly labelled electrical products and power supplies that could cause electric shock.
This is not a claim that every product on Temu is unsafe. It is that some purchases require more scrutiny than others, particularly when a product can affect your health or physical safety.
Watch out for misleading product listings
Sometimes the problem is not the product itself but the way it is presented.
A photograph can make a small item appear much larger. A listing can show accessories that are not included in the actual purchase. A product can resemble a popular brand without being an authentic version. In other cases, important details about materials, dimensions or functionality are missing.
Read the product title and description together. Check what is included in the package, and look for wording that distinguishes the main product from accessories or decorative items.
Be suspicious of luxury products offered at prices that seem too good to be true, particularly when the seller provides little information about the brand or product origin.
If the listing does not clearly explain what you are paying for, do not assume the missing information will work in your favour.
Understand Temu’s payment and shopping safety
A genuine Temu listing does not mean every message, promotion or website using the Temu name is genuine. Scammers can imitate online stores to collect payment details, passwords and personal information.
Use Temu’s official website or app, and avoid links from unfamiliar emails, text messages and social media accounts promising free gifts or unusually large discounts. Fake delivery notifications and customer-support messages can also be used to direct shoppers to fraudulent websites.
Keep payments and conversations within Temu. The company warns that it cannot verify or assist with transactions completed outside its platform. No seller from Temu will ask for your card details, password or verification codes through messages or email.
Use a strong, unique password and check your bank or card statements after making purchases. Also review the app’s privacy permissions and think carefully about the personal information you share.
There is a reason to take privacy seriously in Nigeria. In February 2026, the Nigeria Data Protection Commission opened an investigation into Temu’s data-processing prac

articles.title: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump’s troubles with Iran could open the door to China  The GuardianChina Won’t Bail Out Trump’s Lost War  Foreign PolicyBeijing launches diplomatic flurry amid threat of renewed U.S. war with Iran  The Washington PostChina's Wang urges Middle East dialogue in meetings with Iranian, Saudi officials  ReutersIran looks to China and Russia for leverage in US talks  Iran International
articles.full_text:
China has held a flurry of meetings with Gulf leaders in a sign that Beijing is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East.
The diplomatic salvo comes before a highly anticipated meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping when the US president is expected to attend the Apec conference in Shenzhen, China, on 18 and 19 November.
Xi held talks with Haitham bin Tariq, Oman’s sultan, in a historic state visit to Beijing on Monday.
President Xi’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, met Saudi Arabia’s national security adviser, Musaad bin Mohammed Al Aiban, and the deputy secretary of Iran’s national security council, Ali Bagheri Kani.
Haitham’s trip to Beijing is the first time that an Omani head of state has visited China since the two countries established diplomatic relations nearly 50 years ago. According to a Chinese readout of the meeting, Xi warned that the Middle East should not become an arena for “great power rivalry and geopolitical conflicts”.
He said: “China has always been actively committed to stopping conflict and promoting peace, and hopes to contribute wisdom and solutions to resolving the regional security dilemma.”
Wang said after his separate talks that China was willing to “play a constructive role in helping the region emerge from the shadow of the pandemic and achieve lasting peace and stability”. In his meeting with Bagheri Kani, Wang said China supported Iran “in safeguarding its sovereignty and security”. According to China, the Iranian official said his country looked forward to China “playing a more important role in international and regional peace”.
When the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February, China was credited with pushing Tehran toward ceasefire talks in Pakistan, bolstering its status as a regional mediator.
Beijing’s influence in the Middle East is “no longer what it used to be”, said Shen Dingli, a Shanghai-based scholar of international relations. But he added: “Given China’s increased investment and trade in the region … its influence cannot be ignored.”
As the war has dragged on, China’s diplomatic efforts have been muted. Its biggest economic leverage over Iran is the fact that it buys about 90% of the Middle Eastern country’s crude oil exports. Between April and June, it slashed its crude imports by 30%, with the total in June plunging to the lowest level in a decade. That saved the global economy from a major spike in inflation. According to some estimates, China’s cut in oil imports shaved $30 or more off barrel prices of Brent crude, a global benchmark.
Beijing has otherwise done little to broker peace in the Middle East. That is partly because it does not see the conflict as being its responsibility to resolve. In March, Wang said the war “should never have happened” and that the US and Israel would find “no popular support” for the strikes.
China is also a beneficiary from the damage that the fighting has done to the US’s global reputation.
According to findings published in July by the Pew Research Center, a Washington-based thinktank, China is now viewed more favourably than the US in a majority of 36 countries surveyed.
The pain caused by the long-term disruption to the strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which much of the world’s oil and gas flows, also poses a risk to China’s economy. Shortages of energy cause inflation, which risks reducing global demand for Chinese goods.
Tehran and Washington are locked in intensive talks to reach an agreement, which could include reopening the strait. Trump has repeatedly threatened to renew military action against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US, a move which would cause alarm in Beijing.
Trump’s desperation to reach a deal in the Middle East may also provide an opportunity for China to present itself as a regional peacemaker, bolstering Xi’s status before their meeting. Beijing brokered a detente between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023 but since then its diplomatic impact in the region has been limited.
Shen said China’s desire to improve diplomatic relations with Middle Eastern countries as well as the US were “mutually reinforcing” trends.
China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, Mao Ning, said on Monday that China would send special envoy Zhai Jun to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November.
