articles.summary: Knowing foreign markets matters for going global  China Daily Global Edition
articles.full_text:
Editor's note: As a growing number of Chinese enterprises venture abroad, understanding their role in local economies has become crucial. 21st Century Business Herald spoke to Lin Xueping, an expert of industrial studies, on what Chinese companies should focus on when they expand overseas. Below are excerpts of the interview. The views don't necessarily represent those of China Daily.
The overseas footprints of Chinese enterprises cannot be measured merely by the number of factories they have built. The more pertinent question is what role do these factories play in the local economy.
The overseas businesses of many Chinese companies still focus on establishing factories, equipment and production lines locally, which does not entail the full relocation of supply chains.
The more challenging step is to export innovation capacity alongside production. Many overseas factories of Chinese companies still depend heavily on teams back in China for R&D, design and product iteration capabilities. This model enables Chinese enterprises to set up overseas production capacity rapidly. However, these overseas factories are not yet able to operate independently and engage in local industrial innovation.
When they enter overseas markets, Chinese companies need to understand different working norms, cultures and social rules, while managing compliance, labor relations and community outreach. A company that has been supplying multinational companies or participating in the global supply chain doesn't necessarily have what it takes to operate independently overseas.
Localization is not merely about transplanting equipment and management systems, but also about understanding the host society where the business operates. Industrial parks can lend support in this regard by lowering entry barriers concerning land, factory premises and infrastructure and helping enterprises settle in faster. But they cannot resolve all the challenges. For instance, they may not be able to build stable communication channels with local governments on a company's behalf, nor automatically foster trust within communities.
Enterprises should adopt a more proactive approach to establishing essential communication channels with local media and communities. By articulating the jobs they create, the taxes they contribute and the benefits they provide to local communities, they can make their localized value tangible. Successful overseas operations demand more than legal compliance; they also require becoming an understandable and approachable part of the host society.
Treating the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation as a monolithic bloc tends to obscure the vast differences among its member economies. It encompasses mature economies such as the United States alongside some Southeast Asian economies still striving for industrialization. Chinese enterprises face diverse industrial policies, resource allocations and political and economic priorities across APEC economies.
APEC's value lies not in transforming its economies into a single customs union, but in enabling economies at various stages of development to reach a consensus and identify opportunities for cooperation in trade, investment and industrial development. Chinese enterprises should seek market opportunities while also understanding what host countries aim to gain from such investments.

articles.title: Thailand drastically increases tax on EV imports - electrive.com
articles.summary: Thailand drastically increases tax on EV imports  electrive.com
articles.full_text:
From 1 January 2027, Thailand will drastically increase the consumption tax on imported electric vehicles to 35 per cent. This affects battery-electric vehicles, which currently have a tax rate of 10 per cent, as well as range-extended electric vehicles, previously taxed at 15 per cent. The regulation targets vehicles imported as finished products or those that do not use components manufactured in Thailand.
The tax adjustment is based on decisions made in 2025 and 2026 by the National Committee for Electric Vehicle Policy. It follows significant pressure on the domestic market, as Thai industry associations warned of a crisis for local automakers, which cannot compete with the significantly cheaper imports from China. Although 2026 figures show that electromobility in Thailand experienced a surge in demand – with electrified vehicles accounting for 55 per cent of all new registrations for the first time – this growth primarily benefited imports of foreign vehicles.
To maintain the attractiveness of the industrial location, the Ministry of Finance has instructed the consumption tax authority to hold direct discussions with foreign investors and companies. Manufacturers that commit to new investments in the production or assembly of key components in Thailand can expect special tax rates from the authority.
With existing funding programmes, tax incentives, and purchase subsidies, Thailand has already attracted over €3.5 billion in investments, including from Chinese manufacturers such as BYD, Changan, and Great Wall Motor. By August 2026, approved investments in the entire electromobility ecosystem had risen to the equivalent of €4.1 billion, spread across 189 projects. The tax adjustment from 2027 aims to sustainably retain these capital inflows in the country and secure the location based on the following principle:
Investment-driven vehicle imports will be directly linked to a willingness to invest locally. This ensures Thailand does not remain merely a consumer market but establishes itself as a hub for the production and export of environmentally friendly vehicles. The strategy focuses on high local value creation by specifically increasing the share of Thai-made components to secure market shares for domestic suppliers.

articles.title: Thailand to Raise Imported EV Taxes to 35% in Push to protect Local Production - Thailand Business News
articles.summary: Thailand to Raise Imported EV Taxes to 35% in Push to protect Local Production  Thailand Business News
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK — In a major policy intervention aimed at safeguarding domestic vehicle production and encouraging localized industrial investment, the Thai cabinet has approved substantial excise tax increases on imported battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs), effective January 2027.
According to Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas, the excise tax rate on fully imported BEVs will rise sharply from 10% to 35%. Similarly, the tariff on imported REEVs will jump from 15% to 35%. The regulatory overhaul follows urgent warnings from domestic automotive industry groups, which cautioned that local manufacturers faced a severe competitive crisis due to an influx of low-cost Chinese imports under previous tax structures.
The strategic shift underscores the government’s determination to reinforce Thailand’s position as Southeast Asia’s primary automotive manufacturing and export hub—a market historically dominated by traditional Japanese original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) such as Toyota Motor, but increasingly shaped by global EV leaders like BYD.
Key Takeaways
- Significant Excise Tax Structure Shift: Excise taxes on fully imported BEVs and REEVs will increase to 35% starting in January, closing the price gap between foreign-built vehicles and locally assembled models.
- Protecting $4.5+ Billion in Capital Investments: The policy safeguards existing investments, supporting the Board of Investment’s (BOI) cumulative approval of $4.59 billion across 189 projects within the country’s EV ecosystem as of August 2026.
- Rapid Electrification Dynamics: Alternative powertrain vehicles—including BEVs, hybrids, and plug-in hybrids—accounted for 55% of all new car registrations in Thailand during the first seven months of 2026, surpassing internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles for the first time in history.
Market Implications and Economic Landscape
The updated tax policy signals a pivotal transition in Thailand’s EV roadmap from initial market penetration to localized industrialization. Early government incentives—such as direct price subsidies and lowered import tariffs—successfully catalyzed rapid consumer adoption. However, this surge in demand primarily benefited foreign assembly lines, putting immediate pressure on local supply chains and automotive component manufacturers.
By raising the barrier on completely built-up (CBU) imports, the Thai government is forcing foreign automakers to transition rapidly from importing finished vehicles to localized assembly (CKD operations). Global brands including BYD and Great Wall Motor, which have already committed substantial capital to local production facilities, stand to benefit relative to brands relying exclusively on cross-border shipments.
Chinese firms BYD and Great Wall Motor have invested in Thailand’s electric vehicle ecosystem. These investments are part of a larger wave of activity that has attracted over $4 billion into the sector.
BYD operates an electric vehicle manufacturing plant in Rayong, which began producing vehicles in 2024 and has an annual capacity of 150,000 units. Additionally, cumulative investment approvals for the electric vehicle ecosystem in Thailand reached $4.59 billion across 189 projects as of August 2026. The rise of these Chinese manufacturers has significantly increased their market share in the country, even as the government introduces new tax measures to encourage local production and protect existing supply chains.
For the local business landscape, this policy pivot offers critical support to domestic auto parts suppliers and protects employment within the manufacturing sector. As EVs now represent the majority of new vehicle registrations in the country, forcing localized production guarantees that supply chain value, technological transfer, and high-skilled labor opportunities remain within the domestic economy.

articles.title: Australia raises rates to highest level since 2008 financial crisis - Financial Times
articles.summary: Australia raises rates to highest level since 2008 financial crisis  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Australia’s central bank has raised interest rates to an 18-year high as it warned that inflation remained above target in an economy grappling with high unemployment and a collapse in house prices.
The Reserve Bank of Australia on Tuesday opted to raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points to 4.85 per cent, its fifth increase this year, as it said that the inflation outlook was now “materially higher”, with fuel, commodities and AI-related investments driving up prices.
The bank said it did not expect inflation to drop into its target range of 2 to 3 per cent — which it has been above for two years — until late next year, three quarters later than previously forecast.
Official data released last week showed underlying inflation — which strips out volatile items such as fuel — hit 3.6 per cent in the year to September, a slight increase on the month before, while overall inflation was up 4.3 per cent.
RBA governor Michele Bullock told reporters that the central bank’s fifth rate rise in 2026 reflected a worsening inflation outlook. “I know this is not the news many Australians wanted to hear but it is what is needed,” she said.
Bullock added that high inflation affected everyone, not just mortgage holders. “This is the right thing for the Australian economy,” she said.
The Australian dollar weakened as much as 0.35 per cent to under US$0.70 following the announcement of the rise, which was widely expected, and was decided in a 6-3 vote.
The latest rate move, which arrived shortly before the start of the Melbourne Cup horse race, one of Australia’s biggest annual sporting events, added to growing concerns about the health of the economy with house prices slumping and unemployment rising to 4.7 per cent last month.
It will also heap pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s government, which has signalled that it is preparing to cut public spending next month. The government has repeatedly pointed to external factors, including the war in the Middle East, as critical factors driving inflation.
Paul Bloxham, chief economist at HSBC Australia, said there was “a risk the Australian economy tips into recession”, adding: “We put the risk at a 50-50 chance.”
Bullock said the central bank’s baseline forecast did not foresee a recession but warned that, with house prices tumbling and unemployment rising, many Australians might perceive one had arrived.
“I think that is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer,” she said.
Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP, said that the cumulative rate rises would increase annual mortgage interest payments for many homeowners by A$6,600 (US$4,610) a year. “We may be close to a tipping point for some mortgage holders,” he said in a note.
The rate move also put the RBA out of step with other central banks, such as the US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, Bank of Japan and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, which opted to hold rates at recent meetings.
Bullock countered that the bank’s aggressive strategy was needed to reduce excess demand in the Australian economy. She added that the disparity between the RBA’s inflation targets and monthly readings was broadly similar across different markets.
“I wouldn’t say we’re completely Robinson Crusoe here,” she said in response to a question from the FT.

articles.full_text:
Thailand's cabinet on Tuesday approved raising the excise tax on fully imported battery electric vehicles to 35% from 10%, effective in January, Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas said.
The same 35% rate will apply to imported range-extended electric vehicles, up from 15%, he told a briefing. The government is adopting a tiered tax structure meant to pull investment into domestic assembly and keep manufacturers that employ Thai workers, the minister said.
Thailand has built itself into a regional automotive production and export base, with BYD and Toyota Motor among the manufacturers operating there. Its EV program, which combines tax incentives with price subsidies, has drawn more than $4 billion in investment, including commitments from China's BYD and Great Wall Motor. The Board of Investment counted $4.59 billion in cumulative approved investment across 189 EV-related projects as of August 2026.
Electrified models now dominate the market. EVs, hybrids and plug-in hybrids made up 55% of new-car registrations in the first seven months of 2026, overtaking combustion-engine vehicles for the first time, the board said.
The shift follows warnings from Thai auto industry groups in May that the sector faced a crisis unless EV policy changed, as local manufacturers struggled to compete with cheaper Chinese imports.

articles.summary: AerosoarX, UFORCE sign MOU on supply chain cooperation  Taipei Times
articles.full_text:
AerosoarX yesterday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Ukrainian uncrewed systems company UFORCE to explore ways to cooperate on supply chains, including finding alternative component suppliers.
The agreement established a framework in which the companies would use Taiwan’s technology and manufacturing capabilities to help UFORCE diversify its component suppliers, and build a more flexible and resilient supply chain, AerosoarX said in a statement.
The partnership comes as the global uncrewed vehicle industry faces challenges, including limited access to key components, reliance on a limited number of suppliers and uncertainty over production capacity and delivery schedules, the company said.
Photo courtesy of AerosoarX Technology
AerosoarX chairman Lo Cheng-fang (羅正方) said uncrewed systems companies worldwide are having difficulties securing reliable supplies of critical components.
Through the agreement, AerosoarX hopes to use Taiwan’s technological and manufacturing capabilities to meet UFORCE’s global needs, Lo said.
UFORCE develops uncrewed platforms for maritime, land and aerial applications, as well as artificial intelligence (AI) software and command-and-control systems.
AerosoarX said it can provide UFORCE access to Taiwan’s semiconductor, electronic component, communications and precision manufacturing industries.
It aims to improve its ability to coordinate suppliers by connecting Taiwanese manufacturers with international suppliers, while continuing to develop expertise in AI computing, advanced communications and critical components, AerosoarX said.
The agreement reflects its strategy of building international partnerships through Taiwan’s technology industry and supporting the global uncrewed vehicle industry, it added.

articles.title: Major Australian retailer David Jones folds after 188 years in operation - BBC
articles.summary: Major Australian retailer David Jones folds after 188 years in operation  BBCAustralian department store chain enters administration after 188 years  Financial TimesAustralian Chain David Jones Collapses After Almost 200 Years  Bloomberg.comDevastating scenes in David Jones store  News.com.auAustralia's 188-year-old retailer David Jones enters administration, faces sale  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Australia's oldest department store David Jones folds after 188 years
David Jones, Australia's oldest department store chain, has gone into voluntary administration, putting thousands of jobs at risk.
It comes after years of financial struggles for the 188-year-old retailer - known locally as DJs - as customers desert traditional shops for online shopping.
David Jones's physical and online stores will continue to operate while receivers FTI Consulting review the company, said voluntary administrators McGrathNicol.
"David Jones is an iconic company and so many Australians have stories and memories of visiting DJ's stores," said its CEO Erica Berthold, adding the brand has a "well-developed plan" to "reset the business for the future".
Berthold thanked "customers, our team members and our partners for their continued support of David Jones through this period".
David Jones employs about 6,000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres.
Hours before the board voted to go into administration, Scentre - which owns Westfield - said the retailer had not paid its rent for October and was "therefore in breach" of its tenancy agreement.
"We understand the current retail trading environment, rising costs, a significant and outdated retail footprint, and supply chain challenges have led to this point," said Christopher Hill from receivers FTI Consulting.
By appointing administrators and receivers, David Jones will get "breathing space" and a chance to restructure the business, Hill said.
For many Australians, David Jones - and its trademark black-and-white houndstooth design - represented luxury.
But its collapse signalled the "death knell" for the department store format, said Jana Bowden, who teaches marketing at Macquarie University's Business School.
"It was once the epitome of glamour shopping in Australia - the Aussie version of Harrods," she said, "a place you would go to see and be a part of the glitz and glamour, where you could marvel at all the premium luxury labels, and feel like you'd made it."
Visiting the flagship city stores in Sydney and Melbourne was also a ritual for many Australian families, especially to see the festive Christmas window displays.
"People would travel from hours away from the city just to see those windows and experience the magic," Bowden said, but in recent years, the brand had lost its shine.
"The city stores have retained their upper end airs and graces, but the suburban stores leave a lot to be desired – they're mundane, they lack excitement and there's definitely no glitz," she said.
During Queen Elizabeth II's first visit to Sydney in 1954, the then-27-year-old monarch attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth St store, according to the Sydney Morning Herald.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that Hangzhou Ailong Metal Products Co., Ltd. (Ailong) failed to establish its eligibility for a separate rate and, therefore, is part of the China-wide entity. The period of review (POR) is August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025. In addition, we are rescinding the review with respect to 39 companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results of review.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Krisha Hill, AD/CVD Operations, Office IV, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-4037.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i), we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty
Order
on light-walled rectangular pipe and tube (LWR pipe) from the People's Republic of China (China), including Ailong.[1]
On December 17, 2025, we released U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) information for comment.[2]
We received no comments on the CBP Data Release. On June 16, 2026, we issued an intent to rescind, in part, memorandum.[3]
We received no comments on Intent to Rescind, in Part.
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.[4]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.[5]
On June 24, 2026, we extended the preliminary results of this review to no later than November 2, 2026.[6]
Scope of the Order
The merchandise subject to this
Order
is certain welded carbon quality light-walled steel pipe and tube, of rectangular (including square) cross section, having a wall thickness of less than 4 mm.
The term carbon-quality steel includes both carbon steel and alloy steel which contains only small amounts of alloying elements. Specifically, the term carbon-quality includes products in which none of the elements listed below exceeds the quantity by weight respectively indicated: 1.80 percent of manganese, or
( printed page 69548)
2.25 percent of silicon, or 1.00 percent of copper, or 0.50 percent of aluminum, or 1.25 percent of chromium, or 0.30 percent of cobalt, or 0.40 percent of lead, or 1.25 percent of nickel, or 0.30 percent of tungsten, or 0.10 percent of molybdenum, or 0.10 percent of niobium, or 0.15 percent vanadium, or 0.15 percent of zirconium. The description of carbon-quality is intended to identify carbon-quality products within the scope. The welded carbon-quality rectangular pipe and tube subject to this
Order
is currently classified under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) subheadings 7306.61.50.00 and 7306.61.70.60. While HTSUS subheadings are provided for convenience and CBP's customs purposes, our written description of the scope of the
Order
is dispositive.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of an antidumping duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[7]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.[8]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct CBP to liquidate at the calculated antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.[9]
Commerce notified all interested parties of its intent to rescind the instant review regarding the companies listed in the Appendix because there were no reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR and invited interested parties to comment.[10]
No parties commented on Commerce's intent to rescind this review with respect to these companies. In the absence of any suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review for the companies listed in the Appendix, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and 19 CFR 351.213.
China-Wide Entity
Commerce's policy regarding conditional review of the China-wide entity applies to this administrative review.[11]
Under this policy, the China-wide entity will not be under review unless a party specifically requests, or Commerce self-initiates, a review of the entity. Because no party requested a review of the China-wide entity, the entity is not under review, and the entity's rate (
i.e.,
255.07 percent) [12]
is not subject to change.
Preliminary Results of Review
The deadline for Ailong to submit a separate rate application (SRA) or separate rate certification (SRC) was October 9, 2025, and the deadline to submit a no-shipment certification was October 25, 2026.[13]
Ailong, did not submit an SRA or SRC. Thus, Commerce preliminarily determines that Ailong has not demonstrated its eligibility for a separate rate and, therefore, Ailong is part of the China-wide entity and subject to the China-wide rate of 255.07 percent; thus, no decision memorandum accompanies this notice.
Disclosure
Normally, Commerce discloses to interested parties the calculations performed in preliminary results within five days of any public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of the notice of preliminary results in the
Federal Register

Published Document: 2026-22524 (91 FR 69534)

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) finds that revocation of the antidumping duty (AD) order on certain metal lockers and parts thereof (metal lockers) from the People's Republic of China (China) would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, at the levels indicated in the “Final Results of Sunset Review” section of this notice.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brendan Quinn, AD/CVD Operations, Office III, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-5848.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 20, 2021, Commerce published the
Order
in the
Federal Register
.[1]
On July 2, 2026, Commerce
( printed page 69535)
published the notice of initiation of this first sunset review of the
Order,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930 (the Act).[2]
On July 16, 2026, Commerce received a timely and complete notice of intent to participate in the sunset review from List Industries, Inc. (List) and Tennsco LLC (Tennsco) (collectively, the domestic interested parties), within the deadline specified in 19 CFR 351.218(d)(1)(i).[3]
The domestic interested parties claimed interested party status within the meaning of section 771(9)(C) of the Act as producers of the domestic like product.[4]
On July 31, 2026, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.218(d)(3)(i), the domestic interested parties filed a timely and adequate substantive response.[5]
Commerce did not receive a substantive response from any respondent interested party.[6]
As a result, pursuant to section 751(c)(3)(B) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(e)(1)(ii)(C)(2), Commerce conducted an expedited (120-day) sunset review of the
Order.
Scope of the Order
The products covered by this
Order
are metal lockers from China. For the full description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.[7]
Analysis of Comments Received
A complete discussion of all issues raised in this sunset review, including the likelihood of continuation or recurrence of dumping in the event of revocation of the
Order
and the magnitude of the margins likely to prevail if the
Order
were to be revoked, is provided in the accompanying Issues and Decision Memorandum.[8]
A list of the topics discussed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum is attached in the Appendix to this notice. The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be directly accessed at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Final Results of Sunset Review
Pursuant to sections 751(c)(1), 752(c)(1) and (3) of the Act, Commerce determines that revocation of the
Order
would be likely to lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, and that the magnitude of the dumping margins likely to prevail would be weighted-average dumping margins up to 322.25 percent.
This notice also serves as the only reminder to parties subject to administrative protective order (APO) of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305. Timely notification of the return or destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective, orders is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation which is subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
We are issuing and publishing these final results in accordance with sections 751(c), 752(c), and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.218 and 19 CFR 351.221(c)(5)(ii).

Published Document: 2026-22501 (91 FR 69566)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
General notice.
SUMMARY:
This document announces that U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) will conduct a test regarding the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP), a new case management system that is designed to provide a secure centralized location and standardized method for information capture, that may replace the submission of technical assistance requests by telephone or by email. This voluntary test will permit CBP to examine whether the CRTAP meets its intended use and function. This notice
( printed page 69567)
describes the test, invites trade members to participate, and sets forth participation criteria.
DATES:
The CRTAP test will commence on December 4, 2026 and will continue for a period of 45 days, subject to any extension, modification, or termination as announced in the
Federal Register
. CBP will begin to accept requests to participate in the test on November 4, 2026, and CBP will continue to accept such requests until the CRTAP test concludes. Public comments on the test are invited and may be submitted to the address set forth below until the test commences.
ADDRESSES:
Comments and questions concerning this notice or any aspect of the test, including requests to participate in the CRTAP test, may be submitted via email to
gmb.clientrepoutreach@cpb.dhs.gov,
with the subject line reading “Comments/Questions on CRTAP Test.”
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Mary Ann Morris, Client Services Division, Trade Transformation Office, Office of Trade, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, by email at
mary.ann.morris@cbp.dhs.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
Current Trade/Client Representative Case Management System
CBP's Client Services Representatives are located in the Office of Trade (OT), Trade Transformation Office (TTO), Client Services Division (CSD). CSD seeks to improve the stakeholder (trade user) experience through supporting the trade community's use of the Automated Commercial Environment (ACE) for processing cargo transactions, while also protecting the privacy of trade data. CSD operates and supports trade interaction within CBP electronic cargo processing systems by providing expertise for complex CBP trade processing problems. CSD oversees direct trade access into CBP's automated system and ensures the privacy of trade data. CSD is comprised of the following branches: (1) the Post Summary Processing Branch, (2) the Cargo Release and Partner Government Agency (PGA) Branch, (3) the Air and Truck Manifest Branch, (4) the Entry Summary and Post Summary Corrections (PSC) Branch, (5) the Automated Export System (AES) and Free Trade Zone (FTZ) Branch, and (6) the Ocean and Rail Manifest Branch.
Under the existing process, trade members contact their assigned CBP Client Representative by telephone or by email, requesting assistance in resolving technical issues the trade member may encounter and that the member is unable to resolve in-house. The Client Representative responds to trade inquiries and assists with resolving the issues. There is no centralized repository for the intake of this type of trade outreach and no feasible means of tracking the resolution of such matters.
II. General Description of the CRTAP Test
As part of its ongoing effort to modernize its client services trade interactions processes, CBP developed a case management system, entitled the Client Representative Technical Assistance Portal (CRTAP), to streamline operations by automating manual tasks and creating workflows, improve communication and collaboration throughout CSD and with the trade community, provide data analysis and measure the effectiveness of assistance provided to the trade community, and standardize the intake process for submission and resolution of technical issues.
The CRTAP test is a voluntary test that is limited to brokers, self-filers, software providers, Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ) Operators, Automated Export System (AES) users, and/or Automated Manifest Systems (AMS) users. CBP will select participants based on the eligibility criteria discussed in Section IV below. The selected participants will provide their requests for technical assistance to their CBP Client Representative through a designated web address linking them to the CRTAP. CBP Client Representatives will respond to the test participants through the CRTAP, requesting additional information, as needed, and ultimately resolving the technical issues. Once an issue is resolved, the CBP Client Representative will close out the transaction using the CRTAP. At the conclusion of the 45-day test period, CBP will examine any feedback received, assess the feasibility of the CRTAP, and determine whether expanded use of the portal is warranted.
The CRTAP test will commence 30 days from the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
. It will continue for 45-days, unless the test is extended, modified, or discontinued in a subsequent notice published in the
Federal Register
.
CBP will continuously monitor the CRTAP, examining transactions from submission to resolution, to determine whether modifications need to be made to the test while it is ongoing. Upon conclusion of the 45-day test period, CBP will determine whether the test needs to be expanded to additional users, whether the CRTAP meets the needs of CBP and the trade, and whether the CRTAP should become a permanent case management system.
IV. Eligibility Requirements and Application Process
CBP is opening the CRTAP test to a maximum of nine (9) trade members who are brokers, self-filers, software providers, FTZ Operators, AES users, and AMS users. CBP will select a variety of participants to best evaluate the functionality of the CRTAP case management system. Interested parties should apply by submitting an email to
gmb.clientrepoutreach@cbp.dhs.gov,
within 30 day

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Notice; nominations for shark stock assessment advisory panel.
SUMMARY:
NMFS solicits nominations for the Atlantic Highly Migratory
( printed page 69550)
Species (HMS) SouthEast Data, Assessment, and Review (SEDAR) Workshops Advisory Panel, also known as the “SEDAR Pool.” The SEDAR Pool is comprised of a group of individuals who, if selected, review data and advise NMFS on the scientific information, data, and models used in stock assessments for oceanic sharks in the Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of America and Caribbean Sea. NMFS is seeking nominations for a 5-year term beginning in 2027. NMFS will consider individuals with definable interests in recreational and commercial fishing and related industries, including those from the environmental community, academia, and non-governmental organizations, for membership on the SEDAR Pool.
DATES:
Submit nominations on or before December 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit nominations and request the SEDAR Pool Statement of Organization, Practices, and Procedures electronically via email to
SEDAR.pool@noaa.gov.
Karyl Brewster-Geisz or Delisse Ortiz at 301-427-8503.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
HMS fisheries (swordfish, sharks, tunas, and billfish) are managed under the 2006 Consolidated HMS Fishery Management Plan (FMP) and its amendments pursuant to the authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act; 16 U.S.C. 1801et seq.) and consistent with the Atlantic Tunas Convention Act (16 U.S.C. 971et seq.). HMS implementing regulations are at 50 CFR part 635.
Background
NMFS established the SEDAR Pool consistent with section 302(g) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. NMFS may select individuals of the SEDAR Pool to review and advise NMFS on the scientific information, data, and models used in stock assessments for oceanic sharks in the Atlantic Ocean, including the Gulf of America and Caribbean Sea. While NMFS created the SEDAR Pool specifically for consultation on Atlantic shark stock assessments, NMFS may expand consultation to other HMS, as needed.
NMFS may select individuals in the SEDAR Pool to participate in the various data and assessment workshops during the stock assessment process. The primary responsibility of selected individuals is to review and provide advice regarding the scientific information, data, and models that NMFS will use or consider for use in the relevant stock assessment. To ensure that the peer review is unbiased, individuals who participated in a data and/or assessment workshop for a particular stock assessment cannot serve as a peer reviewer for the same stock assessment. However, these individuals may be asked to attend the review workshop to answer specific questions from the reviewers concerning the data and/or assessment workshops. Members of the SEDAR Pool may serve as members of other advisory panels or committees established under section 302(g) concurrent with, or following, their service on the SEDAR Pool.
Procedures and Guidelines
A. Participants
The SEDAR Pool is comprised of individuals that represent the commercial and recreational fishing communities for Atlantic sharks, the environmental community active in the conservation and management of Atlantic sharks, and the academic community that have relevant expertise with sharks and/or stock assessment methodologies for marine fish species. Additionally, individuals who may not necessarily work directly with sharks, but who are involved in fisheries with similar life history, biology, and fishery issues may be part of the SEDAR Pool. Members of the SEDAR Pool must have demonstrated experience in the fisheries, related industries, research, teaching, writing, conservation, or management of marine organisms. The distribution of representation among the interested parties is not defined or limited.
Additional members of the SEDAR Pool may also include representatives from the 5 Atlantic Regional Fishery Management Councils, the 18 Atlantic states, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico, and the relevant interstate commissions (Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission and Gulf States Marine Fisheries Commission).
If NMFS requires additional members to ensure a diverse pool of individuals for data or assessment workshops, NMFS may request individuals to become members of the SEDAR Pool outside of the annual nomination period.
SEDAR Pool members serve at the discretion of the Secretary. Not all members will attend each SEDAR workshop. Rather, NMFS will invite certain members to participate at specific stock assessment workshops dependent on their ability to participate, discuss, and offer scientific input and advice regarding the species being assessed.
NMFS is not obligated to fulfill any requests (
e.g., requests for an assessment of a certain species) that may be made by the SEDAR Pool or its individual members. Members of the SEDAR Pool who are invited to attend stock assessment workshops will not be compensated for their services, but may be reimbursed for their travel-related expenses to attend such workshops.
B. Nomination Procedures for Appointments to the SEDAR Pool
Member tenure is 5 years. Nominations are sought for terms beginning early in 2027 and expiring at the end of 2031. Nomination packages should include:
1. The name, address, phone number, and email of the applicant or nominee;
2. A description of the applicant's or nominee's interest in Atlantic shark stock assessments or the Atlantic shark fishery;
3. A statement of the applicant's or nominee's background and/or qualifications; and
4. A written commitment that the applicant or nominee shall participate actively and in good faith in the tasks of the SEDAR Pool, as requested.
C. Meeting Schedule
Individual members of the SEDAR Pool meet to participate in stock assessments at the discretion of the Office of Sustainable Fisheries, NMFS. Stock assessment timing, frequency, and relevant species will vary depending on the needs determined by NMFS and SEDAR staff. In 2027, NMFS plans to finalize the sandbar shark stock assessment and begin the bull shark stock assessment. All meetings are open for observation by the public.
Dated: November 2, 2026.
Kelly Denit,
Director, Office of Sustainable Fisheries,
National Marine Fisheries Service.

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA)
ACTION:
Interim final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is amending its regulations governing member business loans and commercial lending. This interim final rule eliminates an outdated, transitional provision that is no longer necessary. This action is necessary to reduce regulatory complexity and improve the clarity of the NCUA's regulations. The intended effect is to enhance clarity and simplify compliance for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).
DATES:
This rule is effective on November 4, 2026. Comments must be received on or before January 4, 2027.
DATES:
Comments may be submitted in one of the following ways. (Please send comments by one method only):
Federal eRulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov. The docket number for this rule is NCUA-2026-
( printed page 69496)
1884. Follow the “Submit a comment” instructions. If you are reading this document on
federalregister.gov,
you may use the green “SUBMIT A PUBLIC COMMENT” button beneath this rulemaking's title to submit a comment to the
regulations.gov
docket. A plain language summary of the rule is also available on the docket website.
Mail:
Address to Melane Conyers-Ausbrooks, Secretary of the Board, National Credit Union Administration, 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, Virginia 22314-3428.
Hand Delivery/Courier:
Same as mailing address. Mailed and hand-delivered comments must be received by the close of the comment period.
Mailed and hand-delivered comments must be received by the close of the comment period.
Public inspection:
Please follow the search instructions on
https://www.regulations.gov
to view the public comments. Do not include any personally identifiable information (such as name, address, or other contact information) or confidential business information that you do not want publicly disclosed. All comments are public records; they are publicly displayed exactly as received and will not be deleted, modified, or redacted. Comments may be submitted anonymously. If you are unable to access public comments on the internet, you may contact the NCUA for alternative access by calling (703) 518-6540 or emailing
OGCMail@ncua.gov.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Office of Examination and Insurance:
Naghi Khaled, Associate Director, the Office of Examination and Insurance, at (703) 518-6360 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
Office of General Counsel:
Ariel Woodard-Stephens, Staff Attorney, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at the above address.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
The Board is publishing this interim final rule (IFR) amending its regulations at 12 CFR part 723, which governs member business loans and commercial lending for FICUs. This part establishes the safety and soundness standards FICUs must adopt for their commercial lending programs and implements the statutory limits on the aggregate amount of member business loans a credit union may hold, as established by the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act). The Board's statutory authority for this part is derived from several provisions of the FCU Act, including 12 U.S.C. 1756, 1757, 1757A, 1766, 1785, and 1789.
On March 14, 2016, the Board published a final rule that substantially revised part 723.[1]
The primary purpose of the 2016 rulemaking, which was part of the NCUA's Regulatory Modernization Initiative, was to modernize the agency's regulation of member business lending by shifting from a prescriptive, rules-based framework to a broad, principles-based regulatory approach. The prior rule included prescriptive requirements and limitations related to collateral, security, equity, and loan amounts. The Board determined that this approach caused credit unions to manage their lending practices based on rigid regulatory restrictions rather than on sound, individualized risk management practices. Furthermore, the prior rule's associated waiver process had become burdensome for both credit unions and the NCUA, requiring significant time and resources and sometimes preventing credit unions from acting on borrower applications in a timely manner.
The 2016 final rule was designed to provide FICUs with greater flexibility and individual autonomy to safely and soundly offer commercial loans to their members. It eliminated many of the prescriptive requirements and the associated waiver process, focusing instead on broad principles that clarified regulatory expectations for safe and sound commercial lending. To facilitate the shift, the 2016 final rule included transitional provisions at § 723.9, which became generally effective on January 1, 2017. This section was intended to govern circumstances where, at the time the new rule took effect, a FICU was operating under a waiver approved by the NCUA or was subject to an enforcement constraint related to its commercial lending activities.
Section 723.9(a) addresses previously approved waivers. Because the 2016 rule eliminated the prescriptive requirements for which waivers were typically granted, it rendered most such waivers moot as of the effective date. The provision established a specific exception, however, for waivers that had been granted for borrowing relationship limits. These specific waivers were grandfathered, allowing the existing debt relationship to continue, but prohibited any increase in the debt associated with those relationships.
Section 723.9(b) addresses ongoing enforcement constraints. This provision clarified that any limitations or other conditions imposed on a FICU through a written directive from the NCUA, such as a Document of Resolution or a Letter of Understanding and Agreement, were unaffected by the adoption of the new part. All such pre-existing constraints were to remain in place until formally modified or removed by the NCUA.
B. Legal Authority
The Federal Credit Union (FCU) Act grants the Board a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both insured federal and state-chartered credit unions. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority, and it authorizes the Board to prescribe regulations for the administration of the FCU Act. Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to the NCUA to issue regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all insured credit unions.

articles.full_text:
How did trade and economic activity evolve at the End of Antiquity, when political power shifts away from the Mediterranean towards the Middle East and northern Europe? No records of ancient production, consumption, and trade exist. Yet the composition of coin finds reveals information about monetized transactions, as coins gradually diffused along trade routes. To recover trade and consumption time series, we assemble a database of half a million ancient coins from the fourth to the tenth century and estimate a dynamic model of trade and money. Our estimates suggest that: Mediterranean trade was disrupted by the newly formed border between Islam and Christianity; economic activity shifts away from the Mediterranean starting in the sixth century; real consumption peaks in the Middle East in the eighth century; and by the end of the ninth century, Islamic Spain and Frankish northwestern Europe are the wealthiest regions of the ancient western world.
Recently published in Econometrica, by Johannes Boehm.

The post What Drives Censorship on College Campuses? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
There has been widespread concern about self-censorship on university campuses, and especially that conservative voices are being stifled. Using survey data from a private elite college, we show that self-censorship is not simply about being conservative: it is students with the most moderate views who self-censor the most. This pattern is associated with confidence and salience — students who are more confident in their views or who see an issue as especially important tend to hold more extreme views and to self-censor less. At the same time, conservatives self-censor at higher rates than liberals, and the same individual is more likely to self-censor on the views where they are relatively more conservative than on those where they are relatively more liberal; conservatives are also far more likely than liberals to cite concerns about social exclusion as a reason for self-censoring, and report self-censoring less outside the university community. Groups perceived as marginalized self-censor less than majority groups, and especially so on issues salient to them (e.g., Black students on BLM).
That is from a new NBER working paper by  Peter Arcidiacono,   Cory Dowd   & Matthew Lilley.

articles.title: CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance
articles.summary: CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager CaremarkCVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business in...
articles.full_text:
CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its health insurance and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.
In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.
A second company will keep the name CVS Health and house the major insurer Aetna and the giant pharmacy benefits manager Caremark, along with other businesses that provide home visits and primary care to older people.
The company has come under pressure from lawmakers and regulators over concerns that the healthcare giants, including CVS Health, UnitedHealth Group and Cigna, have become too dominant, leading to higher medical costs. The three companies control roughly 80% of the market. CVS Health in particular generated over $400bn in revenue last year.
A political pushback against healthcare gigantism has led Arkansas and Tennessee to pass laws aimed at preventing the companies from managing prescription benefits and running retail and mail-order pharmacies.
The Arkansas state representative Jeremiah Moore, a Republican who sponsored the state’s bill, told Politico last week: “The average American citizen is really tired of being pushed around and bullied, whether it be from the government or a monopolistic company.”
He added: “For far too long, they’ve taken advantage of these sick people, and it’s what I consider to be crony capitalism. They’re bending the rules to benefit their own bottom line.” Other states have proposed similar restrictions.
At the federal level, a bill introduced by the Missouri Republican senator Josh Hawley and Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren proposes an antitrust crackdown.
Hawley has described the legislation as “a major step toward restoring transparency and making healthcare more affordable for every American.”
David Joyner, CVS’s chief executive and chair, will run the healthcare solutions business.
 
“Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement.
That marks a stark turnaround from CVS Health’s earlier opposition to legislative efforts to break up the healthcare giant, which a company spokesman said would “open the door to private equity stripping the entire U.S. healthcare system for parts”.
The announcement comes after a series of acquisitions that saw CVS Health expand into nearly every corner of the healthcare system. It began in 2018, when CVS and Aetna merged in a $70bn deal. Healthcare rivals, UnitedHealth and Cigna, also brought into the trend of harnessing an insurer, pharmacy benefits, and a mail-order business under one operation.
CVS Health, however, did not meet investors’ expectations for growth. In late 2024, its share price fell to $44, though it has since rebounded. The CVS Health breakup is planned for early 2028.

articles.full_text:
Procedurally it seems to have gone just fine, and the people predicting “the end of democracy in America” now look foolish.  They have been suffering under fundamental misunderstandings of how this country works.  During this election cycle, democracy never was under threat and the United States has not been under risk of fascism.
Rising in status:
Matt Yglesias (socially moderate Democrats did very well)
Normie social science results on campaign finance
Nate Silver predictions
Falling in status:
Tariffs
Corruption
War with Iran
Wealth taxes (losing in CA)
Gerrymandering (came back to hurt Republicans, given the Blue wave)
And there you go.

AGENCY:
Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
30-Day notice.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Justice (DOJ), will be submitting the following information collection request to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and approval in accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. The proposed information collection was previously published in the
Federal Register
on September 1, 2026, 91 FR 56212, allowing a 60-day comment period.
DATES:
Comments are encouraged and will be accepted for 30 days until December 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have comments especially on the estimated public burden or associated response time, suggestions, or need a copy of the proposed information collection instrument with instructions or additional information, please contact: Counter-UAS Operations Unit, Unmanned Aviation Section, Critical Incident Response Group, Federal Bureau of Investigation, email:
cuas@fbi.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Written comments and suggestions from the public and affected agencies concerning the proposed collection of information are encouraged. Your comments should address one or more of the following four points:
—Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
—Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
—Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and/or
—Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses.
Written comments and recommendations for this information collection should be submitted within 30 days of the publication of this notice on the following website
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function and entering either the title of the information collection or the OMB Control Number 1110-0090. This information collection request may be viewed at
www.reginfo.gov.
Follow the instructions to view Department of Justice, information collections currently under review by OMB. If you do submit a comment, please send a copy to
cuas@fbi.gov.
DOJ seeks PRA authorization for this information collection for three (3) years. OMB authorization for an ICR cannot be for more than three (3) years without renewal. The DOJ notes that information collection requirements submitted to the OMB for existing ICRs receive a month-to-month extension while they undergo review.
Abstract:
The SAFER SKIES Act, Title LXXXVI of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, as implemented by the interim final rule codified at 6 CFR part 124 and 28 CFR part 124, extends counter-UAS detection and mitigation authority to State, local, tribal, and territorial (SLTT) law enforcement and correctional agencies under 6 U.
S.
C.
124n(a)(2).
This collection covers the coordination, authorization, reporting, and recordkeeping submissions the rule requires, made through the designated Federal C-UAS coordination portal.
The current approval was granted on an emergency basis and expires November 30, 2026.
This revision requests a standard three-year approval, reflects revisions to five instruments (C-UAS-AN, C-UAS-OPLAN, C-UAS-TTE, C-UAS-ATT, and C-UAS-POR) made during initial implementation, and re-estimates burden for every instrument.
The FBI received one public comment in response to the 60-day notice, from an independent researcher.
The commenter supported the collection and raised questions about the cost burden, the basis for the recordkeeping and plan estimates, the treatment of filed forms under the retention provisions of 6 CFR and 28 CFR 124.
14, access to the instruments, and opportunities to reduce burden through data reuse and machine-readable filing.
In response, the FBI has added a one-time form training line to the burden table, split the recordkeeping estimate by agency tier and raised the mitigation-tier figure, documented the task-level basis for each estimate in the supporting statement, explained the basis for the cost estimate, provided the instruments to the commenter, and committed to adding a State-law citation field to the Extended Retention Notification, publishing the data schema for each instrument, extending data reuse to the Post-Operation Report and Semiannual Summary, and offering a one-step no-activity summary for detection-tier agencies.
The comment and the FBI's response are summarized in the supporting statement.
The FBI is transitioning the instruments from the current offline, emailed workflow to a secure web portal that will host the same instruments with the same data elements, authenticate users through existing federated identity providers, and capture completion timing for future burden estimates; go-live is expected in the second or third quarter of fiscal year 2027.
Following publication of the 60-day notice, the FBI also made minor clarifying edits to the instruments; those edits did not add or remove data elements.

Published Document: 2026-22532 (91 FR 69532)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that certain oil country tubular goods (OCTG) from Taiwan are being, or are likely to be, sold in the United States at less than fair value (LTFV). The period of investigation (POI) is April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2026. Interested parties are invited to comment on this preliminary determination.
DATES:
Applicable November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Monica Gillis or Braeden Lowe, AD/CVD Operations, Office V, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-6384 or (202) 482-9124, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
This preliminary determination is made in accordance with section 733(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Commerce published the notice of initiation of this investigation on April 28, 2026.[1]
On August 28, 2026, Commerce postponed the preliminary determination of this investigation and the revised deadline is now October 29, 2026.[2]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this investigation,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[3]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included as Appendix II to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Scope of the Investigation
The product covered by this investigation is OCTG from Taiwan. For a complete description of the scope of this investigation,
see
Appendix I.
Scope Comments
In accordance with the
Preamble
to Commerce's regulations,[4]
the
Initiation Notice
set aside a period of time for parties to raise issues regarding product coverage (
i.e.,
scope).[5]
Certain interested parties commented on the scope of the investigation as it appeared in the
Initiation Notice,
whereby they requested that Commerce find certain mechanical pipe products to be outside the scope of this investigation. These products include: mechanical pipe for oilfield tools, mechanical pipe for perforating guns, and expandable mechanical pipe.
We note that there is an ongoing scope inquiry related to the antidumping duty orders on OCTG from Argentina and Mexico with respect to these same mechanical pipe products.[6]
In that inquiry, Commerce preliminarily found that the products were outside the scope of the orders,[7]
based on comments identical to the scope comments received in this investigation. Consistent with that finding, Commerce preliminarily finds and clarifies that mechanical pipe for oilfield tools, mechanical pipe for perforating guns, and expandable mechanical pipe are outside the scope of this investigation. Because this is a clarification, Commerce is not preliminarily modifying the scope language as it appeared in the
Initiation Notice. See
the scope in Appendix I to this notice.
The final determination in the above-referenced scope inquiry is currently scheduled to be made no later than December 22, 2026.[8]
We intend to consider that final determination when making a final scope ruling in this investigation. Case briefs or other written comments regarding the scope of this investigation may be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance no later than 30 days after the preliminary determination of this investigation. Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in the case briefs regarding the scope of this investigation, may be filed not later than five days after the date for filing of the scope-related case briefs.[9]

November 2, 2026.
I. Introduction
Section 15E(t) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”) requires that each nationally recognized statistical rating organization (“NRSRO”) implement certain corporate governance measures.[1]
Specifically, Section 15E(t)(1) requires each NRSRO to have a board of directors, and Section 15E(t)(3) sets forth specified, mandatory duties of such board of directors.[2]
Section 15E(t)(2)(A) provides that at least half of the board of directors, but not fewer than two members thereof, shall be independent of the NRSRO, and that a portion of the independent directors shall include users of ratings from an NRSRO.[3]
Section 15E(t)(2)(C) provides that the compensation of the independent members of the board of directors of the NRSRO shall not be linked to the business performance of the NRSRO, and shall be arranged so as to ensure the independence of their judgment. Such section also provides that the term of office of the independent directors shall be for a pre-agreed fixed period, not to exceed five years, and shall not be renewable.
Section 36 of the Exchange Act authorizes the Commission, by rule, regulation, or order, to exempt, either conditionally or unconditionally, any person, security, or transaction, or any class or classes of persons, securities, or
( printed page 69615)
transactions, from any provision of the Exchange Act or any rule or regulation thereunder, to the extent that such exemption is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, and is consistent with the protection of investors.[4]
II. Exemption Request of Japan Credit Rating Agency, Ltd.
Japan Credit Rating Agency, Ltd. (“JCR”)
is
a credit rating agency registered with the Commission as an NRSRO under Section 15E of the Exchange Act for the classes of credit ratings described in clauses (i) through (iii) and clause (v) of Section 3(a)(62)(A) of the Exchange Act.[5]
On August 20, 2015, the Commission granted JCR a three-year, conditional exemption, pursuant to Exchange Act Section 36, allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3) through its supervisory committee.[6]
On August 17, 2018, pursuant to Exchange Act Section 36, the Commission granted JCR a subsequent three-year conditional exemption, that renewed for an additional two years in accordance with its terms, allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3) through its supervisory committee.[7]
On September 28, 2023, pursuant to Exchange Act Section 36, the Commission granted JCR another temporary, conditional exemption allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3) through its supervisory committee through October 30, 2026.[8]
JCR has requested a continuation of such exemption that is not time-limited on the basis that Japanese law applicable to credit ratings agencies registered in Japan, including JCR, imposes requirements for strong independent oversight of credit rating agencies on the supervisory committee, a body separate from the board of directors.
Specifically, JCR has represented to the Commission that Japanese law requires (1) all Japanese credit rating agencies to adopt certain control systems for ensuring the “fair and appropriate performance” of their credit rating business, including establishment of a “supervisory committee” as a Japanese credit rating agency's internal oversight body and (2) at least one-third of the supervisory committee members (or at least two where there are three or fewer members) to be “independent members” of the supervisory committee, and prohibits the directors of the Japanese credit rating agency from serving as independent members.[9]
JCR also represented to the Commission that it has established processes to ensure compliance with the conditions in the 2023 order and that its supervisory committee fulfills the functional equivalent of the requirements applicable to an NRSRO's board of directors under Exchange Act Section 15E(t)(2) and (t)(3). For example, JCR represented to the Commission that: (1) two of the four supervisory committee members are independent members and one of the independent members is a user of ratings; (2) the supervisory committee independent members receive no prohibited compensatory fees, are not associated with JCR or any of its affiliated companies, and are disqualified from deliberation involving a rating where the member has a financial interest in the outcome of the rating; and (3) the supervisory committee independent members receive no prohibited compensation and have no more than a five-year term of office.
III. Discussion
Section 15E(p) of the Exchange Act, as added by Section 932(a)(8) of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act,[10]
requires Commission staff to conduct an examination of each NRSRO at least annually. Commission staff has examined JCR's satisfaction of the conditions in the prior orders as part of each annual examination conducted since 2016 and has determined that JCR currently satisfies the conditions in the 2023 order.
Accordingly, the Commission finds, based on such determination and on JCR's representations referred to in Section II above, that it is appropriate in the public interest and is consistent with the protection of investors to grant JCR a conditional exemption, allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Section 15E(t)(2) and Section 15E(t)(3) through the supervisory committee, subject to the conditions specified below. In addition, Commission staff will continue to examine JCR's satisfaction of the conditions to this order set forth in Section IV below. If the conditions are not being fulfilled to the staff's satisfaction, the staff will consider whether to make recommendations to the Commission, as appropriate.[11]
IV. Conclusion
For the foregoing reasons, the Commission finds that it is appropriate in the public interest and consistent with the protection of investors to grant JCR a conditional exemption allowing JCR to satisfy the requirements of Section 15E(t)(2) and Section 15E(t)(3) of the Exchange Act through the supervisory committee.

articles.full_text:
ACTION:
60-day notice and request for comments
                    SUMMARY:
                        The Small Business Administration (SBA) intends to request approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the collection of information described below. The Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) requires Federal agencies to publish a notice in the 
                        Federal Register
                         concerning each proposed collection of information before submission to OMB, and to allow 60 days for public comment in response to the notice. This notice complies with that requirement.
                    
                    DATES:
Submit comments on or before January 4, 2027.
                    ADDRESSES:
                        Send all comments via email to, Robert Camacho, Small Business Administration, Office of Financial Assistance, at 
                        robert.camacho@sba.gov.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
For SBA financial assistance programs, SBA Form 413 Personal Financial Statement (PFS) collects information regarding the assets and liabilities of certain owners, officers and guarantors of the small business applicant benefiting from such assistance and is used when analyzing the applicant's repayment abilities or creditworthiness. SBA's Surety Bond Guaranty Program uses the Form 413 PFS information during the claim recovery process. The information is also collected from applicants and participants in SBA's 8(a) Business Development (BD) and Women-Owned Small Business (WOSB) Program certification process to determine whether they meet the economic disadvantage requirements of the program.
All program offices use the same Form 413. SBA plans to revise the authorization language for Form 413 to provide consent for SBA to obtain information from the Social Security Administration (SSA) confirming name, social security number, and date of birth. SBA will also update the certification to state that information provided in the Disaster loan application is accurate to the best of their knowledge.
Solicitation of Public Comments
SBA is requesting comments on (a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the agency to properly perform its functions; (b) whether the burden estimates are accurate; (c) whether there are ways to minimize the burden, including through the use of automated techniques or other forms of information technology; and (d) whether there are ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information.
Summary of Information Collection

                     3245-0188.
                
                    (1) Title:
                     Personal Financial Statement.
                
                    Description of Respondents:
                     7(a) and 504 loan Program applicants, Surety Bond Program recovery claimants, Disaster Loan Program business applicants 8(a)/BD and WOSB Program applicants.
                
                    Form Number:
                     SBA Form 413.
                
                    Total Estimated Annual Responses:
                     134,921.
                
                    Total Estimated Annual Hour Burden:
                     202,382.
                
                    Shauniece Carter,
Records and Information Management Specialist.
