AGENCY:
U.S. Geological Survey, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is proposing to renew an information collection.
DATES:
Interested persons are invited to submit comments on or before January 4, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by one of the following methods:
U.S. Mail:
USGS, Information Collections Clearance Officer, 12201 Sunrise Valley Drive, MS 159, Reston, VA 20192.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
To request additional information about this information collection request (ICR), contact Stephen Slaughter by email at
sslaughter@usgs.gov,
or by telephone at 720-483-3945. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with the PRA (44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.) and 5 CFR 1320.8(d)(1), all information collections require approval under the PRA. We may not conduct or sponsor and you are not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
As part of our continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burdens, we invite the public and other Federal agencies to comment on new, proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. It also helps the public understand our information collection requirements and provide the requested data in the desired format.
We are especially interested in public comments addressing the following:
(1) Whether or not the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility.
(2) The accuracy of our estimate of the burden for this collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used.
(3) Ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
(4) How might the agency minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including using appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of response.
Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of public record. We will include or summarize each comment in our request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personally identifiable information (PII) in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment—including your PII—may be made publicly available at any time. While you can ask us in your comment to withhold your PII from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.
Abstract:
USGS collects this information under the authority of 43 U.S.C. 3101-3104 (National Landslide Preparedness Act), which supports the mission of the USGS Landslide Hazards Program to reduce loss of life and property from landslides and improve public safety and community resilience. Under this authority, the USGS provides competitive grants to State, territorial, local, and Tribal governments to research, map, assess, and collect data on landslide hazards within their jurisdictions.
In response to USGS program announcements, applicants submit proposals describing proposed work in one or more priority areas: (a) advancing landslide hazard mapping and assessments, (b) improving landslide hazard planning and coordination, and (c) improving the dissemination and effectiveness of landslide hazard information to mitigate losses. Proposals include a project narrative, a detailed budget, resumes or curricula vitae of key staff, and applicant organization information (organization name, address, and authorized representative).
The USGS collects this information to evaluate and select proposals for funding that best meet the priorities of the Cooperative Landslide Hazard Mapping and Assessment Grant Program. Award recipients must also submit final technical reports summarizing project outcomes and, for awards spanning more than two years, annual progress reports describing work completed to date. The USGS uses these reports to monitor grantee progress and performance and to ensure accountability for federal funds. Final technical reports are made publicly available at
https://www.usgs.gov/programs/landslide-hazards/science/external-grants-overview.

In accordance with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (Commission or FERC) regulations, 18 CFR part 380, Commission staff reviewed PacifiCorp's, application seeking an exemption from the licensing requirements of Part 1 of the Federal Power Act for the Stairs Project No. 15372, and an administrative surrender of the license for the Stairs Project No. 597, and have prepared an Environmental Assessment (EA) for the projects.[] 
                    
                     The project is located along Big Cottonwood Creek, near the city of Cottonwood Heights, in Salt Lake County, Utah, and occupies federal lands within the Uinta-Wasatch-Cache National Forest managed by the U.S. Forest Service.
                
The EA contains Commission staff's analysis of the potential environmental effects of the proposed surrender and issuance of an exemption, alternatives to the proposed action, and concludes that the proposed surrender and issuance of an exemption would not constitute a major federal action that would significantly affect the quality of the human environment.
                    The EA may be viewed on the Commission's website at 
                    http://www.ferc.gov
                     using the “eLibrary” link. Enter the docket number (P-597-025 or P-15372-000) in the docket number field to access the document. For assistance, contact FERC Online Support at 
                    FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
                     or toll-free at 1-866-208-3676, or for TTY, (202) 502-8659.
                
                    You may also register online at 
                    http://www.ferc.gov/docs-filing/esubscription.asp
                     to be notified via email of new filings and issuances related to this or other pending projects. For assistance, contact FERC Online Support.
                
All comments must be filed by November 30, 2026, 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.

The first page of any filing should include docket numbers P-597-025 and P-15372-000.
                
                    For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions, comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202) 502-6595 or 
                    OPP@ferc.gov.
                    For further information, contact Chris Chaney at (202) 502-6778 or 
                    christopher.chaney@ferc.gov.

Published Document: 2026-22509 (91 FR 69524)
This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Agricultural Marketing Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Referendum order; amendment to referendum order.
SUMMARY:
This document extends the voting period for the referendum being conducted among eligible Florida citrus producers to determine whether they favor continuance of the marketing order regulating the handling of oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, and pummelos produced in Florida. The voting period was originally set to close November 9, 2026, and is now being extended through December 1, 2026.
DATES:
The voting period for the referendum will be extended from November 9 through December 1, 2026. Only current Florida citrus producers within the production area that produced oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, or pummelos for the fresh market during the period of August 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, are eligible to vote in this referendum. Ballots delivered to AMS via U.S. mail or electronic ballot must show proof of delivery by no later than 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 1, 2026, to be included in the vote tabulation.
ADDRESSES:
Copies of the marketing order may be obtained from the office of the referendum agents at the Southeast Region Branch, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, 1124 1st Street South, Winter Haven, FL 33880; telephone: (863) 324-3375; or from the Docket Clerk, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, 1400 Independence Avenue SW, STOP 0237, Washington, DC 20250-0237; telephone (202) 720-8085; or on the internet:
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/subtitle-B/chapter-IX/part-905.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Rebecca Geller, Marketing Specialist, or Christian D. Nissen, Branch Chief, Southeast Region Branch, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, 1124 1st Street South, Winter Haven, FL 33880; telephone: (863) 324-3375; or email:
Rebecca.Geller@usda.gov
or
Christian.Nissen@usda.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Pursuant to Marketing Order No. 905, as amended (7 CFR part 905; the Order), and the applicable provisions of the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, as amended (7 U.S.C. 601-674) (the Act), it is hereby directed that a referendum be conducted to ascertain whether continuance of the Order is favored by fresh citrus producers. The referendum voting period started October 19 and will run through December 1, 2026, among Florida fresh citrus producers in the Order's production area. Only current Florida citrus producers engaged in the production of oranges, grapefruit, tangerines, or pummelos for the fresh market during the period of August 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, may participate in the continuance referendum.
A referendum order was published in the
Federal Register
on September 18, 2026 (91 FR 59101). The referendum order specified that the voting period would be from October 19 through November 9, 2026. USDA has received requests from industry organizations to extend the voting period for the referendum, citing the significant production, recovery, and business challenges currently facing Florida citrus producers and the need for additional time to ensure informed participation in the referendum process. To facilitate full producer participation in the referendum, USDA is extending the voting period from November 9 through December 1, 2026. During this time, USDA will continue to mail ballots to eligible voters who request a ballot. All ballots received from October 19 through December 1, 2026, will be accepted. Voters who have already submitted a ballot do not need to take further action.
USDA has determined that continuance referenda are an effective means for determining whether producers favor the continuation of marketing order programs. In accordance with § 905.83(c), USDA must conduct a referendum every six years. USDA would consider termination of the Order if less than two-thirds of the producers voting in the referendum, and less than two-thirds of the citrus volume represented in the referendum, vote in favor of continuance. In evaluating the merits of continuance versus termination, USDA will not exclusively consider the results of the continuance referendum. USDA will also consider all other relevant information concerning the operation of the Order and relative benefits and costs to producers, handlers, and consumers to determine whether continued operation of the Order would tend to effectuate the declared policy of the Act.
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. chapter 35), the ballot materials used in the referendum have been approved by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and have been assigned OMB No. 0581-0189, Fruit Crops. It has been estimated it will take an average of 20 minutes for each of the approximately 200 citrus producers to cast a ballot. Participation is voluntary. Ballots delivered to AMS via U.S. mail or electronic ballot must show proof of delivery by no later than 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on December 1, 2026, to be included in the vote tabulation.
Delaney Fuhrmeister, Rebecca Geller, Steven Kauffman, Christian Nissen, and Jennie Varela of the Southeast Region Branch, Market Development Division, Specialty Crops Program, AMS, USDA, are hereby designated as the referendum agents of the Secretary of Agriculture to conduct this referendum. The procedure applicable to the referendum shall be the “Procedure for the Conduct of Referenda in Connection with Marketing Orders for Fruits, Vegetables, and Nuts Pursuant to the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act of 1937, as Amended” (7 CFR part 900.400et seq.).
Ballots and voting instructions will be sent by U.S. mail or through electronic mail to all Florida citrus producers of record and may also be obtained from the referendum agents or their appointees.

AGENCY:
Bureau of Land Management, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of information collection; request for comment.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) proposes extending an information collection.
DATES:
Interested persons are invited to submit comments on or before January 4, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Send your written comments on this information collection request (ICR) by mail to Darrin King, Information Collection Clearance Officer, U.S. Department of the Interior, Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Department of the Interior, Director (630), Bureau of Land Management, 1849 C St. NW, Room 5646, Washington, DC 20240, Attention: Attention PRA Office; or by email to
BLM_HQ_PRA_Comments@blm.gov.
Please reference Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Control Number 1004-0194 in the subject line of your comments. The electronic submission of comments is recommended.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
To request additional information about this ICR, contact Kirk Rentmeister by email at
krentmei@blm.gov,
or by telephone at (775) 453-5514. Individuals in the United States who are deaf, deafblind, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability may dial 711 (TTY, TDD, or TeleBraille) to access telecommunications relay services. Individuals outside the United States should use the relay services offered within their country to make international calls to the point-of-contact in the United States. You may also view the ICR at
http://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
In accordance with the PRA (44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.) and 5 CFR 1320.8(d)(1), all information collections require approval under the PRA. We may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
As part of our continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burdens, we invite the public and other Federal agencies to comment on new, proposed, revised, and continuing collections of information. This helps us assess the impact of our information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting burden. It also helps the public understand our information collection requirements and provide the requested data in the desired format.
We are especially interested in public comment addressing the following:
(1) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(2) The accuracy of our estimate of the burden for this collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(3) Ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
(4) How the agency could minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of response.
Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of public record. We will include or summarize each comment in our request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, phone number, email address, or other personally identifying information (PII) in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment, including your PII, may be made publicly available at any time. While you can ask us in your comment to withhold your PII from public review, we cannot guarantee that we will be able to do so.
Abstract:
The collection of information under 43 CFR subpart 3809 enables the BLM to determine whether operators and mining claimants are meeting their responsibility to prevent unnecessary or undue degradation while conducting exploration and mining activities on public lands under the mining laws. The information collection requirements contained in 43 CFR subpart 3809 are approved under OMB Control Number 1004-0194 which is currently scheduled to expire on February 28, 2027. The BLM plans to request that OMB renew this OMB control number for an additional three (3) years.

On occasion.

A. Background
On December 13, 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) adopted amendments to Rule 17a9(a) and (e)(18)(iv)(A) and (B) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”).[1]
Under these amendments, covered clearing agencies that provide central counterparty services for U.S. Treasury securities (“U.S. Treasury securities CCAs”) must establish, implement, maintain, and enforce written policies and procedures reasonably designed to establish objective, risk-based, and publicly disclosed criteria for participation which require that any direct participant of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA submit for clearance and settlement all of the eligible secondary market transactions to which such direct participant is a counterparty, and identify and monitor the U.S. Treasury securities CCA's direct participants' submission of transactions for clearing as required under the amendments (together, the “Trade Submission Requirement”).[2]
The amendments defined what constitutes an “eligible secondary market transaction” to include, among other things, a secondary market transaction in U.S. Treasury securities of a type accepted for clearing by a registered covered clearing agency that is a repurchase or reverse repurchase agreement collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities (“repo transactions”), in which one of the counterparties is a direct participant of a covered clearing agency.[3]
The amendments also included an exclusion from the definition of an eligible secondary market transaction for any repo transactions entered into between a direct participant and an affiliated counterparty (the “Inter-Affiliate Exclusion”), provided that the affiliated counterparty submit for clearance and settlement all other repo transactions to which the affiliate is a party (the “outward facing condition”).[4]
The amendments define “affiliated counterparty” as any counterparty which meets the following criteria: (i) the counterparty is either a bank (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 78c(6)), broker (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 78c(4)), dealer (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 78c(5)), or futures commission merchant (as defined in 7 U.S.C. 1a(28)), or any entity regulated as a bank, broker, dealer, or futures commission merchant in its home jurisdiction; (ii) the counterparty holds, directly or indirectly, a majority ownership interest in the direct participant, or the direct participant, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in the counterparty, or a third party, directly or indirectly, holds a majority ownership interest in both the direct participant and the counterparty; and (iii) the counterparty, direct participant, or third party referenced in paragraph (ii) of this definition as holding the majority ownership interest would be required to report its financial statements on a consolidated basis under U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles or International Financial Reporting Standards, and such consolidated financial statements include the financial results of the majority-owned party or of both majority-owned parties.[5]
B. IIB's and SIFMA's Requests for Exemptive Relief
The Commission has received requests for exemptive relief related to transactions by non-U.S. persons and related to the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion.
On February 27, 2026, the Institute of International Bankers (“IIB”) submitted a letter to the Commission requesting exemptive relief from the Trade Submission Requirement for certain non-U.S. transactions, specifically, the transactions of foreign financial institutions who are direct participants of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA when transacting with non-U.S. clients.[6]
IIB explained that exemptive relief was appropriate because of legal uncertainty in certain foreign jurisdictions regarding the enforceability of fundamental clearing requirements, potential registration requirements for clearing firms operating in those jurisdictions, and practical concerns about repo transactions occurring when no U.S. Treasury securities CCA is operating.[7]
On March 6, 2026, the Commission published the notice and encouraged interested persons to comment on the request for exemptive relief pursuant to Section 36 of the Exchange Act.[8]
The initial comment period for the IIB Notice closed on April 10, 2026, and the Commission then reopened the comment period, which then closed on May 29, 2026.[9]
On April 10, 2026, the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association (“SIFMA”) submitted a letter to the Commission requesting exemptive relief in two areas related to the Trade Submission Requirement.[10]
First, SIFMA requested exemptive relief to expand the list of permitted affiliates with whom direct participants of a U.S. Treasury securities CCA could transact and rely upon the Inter-Affiliate Exclusion beyond the current set (
i.e.,
banks, broker-dealers, futures commission merchants, and their foreign equivalents) (the “SIFMA First Request”). Specifically, SIFMA requested that the Commission exercise its exemptive authority to allow a firm to treat all counterparties that meet clauses (ii) and (iii) of the definition in Rule 17ad-22(a) as affiliated counterparties, except for an affiliate that is an “investment company” as defined in Section 3 of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (regardless of whether such investment company is registered or required to be registered under that act).[11]
Second, SIFMA requested that the outward-facing condition not include repo transactions between non-U.S.
( printed page 69579)
affiliates and non-U.S. counterparties, to the extent that the direct participant does not exceed a specific activity level percentage threshold for those transactions (the “SIFMA Second Request”).[12]
SIFMA explained that such relief was appropriate because non-U.S. affiliates commonly enter into transactions with each other for treasury, liquidity, and collateral management purposes that would raise serious logistical and cost concerns under the adopted rule.[13]

This document has been published in the Federal Register. Use the PDF linked in the document sidebar for the official electronic format.
AGENCY:
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
ACTION:
30-Day notice of information collection; request for comment; extension of previously approved collection 1670-0013.
SUMMARY:
The Office of the Chief Security Officer (OCSO) within Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) submits the following information collection request (ICR) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review and clearance. CISA previously published this information collection request (ICR) in the
Federal Register
on September 10, 2026 for a 60-day public comment period. No comments were received by CISA. The purpose of this notice is to allow additional 30-days for public comments.
DATES:
Comments are encouraged and will be accepted until December 4, 2026. Submissions received after the deadline for receiving comments may not be considered.
ADDRESSES:
Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function.
The Office of Management and Budget is particularly interested in comments which:
1. Evaluate whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
2. Evaluate the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
3. Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
4. Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submissions of responses.
Partnerships between the U.S. Government and the state, local tribal and private sector at times necessitate the sharing of classified information. The State, Local, Tribal and Private Sector (SLTPS) Clearance Request Form facilitates this sharing by sponsoring security clearances for certain members of each sector based on either their membership on a Sector Coordinating Council (SCC)/association or their infrastructure protection job-related duties and their need-to-know. The SLTPS is designed to sponsor security clearances for state, local, tribal and private sector officials involved in the infrastructure protection mission. These partners are subject matter experts within specific industries and have specialized knowledge not available within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and other Federal Departments or Agencies. Private citizens do not receive monetary compensation for their time. CISA created this program to sponsor clearances for these individuals who are not employed by or contracted with another Federal agency (the traditional means of obtaining a clearance) and must have clearances.
CISA collects necessary information through 1670-0013 to facilitate security clearances needed for sharing classified information with the vetted SLTPS Stakeholders.
The U.S. Government is authorized to ask for this information under Sections 201 and 229 of the Homeland Security Act (Pub. L. 107-296, 6 U.S.C. 121, 150), and Executive Orders 12968, 13526, 13549, 13636, and 13691 which authorize the collection of this information.
In order to begin this process of adjudicating a nominee to participate in the clearance program, federal nominators will complete the DHS Form 9014, State, Local, Tribal and Private Sector Clearance Request Form. The federal nominator will sign the form and have it approved by a senior-level official from the corresponding Federal Department or Agency. The signatures indicate the nominator and senior-level official have deemed the applicant has a CISA mission and meets the requirements and criteria as outlined in Executive Order (E.O.) 13549, the Department of Homeland Security, Classified National Security Information Program for SLTPS Implementing Directive and E.O. 13691, Sec. 4(c), and 32 CFR, Part 117, Sec. 117.22 of the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM). Once submitted to the CISA OCSO the SLTPS Administrator will request the Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and a record is created into the Integrated Security Management System (ISMS). The Security Specialist will initiate an eApplication (eAPP), the
( printed page 69570)
Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency secure portal for investigation processing. Once the data is entered into e-App, the nominee is provided a password and can access the system and complete the online security questionnaire.
This information is only available to Security Specialists within OCSO working on the program and is maintained in ISMS, which is “owned” by the OCSO. The two-part PII request process helps minimize the collection of sensitive PII for only those nominees who meet the threshold and are sponsored by CISA.
This is an extension of a previously approved information collection.

November 2, 2026.
I. Introduction
On September 10, 2026, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (the “Board” or the “PCAOB”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”), pursuant to section 107(b) [1]
of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (“SOX”) and section 19(b) [2]
of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Exchange Act”), a proposal to adopt (1) amendments to certain provisions of Quality Control (“QC”) 1000,
A Firm's System of Quality Control
(“QC 1000”); (2) related amendments to PCAOB Rule 2203A and PCAOB forms; and (3) technical amendments to Auditing Standard (“AS”) 2101,
Audit Planning
(each, an “Amendment” and collectively, the “Amendments”).[3]
The Amendments were approved by the PCAOB on September 9, 2026.[4]
On September 11, 2026, the Board adopted a technical correction to one of the proposed rules included in the Amendments and then filed the technical correction with the SEC on September 14, 2026.
The Amendments were published for comment in the
Federal Register
on September 18, 2026.[5]
We received ten comment letters from the public regarding the Amendments.[6]
This Order approves the Amendments, which we find to be consistent with the requirements of Title I of SOX and the rules and regulations issued thereunder and necessary or appropriate in the public interest or for the protection of investors.[7]
The Amendments and the findings with respect thereto are discussed in further detail below.
II. Background and Description of the Amendments
On September 9, 2024, the Commission approved QC 1000, an integrated, risk-based QC standard intended to replace the interim QC standards that the PCAOB had adopted in 2003.[8]
The PCAOB stated it believed QC 1000 would lead registered public accounting firms (“firms”) to significantly improve their QC systems.[9]
QC 1000 was set to become effective on December 15, 2025; however, the PCAOB subsequently delayed the effective date of QC 1000 for one year—until December 15, 2026—after considering information it received from various sources that some firms had encountered implementation challenges that, as a practical matter, may be insurmountable by the effective date.[10]
On September 9, 2026, the Board adopted the Amendments.[11]
The Amendments were preceded by a June 2026 supplemental request for comment [12]
and other outreach engaged in by the PCAOB. The Amendments were targeted to modify only certain provisions of QC 1000, as described in more detail below. Except for the targeted Amendments, QC 1000 would remain unchanged.
In the Notice of Filing of Proposed Rules, the PCAOB stated that it was proposing Amendments to QC 1000 that it believes address concerns regarding the implementation challenges identified by firms and to better align certain provisions with other quality management standards, both internationally and in the United States.[13]
As described by the Board, these Amendments are designed to reduce compliance costs while maintaining the investor protection benefits of QC 1000.[14]
According to the Board, although several of the Amendments the Board adopted better align QC 1000 with other quality management standards with which most firms are already complying,[15]
differences remain in areas where the Board continues to believe that alternative or incremental provisions of QC 1000 better address the United States' legal and regulatory environment, the needs and priorities of the Board's stakeholders, and the Board's statutory mandate of protecting investors and the public interest.[16]
( printed page 69621)
The Amendments consider the feedback the PCAOB received on its Supplemental Request for Comment and information obtained through the PCAOB's implementation support efforts (
e.g.,
workshops, stakeholder outreach, and feedback received from firms and other stakeholders regarding implementation, including implementation guidance provided by the PCAOB), among other sources.[17]
The principal Amendments adopted by the PCAOB are intended to:
Rescind the “design-only” requirement so that QC 1000 imposes requirements only on firms that are required to comply with applicable professional and legal requirements with respect to any “engagement” as defined in QC 1000 (QC 1000.06 and .07d);
Provide increased flexibility in filling certain specified roles in the QC system by permitting those roles to be assigned to non-firm personnel and divided among multiple individuals (QC 1000.12);
Rescind the requirement to have an External QC Function (“EQCF”) (QC 1000.28);
Narrow and simplify communication requirements relating to metrics that the firm communicates to external parties about its audit practice, firm personnel, or engagements (QC 1000.53e);
With respect to identified engagement deficiencies, require evaluation of whether similar engagement deficiencies exist on other engagements only if the identified deficiency resulted or could result in (i) a failure to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence to support the conclusion reached on an engagement or (ii) an inappropriate overall conclusion on the subject matter of an engagement (QC 1000.68d);
Revise the definition of QC deficiency to make clear that, when firms have implemented more than one quality response to address the same quality risk, they can take those other quality responses (e.g.,
compensating responses) into account when determining whether a QC deficiency exists (QC 1000.A8);
Allow firms to select the date as of which they annually evaluate the effectiveness of their QC system, rather than requiring firms to evaluate as of September 30 (QC 1000.77);
Revise the QC system evaluation conclusions to align more closely with the conclusions in other quality management standards,[18]
while retaining a structured process, including specified factors for consideration, to guide the evaluation (QC 1000.77 and .78); and
Simplify the requirements for retention of QC system documentation and abbreviate the retention period from seven to five years (QC 1000.84 and .86).[19]
The Amendments will be effective on December 15, 2026, the same effective date as the rest of QC 1000.[20]

The U.S. Department of Energy installation known as the SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, located in the City of Menlo Park, San Mateo County, California, with a physical address of 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA 94025.

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule adopting as final the revisions to the capital adequacy rule and the member business lending rule made under an interim final rule (IFR) published in the
Federal Register
on April 27, 2020.
DATES:
The final rule is effective on November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John H. Brolin, Senior Staff Attorney, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
On March 27, 2020, President Trump signed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act) into law.[1]
The law provided aid to the U.S. economy during the COVID-19 pandemic. The CARES Act authorized the Small Business Administration (SBA) to create a loan guarantee program, the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), in response to the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on small businesses. The PPP helped participating businesses meet payroll needs and utilities, including employee salaries, sick leave, other paid leave, and health insurance expenses. Provided that credit union lenders complied with the applicable lender obligations set forth in the SBA's interim final rule (IFR), the SBA fully guaranteed loans issued under the PPP. Most federally insured credit unions (FICUs) were eligible to make PPP loans to members.[2]
Under the CARES Act, PPP loans received a zero percent risk weighting under the NCUA's risk-based capital requirements.[3]
On April 27, 2020, the Board issued an IFR (April 27th IFR) to make a conforming amendment to its capital adequacy regulation following the enactment of the CARES Act.[4]
As noted, the CARES Act required that, under the NCUA's risk-based capital requirements, PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weighting. To reflect the statutory requirement, the April 27th IFR amended the NCUA's capital adequacy regulation to provide that covered PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weight. The April 27th IFR also provided that the covered loan could be excluded from a credit union's accounting of total assets in its net worth ratio calculation if the covered loan was pledged as collateral for a non-recourse loan that was provided as part of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System's (FRB) PPP Loan Facility. The April 27th IFR also made a conforming amendment to the definition of commercial loan in the NCUA's member business loans and commercial lending rule. The Board found good cause to issue the April 27th IFR without advance notice-and-comment procedures and with an effective date upon publication.
This rule adopts as final the revisions to the capital adequacy rule and the member business lending rule published in the
Federal Register
on April 27, 2020.[5]
The Board is adopting this IFR as final. Under this final rule, FICUs may continue to assign a zero percent risk weight to PPP loans under the NCUA's risk-based capital regulations and neutralize the regulatory capital effects of participating in the PPP Liquidity Facility (PPP Loan Facility). Because the IFR was effective immediately upon publication and the final rule does not require affected parties to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect, the Board is issuing this final rule to address the types of matters described in this paragraph with an immediate effective date.[6]
B. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue this final rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act and its specific rulemaking authority under the various provisions the Board administers.[7]
II. Final Rule
A. Zero Percent Risk Weight for PPP Loans
The NCUA's April 27th IFR amended the NCUA's risk-based net worth rules to reflect the requirement that PPP loans receive a zero percent risk weight. In particular, the IFR classified PPP loans as low-risk assets. Under prior § 702.106(d), low-risk assets received a zero percent risk weight.[8]
In addition, § 702.104(d) defined low-risk assets as cash on hand (for example, coin and currency, including vault, ATM and teller cash), the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund deposit, debt instruments unconditionally guaranteed by the NCUA, and loans issued under the SBA's PPP.[9]
Thus, the April 27th IFR provided that PPP loans received a zero percent risk weight under the NCUA's risk-based capital rules as required by the CARES Act.
The NCUA's 2015 final rule regarding risk-based capital (2015 Final Rule) [10]
went into effect on January 1, 2022,[11]
making substantial changes to the NCUA's previous prompt corrective action (PCA) requirements under part 702 of the NCUA's regulations. Among other changes, the 2015 Final Rule eliminated the definition of “low risk asset” under § 702.104(d). To account for this change, in a December 23, 2021, final rule on capital adequacy (December 2021 Final Rule), the NCUA gave covered loans issued under the SBA's PPP a zero percent risk weight.[12]
This amendment finalized the change made to the previous PCA regulations by the April 27th IFR, thus this final rule does not affect the changes that were made by the NCUA's December 2021 Final Rule and no further amendment is required.
B. Definition of Total Assets for Purposes of Calculating the Net Worth Ratio
Pursuant to section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act, the FRB authorized each of the Federal Reserve Banks to participate in the PPP Loan Facility as a means to provide liquidity to small business lenders and the broader credit markets, help stabilize the financial system, and provide economic relief to
( printed page 69494)
small businesses nationwide.[13]
Through the PPP Loan Facility, each of the Federal Reserve Banks extended non-recourse loans to eligible financial institutions to fund PPP loans. Under this construct, only PPP loans that were guaranteed by the SBA with respect to both principal and interest and were originated by an eligible institution could be pledged as collateral to the Federal Reserve Banks. Participation in the PPP Loan Facility affected a FICU's balance sheet because, as a function of participating in the PPP Loan Facility, the FICU was required to originate and hold PPP covered loans (that is, assets that are eligible collateral pledged to the Federal Reserve Banks) on its balance sheet.
As a result, FICUs that participated in the PPP Loan Facility could potentially be subject to increased regulatory capital requirements due to the increase in total assets from originating and holding PPP loans. To facilitate use of the PPP Loan Facility, the April 27th IFR allowed FICUs to neutralize the regulatory capital effects of PPP loans pledged to the PPP Loan Facility.[14]

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
On February 25, 2026, NCUA (or `agency') published a proposed rule to solicit comments on the removal of a provision of NCUA regulations regarding federal credit unions' (FCUs) statutory lien authority. Upon further consideration, and based on the comments received, the Board is issuing this final rule, as proposed, to remove the term, “except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law.” This language does not provide any assistance to FCUs in determining whether such statutory or case law exists, therefore it has no material value.
DATES:
This final rule is effective December 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Gira Bose, Senior Staff Attorney,
Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6562 or
gbose@ncua.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
Section 701.39 of the NCUA's regulations implements the statutory lien authority granted to FCUs under the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act).[1]
The regulation, which converted a prior policy statement into a regulation in 1999, states that an FCU has the power to impress and enforce a lien against a member's shares and dividends to satisfy any outstanding financial obligation owed to the credit union.[2]
The proposed rule, issued on February 25, 2026, put forward an amendment to the regulation by removing the definition of the term “[e]xcept as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law.” [3]
The Board determined that this definition is not helpful. The fact that an FCU must determine which laws apply to its operations and must be aware that some legal requirements supersede others, is a universal consideration and not one that is specific to this regulation. Thus, the Board proposed to repeal paragraph 701.39(a)(1).
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).[4]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.[5]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.[6]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.[7]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the proposed rule and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on April 27, 2026, the Board had received 11 comments. Commenters were two credit unions, five state and regional credit union leagues or associations, three national credit union trade associations, and one individual member of the public who did not disclose a group affiliation. After careful consideration of the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has decided to adopt the proposal without change.
B. Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments. Nine of the eleven commenters expressed support for the proposal generally stating that:
the provision identified for removal is redundant and does not provide substantive guidance to credit unions;
the proposal would remove potentially confusing language from NCUA's regulation and have no effect on lien authority or obligations; and
from an operational perspective, FCUs must already maintain processes to identify and apply applicable statutory and case law when exercising their authorities, including statutory lien rights. The presence or absence of this definitional language does not alter that responsibility.
Two commenters opposed the rule. One stated that preserving the current statutory lien framework best balances member transparency, operational certainty, and safety and soundness. The other commenter did not speak specifically to this proposal, but voiced opposition to deregulation in general. This commenter stated that the suggestion that certain requirements are overly burdensome warrants careful scrutiny. A regulation requiring staff time or administrative effort does not necessarily indicate that the requirement lacks value. Oversight, documentation, and verification processes inevitably require time and resources, but those efforts are part of maintaining responsible governance and protecting member assets.
The Board agrees that deregulatory proposals must be carefully considered and appropriately balanced with the need to maintain the safety and soundness of the credit union system. The Board also believes that this amendment will not jeopardize that balance. As a number of commenters noted, the term “except as otherwise provided by law or except as otherwise provided by federal law” does not provide any assistance to FCUs in determining whether such statutory or
( printed page 69492)
case law exists. And its removal does not diminish an FCU's obligation to determine, as in all cases, if there are other laws that apply to its activities. Thus, this rule is being finalized as proposed.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to Executive Order 12866 (“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order. Executive Order 13563 (“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in Executive Order 12866. This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with Executive Order 12866 and Executive Order 13563. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined in section 3(f) of Executive Order 12866.

AGENCY:
Drug Enforcement Administration, Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Final rule; technical amendment.
SUMMARY:
This final rule updates a Drug Enforcement Administration regulation to clarify that the provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications also applies to applications for registration renewal. This action makes no substantive changes to this regulation.
DATES:
This rule is effective November 4, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heather E. Achbach, Regulatory Drafting and Policy Support Section, Diversion Control Division, Drug Enforcement Administration; Mailing Address: 8701 Morrissette Drive, Springfield, Virginia 22152; Telephone: (571) 776-3882.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Legal Authority
The Controlled Substances Act (CSA) grants the Attorney General authority to promulgate and enforce rules and regulations pertaining to the registration and control of the manufacture, distribution, and dispensing of controlled substances and the maintenance and submission of records and reports related thereto.[1]
The CSA further authorizes the Attorney General to promulgate regulations necessary and appropriate to execute the functions of subchapter I (Control and Enforcement) and subchapter II (Import and Export) of the CSA.[2]
The Attorney General has delegated this authority to the Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).[3]
Technical Amendment
DEA regulations state that an application shall be deemed to be withdrawn if an applicant requests an application to be returned, or if an applicant fails to respond to official correspondence regarding the application when sent by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested.[4]
The use of the term “applicant” may inadvertently suggest that this provision applies only to new registration applications and is not applicable to registration renewal applications. In this final rule, DEA is adding “or registrant” after “applicant” in 21 CFR 1301.16(b) to clarify that this provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications applies to both registration and registration renewal applications.
Regulatory Analyses
Administrative Procedure Act
An agency may find good cause to exempt a rule from certain provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including those requiring the publication of a prior notice of proposed rulemaking and the opportunity for public comment, if such actions are determined to be unnecessary, impracticable, or contrary to the public interest.[5]
The “unnecessary” prong of the APA good cause provision covers amendments that are “ `minor or merely technical' and of little public interest,” [6]
or that involve “routine determination[s], insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry . . . and to the public.” [7]
This rule contains only a technical amendment: it merely resolves a potential ambiguity by clarifying that the DEA regulation [8]
regarding amendments to and withdrawal of applications applies to both registration and registration renewal applications. DEA has always understood and applied the regulation at 21 CFR 1301.16(b) to include renewals. DEA has accordingly determined that notice and comment are not required.
Similarly, the APA provides that a delayed effective date is unnecessary when the agency finds good cause for dispensing with the delay. The APA's delayed-effective-date provision is intended “to give affected parties time to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect.” [9]
Here, regulated parties will not need any time to adjust their behavior to the changes made in this final rule because the rule does no more than ensure that the regulatory text of 21 CFR 1301.16(b) more clearly indicates the way that DEA has always understood and applied that provision.
In addition, the APA excepts from the requirements of notice and comment and a delayed effective date those rules that are non-substantive.[10]
Substantive rules make “substantive changes in prior regulations” or “create new law, rights, or duties.” [11]
Here, as already explained, this final rule makes no substantive changes in DEA's regulations because this rule simply clarifies the way that 21 CFR 1301.16(b) has always been understood and applied.
Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192 (Regulatory Review)
DEA has determined that this rulemaking is not a “significant regulatory action” under section 3(f) of Executive Order (E.O.) 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review). Accordingly, this final rule has not been submitted to the Office of Management and Budget for review. This final rule was developed in accordance with section 1(b) of E.O. 12866, section 1(b) of E.O. 13563 (Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and E.O. 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation).
As stated above, this final rule is a technical amendment to clarify that the provision regarding amendments to and withdrawal of registration applications also applies to applications for registration renewal. DEA has always applied this provision to both new and renewal applications, and therefore, this final rule does not impose any new or substantive requirements on the public or DEA registrants. DEA anticipates that
( printed page 69501)
this final rule will have no economic impact.
This rule is not subject to E.O. 14192 because it is neither a significant regulatory action under section 3(f) of E.O. 12866 nor a significant guidance document that has been reviewed by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.[12]
This final rule meets the applicable standards set forth in sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of E.O. 12988 to eliminate ambiguity, minimize litigation, establish clear legal standards, and reduce burdens.
This final rule does not have federalism implications warranting the application of E.O. 13132. The final rule does not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the Federal Government and the States, or the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
This final rule does not have tribal implications warranting the application of E.O. 13175. It does not have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and the Tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal government and Indian Tribes.

AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
( printed page 69502)
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary special local regulation (SLR) for the navigable waters of the Atlantic Ocean surrounding the Key West Main Shipping Channel and the waters between Sunset Key and Wisteria Island. This action is necessary to provide for the safety of life on these navigable waters near Key West, FL during the Race World Offshore World Championship 2026 event beginning on November 4, 2026, and ending on November 8, 2026. This regulation prohibits persons and vessels from entering the regulated area unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port Key West or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 9:00 a.m. on November 4, 2026, through 6 p.m. on November 8, 2026.
If you have questions about this rule, contact MSTC Mathew Mason, Sector Key West Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 305-292-8823, or email
Mathew.R.Mason@uscg.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
SLR Special Local Regulation
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
On August 5, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that they will sponsor a high-speed powerboat race. The Coast Guard received a request under 33 CFR 100.15 from the Race World Offshore Organization for a Marine Event Permit to host a high-speed powerboat race within the Key West Main Shipping Channel. The event will be held from 9:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m. on November 4, 6, and 8, 2026, in Key West, FL. The races will include approximately 80 participants and 300 spectator craft.
The Captain of the Port Key West (COTP) is issuing this special local regulation (SLR) under the authority in 46 U.S.C. 70041. The COTP has determined that potential hazards associated with the operation of vessels at high speeds include the possibility of collision within the navigable channel, as well as the possibility that participants operating within approaches to local public and private boat facilities might collide with or otherwise interfere with boaters near those facilities. The purpose of this rulemaking is to protect event participants, spectators, and transiting vessels before, during, and after the scheduled event.
Because of these potential hazards, the Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable and contrary to the public interest. The Coast Guard was notified of the final details of the event concerning spectator locations and confirming event boundaries until October 29, 2026, but we must establish this SLR by November 4, 2026, to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment. Therefore, we do not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments.
For the same reasons, the Coast Guard finds that under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3), good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a temporary SLR from 9:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m. on November 4, 6, and 8, 2026. The special local regulation will cover all navigable waters within 800 feet of the Racecourse and the navigable waters extending outward 300 feet from the North shoreline of Sunset Key. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the regulated area without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980, 5 U.S.C. 601-612, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-121), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section. Small businesses may send comments to the Small Business and Agriculture Regulatory Enforcement Ombudsman and the Regional Small Business Regulatory Fairness Boards by calling 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247). The Coast Guard will not retaliate against small entities that question or complain about this rule or any policy or action of the Coast Guard.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501-3520).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under Executive Order 13132, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under Executive Order 13175, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act

articles.title: Thoughts on Owning a Self-Driving Tesla
articles.summary:
My Subaru was showing its years so I recently bought a Tesla. My thinking was I can buy a car or I can buy a car+driver for the same price. Simple choice. I’ve driven about 2000 miles including one long trip (6 hours) to North Carolina and back. FSD is incredible. I don’t mind driving […]
The post Thoughts on Owning a Self-Driving Tesla appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
My Subaru was showing its years so I recently bought a Tesla. My thinking was I can buy a car or I can buy a car+driver for the same price. Simple choice. I’ve driven about 2000 miles including one long trip (6 hours) to North Carolina and back.
FSD is incredible. I don’t mind driving but about 95% of the miles on my Tesla have been FSD. You might wonder why bother with FSD when you still have to supervise but supervising is easier and more pleasant than driving. I was in Washington, DC one evening and I needed to go to an address I was not familiar with. I could have gotten there but it would have required going back and forth between the road and the map, and DC can be confusing–do I drive straight under the mini-underpass or is this the one where I drive over the pass (DC drivers will understand). Instead, FSD drove me at night, flawlessly.
FSD uses 8 cameras to build a 3D, bird’s eye view of the car and everything around it, so it sees in all directions at once. It picks out every car, pedestrian and cyclist and predicts where each is going, much as an LLM predicts the next word. Then it predicts the best move a good driver would make, and makes it. All of this runs on one big neural network, trained on data from billions of miles of Tesla fleet driving. The ride is smooth. Since ChatGPT launched, FSD has improved about as much as LLMs have, and for the same reasons.
Supervision is needed, in my experience, mostly due to navigation. It gets a bit confused on the HOV and normal lanes on I-66 (as does Google Maps). It stopped perfectly, however, for a school bus and even for a police officer who stopped traffic by standing in the middle of the street.
Another example of how supervising is much less taxing than driving. I was listening to Tyler talk with Gita Gopinath on my way home from North Carolina. It’s a great conversation but full-on PhD mode and I became a little lost trying to remember my international econ. No problem, just ask Grok. I had a whole conversation with Grok, reviewed Mundell-Fleming, reminded myself of the great Alan Stockman model (the only international econ model that makes sense) and then returned to the podcast. I could not have done that while driving.
Grok is a significant benefit. Essentially, Grok runs the car’s controls the way it might run your computer, and you just talk to Grok. It’s a more seamless interaction than talking with the car directly. I can even review (verbally) email and send emails as I drive. If you also use Grok Bot you have the bot book an appointment at a dentist or start working on your PowerPoint slides. FSD is $99 a month and the premium connectivity needed for Grok is $10 a month (Grok Bot a bit extra). FSD plus Grok is about what I am saving on gas, so it’s roughly a wash.
My colleague, who long held that self-driving would be worthwhile only if he could sleep, was amazed at the experience of driving my Tesla and immediately ordered two.
It was also pretty cool when I “summoned” the Tesla from the nearby parking lot and we watched it drive itself to us. You might wonder, by the way, how all this innovation is possible. Maxwell Tabarrok, writes about a key part of the answer:
The Department of Transportation (DOT) sets strict safety requirements for cars, but manufacturers are allowed to release new designs without first getting the DOT to sign off that all the requirements have been satisfied. The law is enforced ex post, and the government will impose recalls and fines when manufacturers fail to follow the law.
The FAA, by contrast, enforces all of its safety rules ex ante. Before aircraft manufacturers can do anything with a design, they have to get the FAA’s signoff, which can take more than a decade.
(By the way, it’s amusing to re-read Max’s post in light of Tesla’s flying car.)
If you do enjoy driving, the Tesla is fun, with sports-car acceleration and great responsiveness.
What about range anxiety? If you run out of electrons, the car is dead and no one is going to bring you a portable battery to get you to the nearest charging station. You must be carried–carried on a flatbed, not towed! (Moreover, if you leave the car unplugged for weeks the low-voltage battery can die, in which case you can’t even open the frunk without a special jump start.) You don’t want to run out.
It works fine, however, if you adjust behavior. In a gas car you drive until you are low on fuel and then assume you will find a gas station. If you try this with an electric car, you will be anxious. Tesla chargers are quite common but they are often in odd places like behind a restaurant. There is no big T sign out front. So what do you do? The Tesla knows where the chargers are so put your final destination into navigation, switch on self-driving, and then, if needed, the Tesla will find the nearest charger along your route and drive you there and even back you in nicely. Thus, you trust the Tesla system–car plus network–not just the car. This works much better than with any other electric car.
Normal range for the Model Y is about 250 highway miles on an 80% charge. This is less restrictive than it appears because in many cases you don’t need to charge to full. Returning from North Carolina, for example, I was projected to arrive home with 2% charge–a bit too close for comfort. So the Tesla stopped and charged for 5 minutes (no slower than a gas stop) and I arrived home with 18% charge. I then charged to full overnight. Being able to charge at home is a big advantage (~$1500 to add a charger). Overall, driving the Tesla long distances you will have more frequent stops but unless you are driving cross-country, you will rarely need to stop for longer than a bathroom break and a cup of coffee.
Aside from FSD the rest of the car is nicely designed. I like the flush exterior door handles. The headlights are pixel-based, so when you drive with high beams on and come up behind another car, the pixels aimed at that car turn off while keeping the rest on, so you don’t blind the driver in front. Neat.
A few negatives. Tesla reliability is good but not great; Consumer Reports ranks Tesla 9th among brands. Despite the safety benefits of FSD, Teslas aren’t cheaper to insure than other similarly priced cars, largely I think because repair costs are not low. (Tesla’s own insurance gives lower rates for FSD miles and might be cheaper for me. I had my other car and an umbrella policy with another insurer so I didn’t switch, but I might.) I do find the pure electronic approach a bit much at times–must I really open the glove compartment verbally? Do those nice door handles only work when the battery is working?
Bottom line: FSD is revolutionary–a step change in what it means to drive. I don’t think any other car at a similar price comes close. It’s the best car I have ever owned.

articles.title: The economics of tips
articles.summary:
Tipping is large and growing, but we know little about its consequences for workers and firms. We link point-of-sale and payroll records at 20,000 U.S. firms, which lets us observe tips from customer payment to worker earnings. We find that tips are a nearly constant share of revenue, which means hourly pay moves with revenue. […]
The post The economics of tips appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Tipping is large and growing, but we know little about its consequences for workers and firms. We link point-of-sale and payroll records at 20,000 U.S. firms, which lets us observe tips from customer payment to worker earnings. We find that tips are a nearly constant share of revenue, which means hourly pay moves with revenue. Firms that begin collecting tips claw back between 23 and 33 cents of each dollar of tips through lower base wages. Tips reward effort: workers at tipping firms earn more by serving more customers. We show this with demand shocks constructed from customer spending at other businesses. A demand shock raises revenue nearly twice as much at tipping firms as at non-tipping firms, while base wages and prices do not respond. Output per hour rises more despite a larger increase in hours. Effort drives the gap because each worker is more productive, so the firm expands and recovers about a third of the tips. Yet not every firm adopts tipping: the gain is smaller where customers tip less. A model calibrated to the demand-shock estimates implies that tipping benefits workers and firms, raising job value by about half and firm profit by about 30 percent in firms where customers are prone to tip. These gains may explain why tipping has recently grown in many industries.
That is by Dylan Balla-Elliott and Isaac Norwich, Isaac being on the job market this year from University of Chicago.
